Finally, we are ready to define what it means for an algorithm to compute transformers.

#### Definition 2.7.

An algorithm computes transformers with context length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ and output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ if given any such transformer $T$ and any input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ , the algorithm outputs $T(X)$ .

For circuits, the definition is a bit more subtle. If we were to attempt to say a circuit $\mathcal{C}$ computes a transformer, then the circuit must be able to compute all possible embedding and MLP maps, then the circuit must encode many functions at once, which is too strong of a condition to require. Instead, we aim to give lower bounds against circuits meeting a much weaker requirement: we show lower bounds against circuits $\mathcal{C}$ that compute fixed transformers.

Although we consider fixed transformers, we remark that the embedding map may be parameterized. This corresponds in practice to the learned weights of a model. Formally, consider an attention head $f_{\ell,h}$ with embedding maps $Q_{h,\ell},K_{h,\ell},V_{h,\ell}$ . Then, we require that $(Q_{h,\ell})_{i}=g(w_{Q_{h,\ell}},X_{i})$ where $g$ is an function computable by an eAC, $w_{Q_{h,\ell}}$ denotes the weights associated to this map, and $X_{i}$ denotes the $i$ -th row of the input to the attention head. In our constructions, we require that $g$ is an eAC of size $O(m)$ . Let $W$ denote the concatenation of all the weights of the transformer, and for any eAC transformer $T$ , let $T_{W}(X)$ be the computation of $T$ with weights $W$ on input $X$ . Finally, we define what it means for a circuit to compute a transformer.

#### Definition 2.8.

Let $T$ be a transformer with context length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ and output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ . Suppose $T$ has weights $W$ and input $X$ . A circuit $\mathcal{C}$ computes $T$ if for any input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ and any weights $W$ , $\mathcal{C}(X,W)=T_{W}(X)$ .

To obtain meaningful lower bounds against small eAC computing transformers, we show that transformers can compute functions that are hard for extended arithmetic circuits. Of course, to have a meaningful lower bound, we note that the transformer itself must also be computable with an eAC.

#### Softmax Simulates Hardmax.

We introduce a useful primitive for Transformer computation and show that softmax attention can simulate hardmax attention when there is a sufficient gap between the maximum value and the second largest value. This is similar to a result of [SHT24b].

#### Lemma 2.9.

Let $f\in\mathrm{Att}^{N}_{m}$ be a self-attention unit with embedding functions $Q,K,V$ such that

- 1. $V(X)\in\left\{0,1,2\right\}^{n\times m}$ , and

- 2. for every $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ and $i\in[N]$ :

$$ A(X)_{i,i^{\prime}}\leq\max_{i^{\prime\prime}}A(X)_{i,i^{\prime\prime}}-1,\ \forall i^{\prime}\not\in I_{\max}(A(X)_{i}), $$

where $A(X)=Q(X)K(X)^{\top}$ .

Then there exists an attention unit $f^{\prime}\in\mathrm{Att}^{N}_{m}$ satisfying

$$ \left\lVert f^{\prime}(X)-\mathrm{hardmax}(A(X))V(X)\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)} $$

for an arbitrarily small inverse polynomial.

The idea behind the simulation is simple: by scaling each query vector in $Q$ by a sufficiently large constant $c=\Theta(\log N)$ , we ensure that any probability assigned to non-maximum indices by the softmax operation is exponentially small with respect to $c$ , i.e. less than $\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}$ for any polynomial. We leave the proof to Appendix˜A.

### 2.3 Fine-Grained Complexity

We state our major hypotheses in fine-grained complexity theory in this section. See Section˜1 for more discussions on their applications.

#### Hypothesis 2.10 (Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH)).

For any $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists a positive integer $k$ such that $k\textup{-}\mathsf{SAT}$ requires $\Omega(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n})$ time, where $n$ is the number of variables in the CNF.

We say that $k$ vectors $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ are orthogonal if for all $j\in[d]$ , $v_{\ell}[j]=0$ for some $\ell\in[k]$ . In other words, their $k$ -wise inner product is $0$ . The $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ problem is then defined as follows: given $A_{1},\dots,A_{k}\subset\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ each of size $n$ , determine if there exists $v_{1}\in A_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in A_{k}$ such that $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}$ are orthogonal. The trivial algorithm of checking all $k$ -tuples of vectors requires $O(n^{k}d)$ time. The $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis states that for $d=\Theta(\log n)$ , this is essentially optimal: i.e. any algorithm requires $n^{k-o(1)}$ time.

#### Hypothesis 2.11 ( $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis).

Computing $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ on sets of $n$ vectors with dimension $\Theta(\log n)$ requires $n^{k-o(1)}$ time.

The $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis follows from the popular Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [IP01] which states that satisfiability over $n$ variables requires $2^{(1-o(1))n}$ time [Wil04]. Our lower bound is based on the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, a special case of $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ for $k=3$ .

The unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ problem is defined as follows: given $k$ sets of vectors $A_{1},\dots,A_{k}$ of size $S_{1},\dots,S_{k}$ , determine if there exist $v_{1}\in A_{1},\dots,v_{k}\in A_{k}$ such that $v_{1},\dots,v_{k}$ is orthogonal. The trivial algorithm of checking all $k$ -tuples requires $O(S_{1}S_{2}\dots S_{k}d)$ time. Again, the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis states that this is essentially optimal and it is well-known that the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis is equivalent to the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis.

#### Hypothesis 2.12 (Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis).

$k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ on sets $S_{1},\dots,S_{k}$ of size $n^{s_{1}},\dots,n^{s_{k}}$ with dimension $d=\Theta(\log n)$ requires $n^{s_{1}+\dots+s_{k}-o(1)}$ time.

It is clear that the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis implies the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, by setting $s_{1}=\dots=s_{k}=1$ . The following lemma shows the converse direction, and we include a proof in Appendix˜A for completeness.

#### Lemma 2.13.

Let $0<s_{2}\dotsc,s_{k}\leq 1$ . Let $A_{1},\dots A_{k}\subset\left\{0,1\right\}^{d}$ for $d=\Theta(\log n)$ with $|A_{1}|=n$ and $|A_{i}|=n^{s_{i}}$ for all $i>1$ . Then, any algorithm computing $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ on $A_{1},\dotsc,A_{k}$ requires time $n^{s_{1}+\dotsc+s_{k}-o(1)}$ under the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. In particular, the Unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis holds under the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis.

## 3 Lower Bounds for Small Embedding Dimension

We begin with lower bounds for the small embedding dimension setting (i.e. $m=N^{o(1)}$ ). Our lower bound is based on the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis (or SETH).

First, we show that under the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, when the embedding dimension is small (e.g. $m=\Theta(\log n)$ ), there is no algorithm that computes transformers significantly more efficiently than the naive algorithm that computes each head separately.

#### Theorem 3.1 (Formal Theorem˜1.1).

Let $m=\Theta(\log N)$ and $L,H=\mathrm{poly}(N)$ . Any algorithm computing transformers with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, and input and output dimension $m$ up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ requires $LHN^{2-o(1)}$ time under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. The lower bound holds even if the transformer has no MLPs.

In the above statement, we require $L,H=\mathrm{poly}(N)$ since in $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ the sizes of the three sets must be polynomially related. We remark that this is the interesting regime of the problem since when $L,H=N^{o(1)}$ , we obtain optimal lower bounds directly from the hardness of a single attention head.

#### Lemma 3.2.

Suppose there exists an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that computes any transformer with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $2d+2$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input and output dimension $2d+2$ , up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ in time $B$ , then there exists an algorithm that solves unbalanced $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ with dimension $d$ and size $N,N,LH$ in time $\tilde{O}(LHd+B)$ .

First, we observe that Theorem˜3.1 follows from Lemma˜3.2.

#### Proof of Theorem˜3.1 assuming Lemma˜3.2.

Suppose for contradiction that there is an algorithm computing any transformer with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m=2d+2$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input and output dimension $m$ up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ in time $O\left(LHN^{2-\varepsilon}\right)$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . Then, consider an unbalanced $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance with dimension $d=\Theta(\log N)$ and size $N,N,LH$ . Lemma˜3.2 implies that there is a $\tilde{O}(LHd+LHN^{2-\varepsilon})$ algorithm for this problem, which contradicts the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. ∎

We now prove Lemma˜3.2 to complete the proof of Theorem˜3.1.

#### Proof of Lemma˜3.2.

Consider a $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance $(A,B,C)$ with $|A|=|B|=N$ and $|C|=LH$ . We construct the following transformer $T$ with $m={d_{\textup{in}}}={d_{\textup{out}}}=2d+2$ . Suppose we have an algorithm computing $T$ up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ . Let the input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ be

$$ \displaystyle X \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}^{\top}&b_{1}^{\top}&1&0\\
a_{2}^{\top}&b_{2}^{\top}&1&0\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
a_{N}^{\top}&b_{N}^{\top}&1&0\\
0^{\top}&0^{\top}&2&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $a_{i},b_{i}$ are vectors in $A,B$ . Additionally, we index $C=\left\{c_{h,\ell}:1\leq h\leq H,1\leq\ell\leq L\right\}$ and define

$$ \displaystyle Q_{h,\ell}(X)=-\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
a_{2}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
a_{N}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
0_{1\times d}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\end{pmatrix},K_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}b_{1}^{\top}\odot c_{h,\ell}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
b_{2}^{\top}\odot c_{h,\ell}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
b_{N}^{\top}\odot c_{h,\ell}^{\top}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\\
0_{1\times d}&0_{1\times(d+2)}\end{pmatrix},V_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}0_{1\times(2d+1)}&1\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
0_{1\times(2d+1)}&1\\
0_{1\times(2d+1)}&2\end{pmatrix} $$

such that $Q_{h,\ell}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m},K_{h,\ell}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m},V_{h,\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m}$ where $b\odot c\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the element-wise product of two vectors $a,b$ .

We claim that creating the transformer requires $O(dHL)$ time since each attention head can be created in time $O(d)$ time (i.e. the embedding maps can be specified in $O(d)$ time). In addition, we can encode $Q_{h,\ell}(X),K_{h,\ell}(X)$ as desired. In particular, $Q_{h,\ell},K_{h,\ell}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ apply the following maps to each row:

$$ \displaystyle Q_{h,\ell} \displaystyle:v\mapsto-(v_{1},\dots,v_{d},0,\dots,0)\text{,} \displaystyle K_{h,\ell} \displaystyle:v\mapsto(v_{d+1}\cdot c_{h,\ell}[1],\dots,v_{2d}\cdot c_{h,\ell}[d],0,\dots,0)\text{,} \displaystyle V_{h,\ell} \displaystyle:v\mapsto(0,\dots,0,0,v_{2d+1})\text{.} $$

Observe that the above maps can be expressed using weight matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ :

$$ \displaystyle W_{Q,h,\ell} \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}-I_{d\times d}&0_{d\times(d+2)}\\
0_{(d+2)\times d}&0_{(d+2)\times(d+2)}\end{pmatrix}\text{,} \displaystyle W_{K,h,\ell} \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0_{d\times d}&0_{d\times(d+2)}\\
\mathrm{diag}(c_{h,\ell})&0_{d\times(d+2)}\\
0_{2\times d}&0_{2\times(d+2)}\end{pmatrix}\text{,} \displaystyle W_{V,h,\ell} \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0_{2d\times(2d+1)}&0_{2d\times 1}\\
0_{1\times(2d+1)}&1\\
0_{1\times(2d+1)}&0\end{pmatrix} $$

so that $Q_{h,\ell}(X)=XW_{Q,h,\ell}$ and analogously for $K_{h,\ell},V_{h,\ell}$ .

Firstly, we observe that the first $2d+1$ columns will never change throughout the computation. We remind the readers that $X^{(\ell)}$ is the output of $\ell$ -th transformer layer.

#### Claim 3.3.

For all $\ell$ , the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(\ell)}$ are the first $2d+1$ columns of $X$ .

#### Proof.

The claim follows as the first $2d+1$ columns of $V_{h,\ell}(X)$ are $0$ for all $h,\ell$ . As a result, the output of each head consists of $0$ in the first $2d+1$ columns. Then, since $X^{(\ell)}=X^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{h}f_{h,\ell}(X^{(\ell-1)})$ where $f_{h,\ell}$ denotes the $h$ -th attention head in the $\ell$ -th layer, we have that the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(\ell)}$ are the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(\ell-1)}$ . By induction, the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(\ell)}$ are the first $2d+1$ columns of $X^{(0)}=X$ . ∎

Secondly, we claim that the given hardmax transformer computes the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance. Notice that this suffices because of Lemma˜2.9, as an algorithm computing any softmax transformer can approximate any hardmax transformer with the same dimension. Consider the $(h,\ell)$ -th attention head. Note that

$$ (Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})_{i,j}=\begin{cases}0&\textup{if }\max(i,j)=N+1\\
-a_{i}\cdot b_{j}\cdot c_{h,\ell}&\textup{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

For $1\leq i\leq N$ , the maximum entry in the $i$ -th row is $0$ , since $(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})_{i,N+1}=0$ . Recalling that $I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})$ denotes the set of indices attaining maximum value in the $i$ -th row, we have that $|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})|\geq 2$ if $(a_{i},c_{h,\ell})$ participate in an orthogonal triple and $|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})|=1$ otherwise. In particular, let $t_{i}:=t_{i,(h,\ell)}$ denote the number of $j$ such that $a_{i}\cdot b_{j}\cdot c_{h,\ell}=0$ . Then we have

$$ \mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)=\begin{pmatrix}0&\cdots&0&\frac{t_{1}+2}{t_{1}+1}\\
0&\cdots&0&\frac{t_{2}+2}{t_{2}+1}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&\cdots&0&\frac{t_{N}+2}{t_{N}+1}\\
0&\cdots&0&\frac{N+2}{N+1}\end{pmatrix} $$

In particular, for every $i\leq N$ , the $i$ -th entry in the last column is $2$ if $t_{i}=0$ and at most $\frac{3}{2}$ otherwise. Lemma˜2.9 then implies that there is a transformer such that each attention head computes an output $Y_{h,\ell}$ that approximates the hardmax attention head with embeddings $Q_{h,\ell},K_{h,\ell},V_{h,\ell}$ well. In particular, the output of the $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer, denoted $Y_{h,\ell}$ , satisfies

$$ \left\lVert Y_{h,\ell}-\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{10NHL} $$

for some inverse polynomial in $L,H,N$ .

Let $Z_{h,\ell}$ denote the last column of $\mathrm{hardmax}(Q_{h,\ell}(X)K_{h,\ell}(X)^{\top})V_{h,\ell}(X)$ . If the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance is a no-instance (i.e. there is no orthogonal triple), then every $Z_{h,\ell}[i]=2$ , i.e.

$$ \sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{h,\ell}[i]=2NHL\text{.} $$

On the other hand, if the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ is a yes-instance (i.e. there is an orthogonal triple), then there exists some $i,(h,\ell)$ where $Z_{h,\ell}[i]\leq\frac{3}{2}$ i.e.

$$ \sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{h,\ell}[i]\leq 2NHL-\frac{1}{2}\text{.} $$

Let us then consider the output $X^{(L)}$ , in particular focusing on the last column, since the first $2d+1$ columns are exactly those of $X=X^{(0)}$ by ˜3.3. Observe that our transformer outputs for all $1\leq i\leq N$

$$ X^{(L)}[i,m]=X^{(0)}[i,m]+\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]=\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]\text{.} $$

Since our algorithm computes the given transformer up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ , we in fact obtain in the last column a vector $\hat{X}$ such that $|\hat{X}_{j}-X^{(L)}[i,m]|\leq\frac{1}{10N}$ for all $i\in[N]$ .

Thus, from the computed output of the transformer, we can compute in $O(N)$ time $\sum_{j=1}^{N}\hat{X}[j]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{X}[i]-\sum_{h,\ell}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{h,\ell}[i]\right| \displaystyle\leq\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{X}[i]-\sum_{i=1}^{N}X^{(L)}[i,m]\right| \displaystyle\quad\quad+\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N}X^{(L)}[i,m]-\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]\right| \displaystyle\quad\quad+\left|\sum_{h,\ell}Y_{h,\ell}[i,m]-\sum_{h,\ell}Z_{h,\ell}[i]\right| \displaystyle\leq 0.2\text{.} $$

Here, we apply the triangle inequality, apply the approximation error of our algorithm for the first term, our equation above for the second term and (2) for the third term. Note that from the output of the transformer is a $(N+1)\times m$ matrix, but we sum only the first $N$ entries of the last column.

Thus, the sum $\sum_{j=1}^{N}\hat{X}[j]$ is at least $2NHL-0.2$ if there is no orthogonal triple and at most $2NHL-0.3$ otherwise. Therefore, we can compute the output of the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance.

∎

We conclude with a simple conditional lower bound which suggests that efficient transformers require large size to compute $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ , suggesting that small size transformers cannot handle some instances of $3$ -wise interaction.

#### Theorem 3.4.

Under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, any transformer with linear time embedding and MLP maps computing $d$ -dimensional $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ requires $LHm=N^{1-o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose there is a transformer $T$ with embedding dimension $m=\Theta(\log N)$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension $m$ , output dimension $m$ that computes $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ with dimension $m$ . Recall that in an efficient transformer, all embedding and MLP maps require $\tilde{O}(m)$ time, so that each attention head is computed in $O(Nm+N^{2}m)=O(N^{2}m)$ time. Following the standard algorithm, this transformer can be computed in time $\tilde{O}(N^{2}mHL)$ . In particular, under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, this requires $LHm=N^{1-o(1)}$ . ∎

## 4 Tools for Algebraic Circuits

In this section, we establish some tools for (extended) arithmetic circuits which will be used in our lower bound proofs for large embedding dimensions.

While eAC is a more powerful class in general (e.g. AC cannot compute $\exp(x)$ ), we show that the additional gates are not necessary for computing matrix multiplication. More generally, we argue that we can in fact use standard arithmetic circuits to simulate an eAC that computes low degree functions. For our application, we give the result for quadratic functions. The proof generalizes that of [Str73] which states that division gates are unnecessary for quadratic functions.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Let $F=\{F_{1},\dotsc,F_{m}\}$ where $F_{i}=\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}t_{ik\ell}x_{k}x_{\ell}$ . Suppose there is an eAC $\mathcal{C}$ of size $s$ computing $F$ . Then there is an AC of size $O(s)$ computing $F$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an optimal eAC for computing $F$ , and let $W=(w_{1},\dotsc,w_{s})$ be an ordering of all gates in $\mathcal{C}$ where earlier gates are computed first. Without loss of generality, viewing each $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})$ as a function, we can assume $w_{i}\neq 0$ for any $i$ . Furthermore, since $\mathcal{C}$ computes $F$ for all inputs $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , $\mathcal{C}$ is well defined for all $x$ . In particular, if $w_{i}$ is ever provided as input to a $\ln$ gate, we have that $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})>0$ for all $x$ . Similarly, if $w_{i}$ is ever provided as a denominator to a $/$ gate, we have that $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\neq 0$ for all $x$ . By substituting $\tilde{x}_{i}\leftarrow x_{i}z$ , we can view each gate $w_{j}$ as a formal power series $\tilde{w}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})[[z]]$ with coefficients that are functions on $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}$ . We can do this as all the formal power series are well-defined when $\mathcal{C}$ is well-defined under all the inputs $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ . First, the sum, difference, and product are well defined for any two formal power series, and exponentiation of a formal power series is well-defined (we will show the exact formulation later). For a function $f$ corresponding to some gate, and its formal power series $\tilde{f}$ , observe that $\ln(\tilde{f})$ is well defined as long as $\tilde{f}$ has positive constant coefficient (see exact formulation later). The constant coefficient of $\tilde{f}$ is $f(0,\dots,0)$ , and our assumption that inputs to $\ln$ gates are positive on all inputs ensures that $f(0,\dots,0)>0$ , which implies the constant coefficient of $\tilde{f}$ as needed. For a division gate $w_{j}=g/h$ , our assumption that any gate input to the denominator of a division gates is non-zero for all inputs ensures that the constant coefficient of $\tilde{h}$ is $h(0,\dots,0)\neq 0$ . The following fact then guarantees that the formal power series of $w_{j}$ is well defined.

#### Fact 4.2.

Let $R$ be a ring. A power series $\tilde{h}(z)=\sum_{i}a_{i}z^{i}\in R[[z]]$ is invertible if and only if $a_{0}\neq 0$ . Furthermore, the inverse is given by

$$ \frac{1}{\tilde{h}(z)}=\frac{1}{a_{0}}\left(1+q+q^{2}+q^{3}+\dotsc\right) $$

where $q=-\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_{i}}{a_{0}}z^{i}$ .

Viewing the gates as formal power series, we argue that the desired output can easily be computed from the low order coefficients of the power series of the relevant gates. Specifically, since all $F_{i}$ have degree at most $2$ , we can add a new variable $z$ to all the input $x_{i}$ and only look at the coefficients for $z^{0},z^{1},z^{2}$ . Suppose $w_{j}$ is an output gate $F_{i}$ . Then, we have

$$ F_{i}=w_{j}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}t_{ik\ell}x_{k}x_{\ell}\text{.} $$

Notice that

$$ w_{j}(x_{1}z,\dots,x_{n}z)=\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}t_{ik\ell}x_{k}x_{\ell}z^{2}\text{,} $$

whose formal power series is simply itself. Hence, we can compute $F_{i}$ from the coefficient of $z^{2}$ in the formal power series $\tilde{w}_{j}$ .

We have shown that from the second coefficient of the power series corresponding to the output gates we can compute $F$ efficiently. While we will not be able to compute the full power series of each gate as there could be infinitely many terms, we describe how to compute the low-order coefficients, i.e. the coefficients of $1,z,z^{2}$ , for all $\tilde{w}_{i}$ . We proceed by induction. We denote $\tilde{w}_{i}=\sum_{j\geq 0}c_{j}z^{j}$ and compute $c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}$ . For the input gates, $w_{i}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=x_{j}$ for some $x_{j}$ so that $\tilde{w}_{i}=x_{j}z$ . In particular, $c_{0}=c_{2}=0$ and $c_{1}=x_{j}$ . This requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 1: Addition and Subtraction. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}+\tilde{h}_{i}$ where $\tilde{g}_{i},\tilde{h}_{i}$ are power series with

$$ \tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}\quad,\quad\tilde{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}v_{j}z_{j}\text{.} $$

The first three coefficients can easily be combined via addition and subtraction i.e. $c_{j}=u_{j}\pm v_{j}$ for all $j$ . Again, this requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 2: Multiplication. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}\cdot\tilde{h}_{i}$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}$ and $\tilde{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}v_{j}z^{j}$ . Then, if $\tilde{w}_{i}=\sum_{j}c_{j}z^{j}$ , we have $c_{0}=u_{0}v_{0}$ , $c_{1}=u_{0}v_{1}+u_{1}v_{0}$ , and $c_{2}=u_{2}v_{0}+u_{1}v_{1}+u_{0}v_{2}$ . This requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 3: Division. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}/\tilde{h}_{i}$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}$ and $\tilde{h}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}v_{j}z^{j}$ . Since $v_{0}\neq 0$ , we obtain the inverse via ˜4.2 as

$$ \frac{1}{\tilde{h}_{i}}=\frac{1}{v_{0}}\left(1+q+q^{2}+q^{3}+\dotsc\right) $$

with $q=-\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{v_{j}}{v_{0}}z^{j}$ . In particular, we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\tilde{g}_{i}}{\tilde{h}_{i}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{v_{0}}(u_{0}+u_{1}z+u_{2}z^{2}+\dots)\cdot\left(1+\left(-\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}z-\frac{v_{2}}{v_{0}}z^{2}-\dots\right)+\left(-\frac{v_{1}}{v_{0}}z-\dots\right)^{2}+\dots\right) \displaystyle=(u_{0}^{\prime}+u_{1}^{\prime}z+u_{2}^{\prime}z^{2}+u_{3}^{\prime}z^{3}+\dots)\cdot\left(1+\left(-v_{1}^{\prime}z-v_{2}^{\prime}z^{2}-\dots\right)+\left(-v_{1}^{\prime}z-\dots\right)^{2}+\dots\right) $$

where we set $u_{j}^{\prime}=\frac{u_{j}}{v_{0}}$ and $v_{j}^{\prime}=\frac{v_{j}}{v_{0}}$ . Finally, we have

$$ \displaystyle c_{0} \displaystyle=u_{0}^{\prime} \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=u_{1}^{\prime}-u_{0}^{\prime}v_{1}^{\prime} \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=u_{2}^{\prime}-u_{1}^{\prime}v_{1}^{\prime}+u_{0}^{\prime}(v_{1}^{\prime 2}-v_{2}^{\prime})\text{.} $$

This requires $O(1)$ gates.

Case 4: Exponent. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\exp(\tilde{g}_{i})$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}u_{j}z^{j}$ . Then, using the formal power series of $\exp(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\exp(\tilde{g}_{i}) \displaystyle=\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 0}u_{j}z^{j}\right) \displaystyle=\exp(u_{0})\exp\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}u_{j}z^{j}\right) \displaystyle=\exp(u_{0})\left(\sum_{k\geq 0}\frac{1}{k!}\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}u_{j}z^{j}\right)^{k}\right). $$

Note that for every fixed $j\geq 0$ , there are finitely many terms in the above sum that contribute to the coefficient of $z^{j}$ , so the formal power series is well-defined. In particular,

$$ \displaystyle c_{0} \displaystyle=e^{u_{0}} \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=e^{u_{0}}u_{1} \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=e^{u_{0}}\left(u_{2}+\frac{u_{1}^{2}}{2}\right)\text{.} $$

This requires $O(1)$ gates. Even though the formulas use $\exp(u_{0})$ , it is a constant and can be implemented in an AC.

Case 5: Logarithm. Suppose $\tilde{w}_{i}=\ln(\tilde{g}_{i})$ where $\tilde{g}_{i}=\sum_{j\geq 0}u_{j}z^{j}$ . Then applying the power series identity $\ln(1+x)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k+1}\frac{x^{k}}{k}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\ln(\tilde{g}_{i}) \displaystyle=\ln u_{0}+\ln\left(1+\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{u_{j}}{u_{0}}z^{j}\right) \displaystyle=\ln u_{0}+\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\cdot\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{u_{j}}{u_{0}}z^{j}\right)^{k} $$

Again, for every fixed $j\geq 0$ , there are finitely many terms in the above sum that contribute to the coefficient of $z^{j}$ , so the formal power series is well-defined. In particular,

$$ \displaystyle c_{0} \displaystyle=\ln u_{0} \displaystyle c_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{u_{1}}{u_{0}} \displaystyle c_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{u_{2}}{u_{0}}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{u_{1}}{u_{0}}\right)^{2}\text{.} $$

This requires $O(1)$ gates. Similarly as the $\exp$ case, we only use $\ln$ on a constant, so it can be implemented in the AC model.

Overall, our circuit requires $O(s)$ gates to compute all the relevant coefficients. ∎

The next tool we require is the Baur-Strassen Theorem, which states that given an AC that computes a function, we can compute all the partial derivatives with a similar sized circuit.

#### Theorem 4.3 ([BS83]).

Let $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a function and $F^{\prime}=(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{1}},\dots,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{n}})$ . If there is an AC of size $s$ computing $F$ , there is an AC of size $O(s)$ computing $F^{\prime}$ .

After Baur and Strassen [BS83] obtained this result, Morgenstern [Mor85] showed a simplified constructive proof for the Baur-Strassen theorem. Following the Morgenstern’s proof strategy, we generalize the Baur-Strassen theorem to eAC.

#### Theorem 4.4 (Extended Baur-Strassen Theorem).

Let $F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be a function and let $F^{\prime}=\left\{\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{1}},\dotsc,\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_{n}}\right\}$ . If there is an eAC of size $s$ computing $F$ , there is an eAC of size $O(s)$ computing $F^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\left\{g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s}\right\}$ be a minimum size eAC that computes $F$ . Let $F^{(i)}$ be the function computed by $g_{i},\dotsc,g_{s}$ . Note that $F^{(i)}$ has $s-i+1$ operations and has input variables $\left\{x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n},g_{1},\dotsc,g_{i-1}\right\}$ . We prove the desired claim with induction. For notational simplicity, we define for $1\leq j\leq n+s$ , $z_{j}=x_{j}$ if $j\leq n$ and $z_{j}=g_{j-n}$ if $j>n$ . We claim that partial derivatives of $F^{(i)}$ can be computed with an eAC of size $5(s-i+1)+2$ . Then, the partial derivatives of $F=F^{(1)}$ can be computed with a circuit of size $O(s)$ .

We begin with the base case. Note $F^{(s+1)}(x_{1},\dotsc,x_{n},g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s})=g_{s}$ has partial derivatives $\frac{\partial F^{(s+1)}}{\partial g_{s}}=1$ and $\frac{\partial F^{(s+1)}}{\partial z}=0$ for any $z\in\left\{x_{i}\right\}\cup\left\{g_{1},\dotsc,g_{s-1}\right\}$ . These values are simply constants, so we can compute them using an eAC of size $1$ . While we need gates to store the two distinct values, we do not need to store all derivatives separately. In subsequent computations, we simply remember which value to use at the appropriate gate. This leads to $2$ additional gates in the computed circuit.

We now proceed with the inductive case. Assume that $\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{j}}$ is computed for all $j\leq n+i$ . Then, $F^{(i)}$ is the eAC $F^{(i+1)}$ with input $g_{i}$ substituted with some operation defined in Definition˜2.2. For any variable $z_{j}$ for $j\leq n+i-1$ , we can compute $\frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{j}}$ by the chain rule,

$$ \frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{j}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{j}}+\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial z_{j}}\text{.} $$

The case where $g_{i}$ corresponds to an operation from $\{+,-,\times,/\}$ is already handled in the Morgenstern’s proof for standard Baur-Strassen Theorem [Mor85]. Hence, we focus on the case where $g_{i}$ corresponds to an $\exp$ or $\ln$ gate.

Suppose $g_{i}$ involves input $z_{k}$ for some $k\leq n+i-1$ , and if $j\neq k$ , then $\frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{j}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{j}}$ . Hence, it suffices to compute $\frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{k}}$ .

If $g_{i}=\exp(z_{k})$ for some $k\leq n+i-1$ , we have

$$ \frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{k}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{k}}+\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}\exp(z_{k}) $$

where we have $\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{k}},\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}$ computed by induction and $\exp(z_{k})$ can be computed with one operation. Summing requires an additional operation.

Similarly, if $g_{i}=\ln(z_{k})$ , we have

$$ \frac{\partial F^{(i)}}{\partial z_{k}}=\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial z_{k}}+\frac{\partial F^{(i+1)}}{\partial g_{i}}\frac{1}{z_{k}} $$

where the above term can be computed by $3$ operations. This proves the inductive claim. ∎

Our final ingredient is a lower bound on the size of any arithmetic circuit that computes independent matrix products.

#### Lemma 4.5.

For any integer $\ell\geq 1$ , any arithmetic circuit computing $\ell$ independent $n\times n\times n$ matrix products has size $\ell\cdot n^{\omega-o(1)}$ .

Its proof follows from standard application of the asymptotic sum inequality [Sch81]. We include a proof of this lemma and necessary definitions for completeness.

A tensor $T$ over three sets of variables $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{|X|}\},Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{|Y|}\},Z=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{|Z|}\}$ is defined as

$$ T=\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}a_{ijk}x_{i}y_{j}z_{k} $$

for some coefficients $a_{ijk}\in\mathbb{R}$ . An algebraic circuit computing the tensor is an algebraic circuit that, given inputs $X,Y$ , outputs $\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}a_{ijk}x_{i}y_{j}$ for every $k\in[|Z|]$ .

The rank $R(T)$ of a tensor $T$ is defined as the smallest integer $r$ such that $T$ can be represented as

$$ \sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{|X|}\alpha_{\ell,i}x_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{|Y|}\beta_{\ell,j}y_{j}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{|Z|}\gamma_{\ell,k}z_{k}\right) $$

for some values $\alpha_{\ell,i},\beta_{\ell,j},\gamma_{\ell,k}$ . The asymptotic rank $\tilde{R}(T)$ , which is upper bounded by $R(T)$ , is defined as $\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}(R(T^{\otimes m}))^{1/m}$ , where $T^{\otimes m}$ denotes the $m$ -th tensor power of $T$ .

The matrix multiplication tensor for $n\times n\times n$ matrix products is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{ij}y_{jk}z_{ik}\text{,} $$

and we denote it by $\langle n,n,n\rangle$ . We also denote the disjoint union of $\ell$ copies of $n\times n\times n$ as $\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle$ .

Now we are ready to state the asymptotic sum inequality.

#### Theorem 4.6 (Asymptotic Sum Inequality [Sch81]).

For integers $\ell,n\geq 1$ ,

$$ \ell\cdot n^{\omega}\leq\tilde{R}\left(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle\right). $$

We now prove Lemma˜4.5.

#### Proof of Lemma˜4.5.

Suppose there is an arithmetic circuit of size $O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ for $\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . By definition, this circuit computes $\ell$ independent instances of $n\times n\times n$ matrix products. It is known that the rank of a tensor is at most twice the size of a circuit computing it [Str73] (see also, e.g, [Blä13, Theorem 4.7]), so $R(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle)\leq O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ , which further implies $\tilde{R}(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle)\leq O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ . Hence, by the asymptotic sum inequality [Sch81],

$$ \displaystyle\omega \displaystyle\leq\frac{\log\left(\tilde{R}(\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle)/\ell\right)}{\log n} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\log\left(O(n^{\omega-\varepsilon})\right)}{\log n} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta+(\omega-\varepsilon)\log n}{\log n} \displaystyle=\omega-\varepsilon+\delta/\log n, $$

where $\delta$ is a constant depending on the constant hidden in the big- $O$ notation. As we can take $n\rightarrow\infty$ , this is a contradiction. Hence, $\ell\odot\langle n,n,n\rangle$ does not have an arithmetic circuit of size $O(\ell\cdot n^{\omega-\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon>0$ , i.e., it has size at least $\ell\cdot n^{\omega-o(1)}$ . ∎

## 5 Lower Bounds for Large Embedding Dimension

In this section, we prove lower bounds against transformers with large embedding dimension in the extended arithmetic circuit model. Recall Theorem˜1.2:

#### Theorem 5.1 (Formal Theorem˜1.2).

There exists a transformer $T$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m=2N+3$ , $L$ layers, $H$ attention heads per layer, input dimension and output dimension $2N+3$ satisfying the following:

- 1. $T$ is computable by an eAC, each embedding is computable by an arithmetic circuit of size $O(m)$ , and all MLP maps are the identity map.

- 2. Any eAC computing $T$ has size at least $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}-O\left(LHN^{2}\right)$ .

We begin with defining a transformer that computes row sums of matrix products. First, we give a simple attention head that computes the (normalized) row sums of a single matrix product after taking entry-wise exponential. Our attention head also outputs the normalization factors, which we will later use to recover the entries of the matrix product.

#### Lemma 5.2.

Let $m\geq N$ . There is an attention unit $\mathrm{Att}_{\mathsf{MatMul}}$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m^{\prime}=\max(m+1,2N+3)$ , input dimension $2N+3$ such that for any $N\times m$ matrices $A,B$ and vector $D\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ , there exist embedding weights such that given input $X=\begin{pmatrix}Z_{1}&I_{N}&1_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}\\ Z_{2}&0_{1\times N}&0&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(2N+3)}$ where $Z_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times(N+1)},Z_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times(N+1)}$ are arbitrary matrices, the output $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m^{\prime}}$ satisfies

$$ Y[i,j]=\begin{cases}\frac{N}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $j=1$}\\
\frac{D[j-1]}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
\frac{S_{i}}{1+S_{i}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $j=1$}\\
\frac{D[j-1]}{1+S_{i}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
0&\mathrm{o/w}\end{cases} $$

where $S_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(AB^{\top})_{ij}$ for $i\in[N]$ . Furthermore, all embedding maps can be computed by arithmetic circuits of size $O(Nm)$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the embeddings

$$ Q(X)=\begin{pmatrix}A&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{1\times m}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad K(X)=\begin{pmatrix}B&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{1\times m}&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(m+1)} $$

so that

$$ \exp\left(Q(X)K(X)^{\top}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}\exp(AB^{\top})&1_{N\times 1}\\
1_{1\times N}&1\end{pmatrix} $$

Observe that the embedding maps can be expressed as $Q(X)=XW_{Q},K(X)=XW_{K}$ for matrices $W_{Q},W_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{(2N+3)\times(m+1)}$ :

$$ W_{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{(N+1)\times m}&0_{(N+1)\times 1}\\
A&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{2\times m}&0_{2\times 1}\end{pmatrix},\quad W_{K}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{(N+1)\times m}&0_{(N+1)\times 1}\\
B&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{2\times m}&0_{2\times 1}\end{pmatrix} $$

If $m^{\prime}>m+1$ , we can append columns of zeros to $W_{Q},W_{K}$ and therefore $Q(X),Q(K)$ without changing the value of $Q(X)K(X)^{\top}$ . Then, consider the embedding

$$ V(X)=\begin{pmatrix}1_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}&\dots&0_{N\times 1}\\
0&D_{1}&D_{2}&\dots&D_{N}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(N+1)}\text{.} $$

Observe that $V$ can be expressed as $V(X)=XW_{V}$ where

$$ W_{V}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{(2N+1)\times 1}&0_{(2N+1)\times 1}&0_{(2N+1)\times(N-2)}&0_{(2N+1)\times 1}\\
1&0&0_{1\times(N-2)}&0\\
0&D_{1}&\dots&D_{N}\end{pmatrix} $$

As before, if $m^{\prime}>N+1$ , we can append columns of zeros to $W_{V}$ and therefore $V(X)$ , which only appends columns of zeros to the output $Y$ . Note that $Q(X),K(X),V(X)$ can be computed from $X$ with eAC (in fact AC) circuits of size $O(Nm)$ with the relevant matrices $A,B$ and vector $D$ encoded into the weights. Then, let $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m^{\prime}}$ denote the output of attention and $S_{i}:=\sum_{j}\exp(AB^{T})_{ij}$ . Observe that the outputs are as claimed. ∎

Next, we show how to compute the sum of many matrix products.

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $L,H\geq 1$ and $m\geq N$ . There is a transformer $T$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m^{\prime}=\max(m+1,2N+3)$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension $2N+3$ , output dimension $m^{\prime}$ such that for any collection of matrices $A_{k},B_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ for $k\in[LH]$ and vectors $D_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ , there exist embedding weights such that given input $X=\begin{pmatrix}0_{N\times(N+1)}&I_{N}&1_{N\times 1}&0_{N\times 1}\\ 0_{1\times(N+1)}&0_{1\times N}&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ , the output $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m^{\prime}}$ has entries

$$ Y[i,j]=\begin{cases}\frac{LHN}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $j=1$}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\frac{D_{k}[j-1]}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\frac{S_{ki}}{1+S_{ki}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $j=1$}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\frac{D_{k}[j-1]}{1+S_{ki}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
0&\mathrm{o/w}\end{cases} $$

where $S_{ki}=\sum_{j}\exp(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})_{ij}$ . Furthermore, all embedding maps can be computed by an arithmetic circuit of size $O(LHNm)$ and the MLPs can be taken to be the identity map.

The final stipulation on the size of circuits computing the embedding and MLP maps ensures that these computations do not constitute a computational bottleneck for computing the transformer.

#### Proof.

First, we remark that in the construction of Lemma˜5.2, we may assume the input dimension is in fact $m^{\prime}$ by appending columns of zeros to the input $X$ and rows of zeros to the weight matrices $W_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}$ without changing the computed embeddings $Q(X),K(X),V(X)$ .

We construct a transformer that computes $S_{0},S_{1},\ldots,S_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(N+1)}$ where for $\ell>0$ , $S_{\ell}$ is the matrix satisfying

$$ S_{\ell}[i,j]=\begin{cases}\frac{\ell HN}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $j=1$}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{\ell H}\frac{D_{k}[j-1]}{N+1}&\textsf{if $i=N+1$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{\ell H}\frac{S_{ki}}{1+S_{ki}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $j=1$}\\
\sum_{k=1}^{\ell H}\frac{D_{k}[j-1]}{1+S_{ki}}&\textsf{if $i\in[N]$ and $1<j\leq N+1$}\\
0&\mathrm{o/w}\end{cases} $$

where $S_{ki}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})_{ij}$ and $X$ denotes the input to the transformer.

We proceed inductively. In the base case $S_{0}=X$ , the input to the transformer. Suppose $S_{\ell-1}$ is computed. For any $h\in[H]$ , Lemma˜5.2 implies that we obtain an attention head $\mathrm{Att}^{(h,\ell)}\in\mathrm{Att}^{N+1}_{m+1,2m+1}$ that outputs a matrix $Y^{(h,\ell)}$ such that

$$ S_{\ell}=S_{\ell-1}+\sum_{h}Y^{(h,\ell)}\text{.} $$

This follows as $Y^{(h,\ell)}$ is only non-zero in the first $N+1$ columns, and we show in Lemma˜5.2 that the input to the attention head can be arbitrary in the first $N+1$ columns.

Summing over $H$ heads and the output of the previous layer, we obtain that the output of the $\ell$ -th layer is $S_{\ell}$ as desired. Finally, we observe that $T(X)$ is exactly $S_{L}$ , so we define the output MLP $\Psi$ as the identity map, i.e. each row $v$ of $S_{L}$ is mapped to $\psi(v)=v$ . Note that every embedding can be computed by an arithmetic circuit of size $O(Nm)$ . ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem˜5.1.

#### Proof of Theorem˜5.1.

Suppose there is an eAC of size $s$ that computes the the transformer $T$ with context length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $2N+3$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads per layer, input and output dimension $2N+3$ specified in Lemma˜5.3 (note that this transformer satisfies the first desired property). We construct an eAC with $LHN^{2}$ additional inputs, denoted as $C_{kij}$ and $D_{ki}$ where $k\in[LH]$ and $i,j\in[N]$ . We will now describe an eAC consisting of three parts: a preprocessing stage to construct the input to the transformer, the circuit that simulates the transformer, and a postprocessing stage that sums up the outputs of the transformer.

We begin with the preprocessing stage. For $k\in[LH]$ , define $C_{k}$ to be the $N\times N$ matrix with entries $C_{k}[i,j]=C_{kij}$ and $D_{k}$ to be the dimension $N$ vector with entries $D_{k}[i]=D_{ki}$ . Then, given $A_{k},B_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ we construct matrices $\tilde{A}_{k},\tilde{B}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2N}$ as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{k}=\begin{pmatrix}A_{k}&C_{k}\end{pmatrix},\quad\tilde{B}_{k}=\begin{pmatrix}B_{k}&I\end{pmatrix} $$

Observe that there is an extended arithmetic circuit of size $O\left(LHN^{2}\right)$ that computes $\tilde{A}_{k},\tilde{B}_{k}$ for all $k\in[LH]$ .

Let $T$ be the transformer with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $2N+3$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads per layer, input dimension $2N+3$ , and output dimension $2N+3$ given by Lemma˜5.3 whose output $Y$ is a matrix whose entries are

$$ Y_{i,1}=\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\frac{S_{ki}}{1+S_{ki}} $$

for $i\in[N]$ and

$$ Y_{i,j}=\sum_{k}\frac{D_{k}[j-1]}{1+S_{ki}} $$

for $i\in[N]$ and $1<j\leq N+1$ where $S_{ki}=\sum_{j}\exp\left(\tilde{A}_{k}\tilde{B}_{k}^{\top}\right)_{ij}$ . Recall that we denote the size of the eAC that computes $T$ to be $s$ . With $N$ additional gates, we can sum up the first column and obtain an eAC of size $O\left(s+LHN^{2}\right)$ that computes

$$ f\left(\left\{A_{k},B_{k},C_{k},D_{k}\right\}_{k=1}^{LH}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{i,1}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{(h,\ell)}Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i,1}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\frac{S_{ki}}{1+S_{ki}}\text{.} $$

Now, consider the partial derivatives of $f$ . In particular for any $k\in[LH],i_{0},j_{0}\in[N]$ with $k$ identified with $(h,\ell)$ , the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{(h,\ell)}^{LH}Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i_{,}1} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i_{0},1} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}\frac{S_{ki_{0}}}{1+S_{ki_{0}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\frac{\partial S_{ki_{0}}}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}}{(1+S_{ki_{0}})^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\exp((A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})_{i_{0}j_{0}}+C_{ki_{0}j_{0}})}{(1+S_{ki_{0}})^{2}} $$

where in the second and fifth equality, we only include summands that involve $C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}$ , and in the fifth equality, we use

$$ (\tilde{A}_{k}\tilde{B}_{k}^{\top})_{i0j0}=(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})_{i0j0}+C_{ki0j0}\text{.} $$

Then, if we set the value of all auxiliary $C_{kij}$ to $0$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\exp((A_{k}B_{k}^{\top})_{i_{0}j_{0}})}{(1+S_{ki_{0}})^{2}}\text{.} $$

Similarly, by summing up $Y_{i,i+1}$ , we obtain an eAC that computes the function

$$ g\left(\left\{A_{k},B_{k},C_{k},D_{k}\right\}_{k=1}^{LH}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{LH}\frac{D_{k}[i]}{1+S_{ki}}\text{.} $$

Taking the partial derivative with respect to $D_{k}[i_{0}]$ ,

$$ \frac{\partial g}{\partial D_{k}[i_{0}]}=\frac{\partial}{\partial D_{k}[i_{0}]}Y^{(h,\ell)}[i_{0},i_{0}+1]=\frac{1}{1+S_{ki_{0}}}\text{.} $$

Applying the Extended Baur-Strassen Theorem (Theorem˜4.4) to both $f$ and $g$ , there is an eAC of size $O(s+LHN^{2})$ that computes all partial derivatives of $f$ and $g$ . Then, we can easily compute

$$ \left(A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right)_{i_{0}j_{0}}=\ln\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}\right)-2\ln\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial D_{k}[i_{0}]}\right) $$

for all $k\in[LH]$ and $i_{0},j_{0}\in[N]$ with $O\left(LHN^{2}\right)$ additional gates.

So far, we have obtained an eAC of size $O(s+LHN^{2})$ that computes $A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}$ for $k\in[LH]$ . By Theorem˜4.1, there also exists an AC of size $O(s+LHN^{2})$ that computes $A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}$ for $k\in[LH]$ , i.e., it computes $LH$ independent matrix products of size $N\times N\times N$ . Then, by Lemma˜4.5, any AC that computes these independent matrix products has size $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}$ . Therefore, we must have $s\geq LHN^{\omega-o(1)}-O(LHN^{2})$ as desired.

∎

## 6 Discussion and Open Questions

We provide lower bounds against the efficient computation of transformers. In particular, we show that in the small embedding regime $m=N^{o(1)}$ , an $L$ layer transformer with $H$ heads per layer requires $LHN^{2-o(1)}$ time under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis, thus establishing a conditional lower bound stating that the standard $LHN^{2+o(1)}$ algorithm is optimal up to sub-polynomial factors, improving significantly upon the previous lower bounds based only on the hardness of attention [KWH23, AS24, GHS+26]. In the large embedding regime, we establish that even when the MLP and embedding layers can be computed with small circuits, a circuit computing a transformer can compute many independent matrix products and must be large. In particular, even when the MLP and embedding functions can be computed by linear sized circuits, computing an $L$ layer transformer with $H$ heads per layer and embedding dimension $N$ , a circuit of size $LHN^{\omega\pm o(1)}$ is both necessary and sufficient.

Finally, we conclude with some open questions. First, an interesting direction is to extend Theorem˜5.1 to any algorithms in the Word-RAM model (i.e. generalizing the lower bound beyond the extended arithmetic circuit model).

Second, while Theorem˜5.1 rules out an arithmetic circuit that improves upon the naive algorithm for embedding dimension $m=N$ , it is an interesting open question to rule out any arithmetic circuit improving upon the standard algorithm (when sped up with fast matrix multiplication) for any polynomial $m$ . We remark that our techniques imply a lower bound stronger than that of Theorem˜1.1 for most polynomial $m$ . In particular, we can construct a transformer with embedding dimension $m$ that computes $LH$ independent products of $m\times N$ and $N\times m$ matrices. Thus, any circuit that computes transformers with embedding dimension $m=N^{a}$ for $a>0$ requires $LHN^{\omega(1,a,a)-o(1)}$ size. Here, $\omega(a,b,c)$ denotes the rectangular matrix multiplication exponent, i.e. the smallest constant such that for any $\varepsilon>0$ , there is an arithmetic circuit of size $O\left(n^{\omega(a,b,c)+\varepsilon}\right)$ that computes an $n^{a}\times n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrix product. The question then is to resolve the gap between this lower bound and the $LHN^{\omega(1,a,1)+o(1)}$ upper bound. We remark that even for a single attention head, there is no known reduction from $N\times m\times N$ rectangular matrix multiplication to attention computation with embedding dimension $m$ .

Finally, our work focuses on worst-case lower bounds. Are there input distributions under which we can develop faster algorithms? A similar question can be asked for structural assumptions: what structural assumptions (beyond those known for attention computation [AS24, GHS+26]) admit efficient algorithms?

#### Proof of Lemma˜2.9.

Fix $c\gg\log N$ for some sufficiently large constant. Define embedding maps $Q^{\prime}(v)=c\cdot Q(v)$ to scale the $Q$ embedding by $c$ and $K^{\prime}(v)=K(v),V^{\prime}(v)=V(v)$ to be exactly as in $f$ . Note that these embedding maps can be expressed as weight matrices that are either the $m\times m$ identity $I_{m}$ or a scalar of $I_{m}$ . Fix an index $i$ and assume without loss of generality $1\in I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})$ . Let $A(X)_{i}$ denote the $i$ -th row of $A(X)$ . Then,

$$ \sum_{i^{\prime}\not\in I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})}\exp(cA(X)_{ii^{\prime}})\leq\frac{N}{\exp(c)}\exp(cA(X)_{i1})=\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}\exp(cA(X)_{i1})\text{.} $$

Then, for $i^{\prime}\in I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})$ note that $\frac{1}{|I_{\max}(A_{i})|}\geq\mathrm{softmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}$ so that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathrm{softmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}-\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}\right| \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})|}-\frac{\exp(cA(X))_{i1}}{\sum_{i^{\prime}}\exp(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}}\text{.} $$

Now, we can upper bound

$$ \sum_{i^{\prime}}\exp(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}\leq|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i}|\exp(cA(X))_{i1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)} $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathrm{softmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}-\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{|I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})|}\left(1-\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}}\right)\leq\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}\text{.} $$

For $i^{\prime}\not\in I_{\max}(A(X)_{i})$ , note that $\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}=0$ so that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathrm{softmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}-\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}\right| \displaystyle\leq\frac{\exp(cA(X))_{ii^{\prime}}}{|I_{\max}|\exp(cA(X))_{i1}}\leq\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}\text{.} $$

Then, for a fixed column of $V(X)$ , denoted $V(X)^{j}$ , we use Holder’s inequality to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\left|f^{\prime}(X)_{ij}-\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X)_{i})\cdot V(X)^{j}\right| \displaystyle=\left|(\mathrm{softmax}(cA(X)_{i})-\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X)_{i}))\cdot V(X)^{j}\right| \displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\mathrm{softmax}(cA(X)_{i})-\mathrm{hardmax}(cA(X)_{i})\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert V(X)^{j}\right\rVert_{\infty} \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}\text{.} $$

In particular, every entry of the output is within $\frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(N)}$ for an arbitrary small inverse polynomial by choosing a larger constant factor for $c$ . ∎
