#### Proof of Lemma˜2.13.

Suppose we are given an instance to (balanced) $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ of size $n$ , with sets $B_{1},\dots,B_{k}$ . For $2\leq j\leq k$ , divide $B_{j}$ into $t_{j}:=O(n^{1-s_{j}})$ sets of size $n^{s_{j}}$ , denoted $B_{j}^{(1)},\dots,B_{j}^{(t_{j})}$ . Now, for every $k$ -tuple $(i_{1},\dots,i_{k})\in\prod_{j=1}^{k}[t_{j}]$ , construct an instance of unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ consisting of sets $B_{1},B_{2}^{(i_{2})},\dots,B_{k}^{(i_{k})}$ . Note that this creates $O\left(\prod_{j=2}^{k}t_{j}\right)$ instances of unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ . Suppose there is an algorithm computing unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ in time $O\left(n^{s_{1}+\dotsc+s_{k}-\varepsilon}\right)$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ . We can then compute all of the above instances in time

$$ O\left(\prod_{j=2}^{k}t_{j}n^{1+s_{2}+\dots+s_{k}-\varepsilon}\right)=O\left(n^{k-\varepsilon}\right)\text{.} $$

Since, there is an orthogonal $k$ -tuple in the original $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instance if and only if one of the unbalanced $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ instances contains an orthogonal $k$ -tuple, this violates the $k\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. ∎

### A.1 Denormalized Attention

When thinking about attention, it is frequently useful to be able to ignore the normalization required by softmax. To this end, we define denormalized attention, which replaces $\mathrm{softmax}(v)$ with $\exp(v)$ for every row $v$ of $Q(X)K(X)^{\top}$ .

#### Definition A.1 (Denormalized Attention).

An denormalized attention head is a mapping $g_{Q,K,V}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ defined by

$$ g_{Q,K,V}(X)=\exp(Q(X)K(X)^{\top})V(X) $$

and parameterized by row-wise query, key, and value embeddings $Q,K,V\colon\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ (e.g., $Q(X)=(Q_{1}(X_{1}),\dots,Q_{N}(X_{N}))$ .

We show that denormalized attention can be efficiently computed with a small transformer in the standard setting (i.e. with normalization). Unfortunately, this does not in general imply that a transformer with normalization can simulate a transformer without normalization, as the MLP is applied to the output of each layer (i.e. after summation over heads) whereas the construction below requires an MLP applied immediately to the output of each attention head.

For simplicity, we describe the following transformer

#### Lemma A.2.

Let $g_{Q,K,V}$ be a denormalized attention head with input length $N$ , input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ and embedding dimension $m$ . There is a transformer $T$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m+{d_{\textup{in}}}+1$ , $1$ layer, $1$ head, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ and output dimension $m$ such that

$$ T\left(\begin{pmatrix}X\\
0\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}g_{Q,K,V}(X)\\
1_{1\times N}V(X)\end{pmatrix} $$

for all $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}$ . Furthermore, all embedding and MLP maps can be computed by an arithmetic circuit of size $O(Nm)$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the following embeddings:

$$ \displaystyle Q^{\prime}(X) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}Q(X)&0_{N\times({d_{\textup{in}}}+1)}\\
0_{1\times m}&0_{1\times({d_{\textup{in}}}+1)}\end{pmatrix},\quad \displaystyle K^{\prime}(X) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}K(X)&0_{N\times({d_{\textup{in}}}+1)}\\
0_{1\times m}&0_{1\times({d_{\textup{in}}}+1)}\end{pmatrix},\quad \displaystyle V^{\prime}(X) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0_{N\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}&V(X)&0_{N\times 1}\\
0_{1\times{d_{\textup{in}}}}&0_{1\times m}&1\end{pmatrix} $$

where $Q^{\prime}(X),K^{\prime}(X),V^{\prime}(X)\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(m+{d_{\textup{in}}}+1)}$ . Then

$$ \exp(Q^{\prime}(X)K^{\prime}(X)^{\top})=\begin{pmatrix}\exp(Q(X)K(X)^{\top})&1_{N\times 1}\\
1_{1\times N}&1\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

In particular, the first $N$ rows have row-sum $S_{i}+1$ where $S_{i}$ is the row-sum of the $i$ -th row in the denormalized attention head. Note $S_{i}\geq 0$ so the denominator is always positive. Thus, in the output matrix, the first $N$ rows consist of the input $X^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}X\\ 0\end{pmatrix}$ . Then, for $i\in[N]$ , the $(i,{d_{\textup{in}}}+m+1)$ -th entry is $\frac{1}{1+S_{i}}$ while for $j\in[m]$ the $(i,{d_{\textup{in}}}+j)$ -th entry is $\frac{Y_{i,j}}{1+S_{i}}$ where $Y_{ij}$ is the $(i,j)$ -th entry of the denormalized attention head $g$ . For $i=N+1$ , observe the $(N+1,{d_{\textup{in}}}+m+1)$ -th entry is $\frac{1}{N+1}$ and for $j\in[m]$ , the $(N+1,j)$ -th entry is $\frac{\left\lVert V(X)[;j]\right\rVert_{1}}{N+1}$ . In particular, we obtain the vector $1_{1\times N}V(X)$ scaled by $\frac{1}{N+1}$ .

Then, applying the output MLP $\psi=(\psi_{1},\dotsc,\psi_{m}):\mathbb{R}^{{d_{\textup{in}}}+m+1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ defined by $\psi_{i}:v\mapsto v_{{d_{\textup{in}}}+i}/v_{{d_{\textup{in}}}+m+1}$ , we obtain the desired output $Y$ . Here, note that $v_{{d_{\textup{in}}}+m+1}=\frac{1}{1+S_{i}}>0$ since $S_{i}>0$ . Note that every embedding map and MLP can be implemented with a size $O(m)$ eAC. ∎

## Appendix B MLPs

In standard transformer architectures, MLPs are applied after the attention layers. In our case, $X=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathrm{Att}_{i}(X^{\prime})$ is the sum of the outputs of the attention heads of the corresponding layer. MLPs are functions that are applied to input $X$ .

#### GLU MLPs.

In modern language models, gated linear units (GLUs) are a popular choice of activation function [Sha20], for example in PaLM [CND+23], LLaMA [Tea24], and Gemma [TMH+24]. We will show that without loss of generality, transformers with GLU MLPs can simulate transformers with no MLPs, thus obtaining our lower bounds for transformers with GLU MLPs. We define a gated linear unit below.

#### Definition B.1 (Gated Linear Unit (GLU) MLP).

Given an activation function $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , an GLU with hidden dimension ${d_{\textup{hid}}}$ and activation function $\sigma$ is a map $\psi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ defined

$$ x\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x^{\top}&1\end{pmatrix}W_{0}\odot\sigma\left(\begin{pmatrix}x^{\top}&1\end{pmatrix}W_{1}\right)&1\end{pmatrix}W_{2} $$

where $W_{0},W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+1)\times{d_{\textup{hid}}}}$ , $W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{({d_{\textup{hid}}}+1)\times m}$ and $\sigma$ is applied entry-wise.

We show that transformers with GLU MLPs can simulate transformers with no MLPs whenever the activation function $\sigma$ is not identically $0$ . In particular, our lower bounds for Theorem˜3.1 and Theorem˜5.1 hold also for transformers the GLU MLPs.

#### Proposition B.2.

Suppose there exists some $c\in\mathbb{R}$ with $\sigma(c)\neq 0$ .

Let $T$ be a transformer with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ , output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ with no MLPs.

Then, there is a transformer $T^{\prime}$ with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ , output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ and GLU MLPs with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=m$ and activation function $\sigma$ such that $T^{\prime}(X)=T(X)$ for all inputs $X$ .

Furthermore, if $\sigma$ can be computed by an eAC of size $t$ , the GLU MLPs can be computed with an eAC of size $O(tm)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\sigma(c)=z\neq 0$ . We construct a GLU MLP that computes the identity map. We set ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=m$ and

$$ W_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}z^{-1}\cdot I_{m}\\
0_{1\times m}\end{pmatrix},\quad W_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}0_{m\times m}\\
c\cdot 1_{1\times m}\end{pmatrix},\quad W_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{m}\\
0_{1\times m}\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

Then, for any $x$ , the GLU MLP maps

$$ x\mapsto\frac{x}{z}\odot(\sigma(c)1_{m})=x $$

so that the GLU MLP $\psi$ is the identity map. ∎

In the remainder of this section, we show that our lower bounds also hold for traditional (non-gated) MLPs. Traditionally, an MLP layer, given some input $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ , computes $f(XW_{1})W_{2}$ where $W_{1},W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times{d_{\textup{hid}}}}$ are learned weight matrices and $f$ is an entry-wise activation function. In general, when we multiply by $W_{1},W_{2}$ , we may assume that the input matrix has a column of $1$ ’s appended to allow for a bias term to be added to the linear function computed by $W_{1},W_{2}$ . When it is clear from context, for matrix $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ , we abuse notation and let

$$ XW:=\begin{pmatrix}X&1_{N\times 1}\end{pmatrix}W $$

where $W\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+1)\times{d_{\textup{hid}}}}$ .

#### Definition B.3 (MLP).

Given an activation function $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ , an MLP with hidden dimension ${d_{\textup{hid}}}$ and activation function $\sigma$ is a map $\psi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ defined

$$ x\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}\sigma\left(\begin{pmatrix}x^{\top}&1\end{pmatrix}W_{1}\right)&1\end{pmatrix}W_{2} $$

where $W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+1)\times{d_{\textup{hid}}}}$ , $W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{({d_{\textup{hid}}}+1)\times m}$ and $\sigma$ is applied entry-wise.

In particular, we consider two standard choices of activation function: ReLU and sigmoid.

#### ReLU.

For the ReLU activation function $x\mapsto\max(0,x)$ , we claim that a transformer with ReLU MLP layers can simulate a transformer with no MLPs. Our lower bound then implies that there are transformers with ReLU MLP layers that cannot be computed with an eAC of $LHN^{\omega-c}$ for any $c>0$ . In this case however, it is not clear how to efficiently simulate a ReLU function using an eAC, so it may be the case that an even larger eAC is necessary.

#### Lemma B.4.

Let $T$ be a transformer with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ , output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ with no MLPs.

Then, there is a transformer $T^{\prime}$ with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads, input dimension ${d_{\textup{in}}}$ , output dimension ${d_{\textup{out}}}$ and MLPs with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=2m$ and ReLU activation functions such that $T^{\prime}(X)=T(X)$ for all inputs $X$ .

#### Proof.

Given $X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}$ , we show how to use an MLP with ReLU activation to compute the identity map. Let

$$ W_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{m}&-I_{m}\\
0_{1\times m}&0_{1\times m}\end{pmatrix},\quad W_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{m}\\
-I_{m}\\
0_{1\times m}\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

Now, letting $f(x)=\max(x,0)$ denote the ReLU function, observe

$$ f(XW_{1})W_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}f(X)&f(-X)\end{pmatrix}W_{2}=f(X)-f(-X)\text{.} $$

We conclude the proof by noting that $f(x)-f(-x)=\max(0,x)-\max(0,-x)=x$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$ . ∎

#### Sigmoid.

For the sigmoid activation function (denoted $\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})$ ), we require a more intricate modification of Theorem˜3.1 and Theorem˜5.1. We will in fact prove the results for a more general class of activation functions.

#### Definition B.5.

An activation function $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is gap-preserving if the following hold:

- 1. $\sigma(0)\neq\sigma(1)$ ,

- 2. There exists $c^{*}$ such that for all $x\leq c^{*}-1$ , $\sigma(x)\leq\sigma(c^{*}-1)<\sigma(c^{*})$ .

Note that the sigmoid is gap-preserving with $c^{*}=0$ . We remark that the specific choices of constants (e.g. $0,1,-1,-.1$ ) are not too important, and the proof can be modified for other choices of constants. We show that our lower bound in the small embedding dimension (Theorem˜3.1) holds for MLPs with gap-preserving activation functions.

#### Proposition B.6.

Let $m=\Theta(\log N)$ and $L,H=\mathrm{poly}(N)$ . Any algorithm computing transformers with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads in each layer, input dimension $m$ , and output dimension $1$ up to entry-wise additive error $\frac{1}{10N}$ requires $LHN^{2-o(1)}$ time under the $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ Hypothesis. The lower bound holds even if the transformer has MLPs with hidden dimension $O(m)$ and gap-preserving activation function.

We give a high level overview of the modifications. Recall that in Theorem˜3.1 we construct a transformer such that each layer’s output (1) preserves its input on $m-1$ columns and (2) maintains one column to record whether an orthogonal triple has been found. On this final column, the value is $2H\ell$ if $a_{i}$ has not participated in any orthogonal triple so far and at most $2H\ell-0.5$ otherwise, achieving a $0.5$ additive gap between the yes and no instances. We thus design an MLP that computes the identity map on $m-1$ columns and maintains a gap on the final column. To compute the identity, we observe that each of the first $m-1$ columns has at most $2$ distinct values, thus we can design an appropriate linear function to map the outputs of the sigmoid $\sigma$ back to the input. In the final column, we construct $W_{1}$ to map $x\mapsto x-2H$ and $W_{2}$ to map $\sigma(0)\mapsto 0$ and $\sigma(-1/2)\mapsto y<-0.5$ , maintaining a gap of at least $0.5$ in the output.

#### Proof.

We describe the appropriate modifications to Theorem˜3.1, beginning with the first layer. Let $X^{(0)}$ denote the input to the transformer and $Z_{h,\ell}$ denote the output of $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer of the hardmax transformer defined in Theorem˜3.1. Recall

$$ X^{(0)}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}^{\top}&b_{1}^{\top}&1\\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\
a_{N}^{\top}&b_{N}^{\top}&1\\
0&0&2\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times(m-1)},\quad Z_{h,\ell}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\dots&0&z_{1,h,\ell}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&\dots&0&z_{N,h,\ell}\\
0&\dots&0&\frac{N+2}{N+1}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times m} $$

where $z_{i,h,\ell}=2$ if $a_{i},c_{h,\ell}$ do not participate in an orthogonal triple, and $z_{i,h,\ell}\leq\frac{3}{2}$ otherwise. Then,

$$ \sum_{h}Z_{h,\ell}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\dots&0&z_{1,\ell}\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
0&\dots&0&z_{N,\ell}\\
0&\dots&0&\frac{H(N+2)}{N+1}\end{pmatrix} $$

where $z_{i,\ell}=\sum_{h}z_{i,h,\ell}$ .

We construct an MLP with hidden dimension ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=m$ and gap-preserving activation function. Define linear functions $f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}$ such that $f_{1}$ is an increasing linear function mapping $\sigma(c^{*})\mapsto 0$ and $\sigma(c^{*}-1)\mapsto-1$ and

$$ \displaystyle f_{1}(x) \displaystyle=b_{1}x+b_{2} \displaystyle f_{2}(x) \displaystyle=\frac{x-\sigma(0)}{\sigma(1)-\sigma(0)}=c_{1}x+c_{2} \displaystyle f_{3}(x) \displaystyle=1+f_{2}(x)=c_{1}x+(1+c_{2}) $$

for some constants $b_{1},b_{2},c_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R}$ and observe

$$ \displaystyle f_{1} \displaystyle:\sigma(c^{*})\mapsto 0,\quad\sigma(c^{*}-1)\mapsto-1 \displaystyle f_{2} \displaystyle:\sigma(0)\mapsto 0,\quad\sigma(1)\mapsto 1 \displaystyle f_{3} \displaystyle:\sigma(0)\mapsto 1,\quad\sigma(1)\mapsto 2\text{.} $$

Note that we can construct $f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}$ by the first two properties of Definition˜B.5. Set the weight matrices as

$$ W_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{2d}&0_{2d\times 1}&0_{2d\times 1}\\
0_{1\times 2d}&1&0\\
0_{1\times 2d}&0&2\\
0_{1\times 2d}&-1&c^{*}-4H\end{pmatrix},\quad W_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}c_{1}I_{2d}&0_{2d\times 1}&0_{2d\times 1}\\
0_{1\times 2d}&c_{1}&0\\
0_{1\times 2d}&0&b_{1}\\
(c_{2})_{1\times 2d}&1+c_{2}&b_{2}\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

Note that $W_{1},W_{2}$ have $m+1$ rows (instead of $m$ ) since the last row encodes the bias term of the linear function $W_{1},W_{2}$ .

Since the first $2d$ columns of $X^{(0)}$ is $0$ or $1$ , we ensure that the first $2d$ columns is preserved by the MLP, since $W_{1}$ is the identity map and $f_{2}$ maps $\sigma(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ to $0$ and $\sigma(1)$ to $1$ .

Similarly, since the $(2d+1)$ -th column is $1$ or $2$ , we ensure that this is preserved by the MLP as well. Here, observe that $W_{1}$ maps $1$ and $2$ to $0$ and $1$ respectively, while $f_{3}$ maps $\sigma(0)$ to $1$ and $\sigma(1)$ to $2$ .

Finally, consider an entry in the $(2d+2)$ -th column. As before, if $a_{i}$ does not participate in an orthogonal triple with any $\left\{c_{h,1}\right\}$ then $z_{i,1}=2H$ and otherwise, $z_{i,1}\leq 2H-\frac{1}{2}$ . Then, $\sigma(Y^{(1)}W_{1})[i,m]=\sigma(c^{*})$ in the former case and $\sigma(x)\leq\sigma(c^{*}-1)$ in the latter case. In particular, the MLP layer outputs $X^{(1)}[i,m]=(\sigma(Y^{(1)}W_{1})W_{2})[i,m]=0$ in the former case, and is at most $-1$ (since $f_{1}$ is increasing) in the latter case.

We can proceed inductively for subsequent layers. Note that with the exception of the $m$ -th column, the identical proof as above shows that the contents of the input matrix $X^{(0)}$ are preserved. It suffices to show that the $m$ -th column allows us to distinguish a yes-instance of $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ from a no-instance. We use the following inductive claim: for all $i$ , if $a_{i}$ participates in an orthogonal triple with $c_{h,t}$ for some $h\in[H],t\leq\ell$ , then $X^{(\ell)}[i,m]\leq-1$ . Otherwise, $X^{(\ell)}[i,m]=0$ . Above we have established the base case with $\ell=1$ .

Let $Y^{(\ell)}$ denote the output of the attention layer, we have

$$ Y^{(\ell)}[i,m]=X^{(\ell-1)}[i,m]+\sum_{h}z_{i,h,\ell}\text{.} $$

In a no-instance, we have $X^{(\ell-1)}[i,m]=0$ (by induction) and $\sum_{h}z_{i,h,\ell}=2H$ . Following the proof of the base case, we conclude $X^{(\ell)}[i,m]=0$ .

We now argue that in a yes-instance, whenever $a_{i}$ participate in an orthogonal triple with some $c_{h,t}$ for $t\leq\ell$ , $X^{(\ell)}[i,m]\leq-1$ . By induction, we either have $X^{(\ell-1)}[i,m]\leq-1$ if $t<\ell$ or $\sum_{h}z_{i,h,\ell}\leq 2H-0.5$ . Since $X^{(\ell-1)}[i,m]\leq 0$ and $\sum_{h}z_{i,h,\ell}\leq 2H$ in either case, we have $Y^{(\ell)}[i,m]\leq 2H-0.5$ . Since $W_{1}$ applies an increasing function to the $m$ -th column, we again have that the input to $\sigma$ is $c^{*}$ in the no-instance and at most $c^{*}-1$ in the yes instance. We then conclude the proof identically as in the base case.

Thus, encoding MLPs as above, it suffices to examine the $m$ -th column of the output of the transformer to compute $3\textup{-}\mathsf{OV}$ . In a no instance, all the output entries should be $0$ . In a yes instance, at least one entry will be less than $-1$ . ∎

We now move on to Theorem˜5.1, which we prove a separate class of activation functions (which sigmoid also satisfies).

#### Definition B.7.

An activation function $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is eAC gradient efficient if the following hold:

- 1. $\sigma(0)\neq\sigma(1)$ ,

- 2. $\sigma^{-1}$ can be implemented with an eAC of size $O(1)$ .

- 3. $\sigma^{\prime}(x)=h(\sigma(x))$ for some $h$ such that both $\sigma,h$ can be implemented with an eAC of size $O(1)$ .

Note that the sigmoid function is eAC gradient efficient as $\sigma^{\prime}(x)=\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$ and $\sigma^{-1}$ is computable on the range of the sigmoid function $(0,1)$ . We remark that in the event that the last layer has no MLP, the second condition is unnecessary.

#### Proposition B.8.

There exists a transformer $T$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m=2N+1$ , $L$ layers, $H$ attention heads per layer, input dimension $1$ and output dimension $N+1$ satisfying the following:

- 1. $T$ is computable by an eAC, and each embedding and MLP is computable by an eAC of size $O(m)$ .

- 2. Any eAC computing $T$ has size at least $LHN^{\omega-o(1)}-O\left(LHN^{2}\right)$ .

The lower bound holds even when $T$ has MLPs with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=O(m)$ and eAC gradient efficient activation functions.

#### Proof.

We maintain the construction of Theorem˜5.1, modifying only the MLPs. As in Proposition˜B.6, each MLP weight matrix has an additional row to allow for a bias term in the linear function. We set

$$ W_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{N+1}&0_{(N+1)\times(m^{\prime}-(N+1))}\\
0_{(m^{\prime}-(N+1))\times(N+1)}&I_{m^{\prime}-(N+1)}\\
0_{1\times(N+1)}&0_{1\times(m^{\prime}-(N+1))}\end{pmatrix},W_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{N+1}&0_{(N+1)\times(m^{\prime}-(N+1))}\\
0_{(m^{\prime}-(N+1))\times(N+1)}&c_{1}I_{m^{\prime}-(N+1)}\\
0_{1\times(N+1)}&-(c_{2})_{1\times(m^{\prime}-(N+1))}\end{pmatrix} $$

where $c_{1},c_{2}$ are constants as defined in Proposition˜B.6. Note that to define $c_{1},c_{2}$ we only require the property $\sigma(0)\neq\sigma(1)$ . Thus, the MLP layer applies $\sigma$ entry-wise to the first $N+1$ columns and maps $0,1$ to $0,1$ respectively in the last $m^{\prime}-(N+1)$ columns. Since $\sigma$ can be computed by an eAC of $O(1)$ size, each MLP map can be computed by an eAC of size $O(m)$ , satisfying the first property.

We first argue that the outputs of the attention heads as described in Lemma˜5.2 remain unchanged. Since the guarantees of Lemma˜5.2 holds as long as the last $m^{\prime}-(N+1)$ columns are the same as the input $X^{(0)}$ , it suffices to argue that this is maintained after each layer, which is formalized in the following claim.

#### Claim B.9.

In the transformer defined in Theorem˜5.1 with MLPs specified by $W_{1},W_{2}$ above, the output of each layer $\ell\geq 0$ satisfies $X^{(\ell)}[i,j]=X^{(0)}[i,j]$ for all $i\in[N+1],j>N+1$ i.e., the input is preserved in the last $m^{\prime}-N+1$ columns.

#### Proof.

We proceed inductively. The base case holds trivially, so we consider the inductive case. From Lemma˜5.2, each attention head outputs $0$ beyond the first $N+1$ columns, so that the output of each attention layer is its exactly its input on these columns. Since our input to the transformer, denoted $X^{(0)}$ , contains only $0,1$ in these columns, the MLP computes the identity map on these values, and maintains the input beyond the first $N+1$ columns, proving the inductive hypothesis. ∎

We now argue that we may recover the matrix products efficiently from an eAC that computes the described transformer. Let $h$ be the function such that $\sigma^{\prime}(x)=h(\sigma(x))$ . In the following, assume $j\leq N+1$ , since we only need the entries from the first $N+1$ columns of the output of the transformer to recover the matrix products. As in Proposition˜B.6, we define

$$ Y^{(\ell)}:=X^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{h}Y^{(h,\ell)} $$

where $Y^{(h,\ell)}$ denotes the output of the $h$ -th head in the $\ell$ -th layer. Recall that above we have shown $Y{(h,\ell)}$ are exactly the outputs of the corresponding attention head in the transformer constructed in Theorem˜5.1.

In particular, if $Y$ denotes the output of the transformer, we have for $j\leq N+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Y_{i,j} \displaystyle=\sigma\left(Y^{(L)}_{i,j}\right) \displaystyle=\sigma\left(X^{(L-1)}_{i,j}+\sum_{h}Y^{(h,L)}_{i,j}\right) $$

and for all $\ell>0$ and $j\leq N+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle X^{(\ell)}_{i,j} \displaystyle=\sigma\left(Y^{(\ell)}_{i,j}\right) \displaystyle=\sigma\left(X^{(\ell-1)}_{i,j}+\sum_{h}Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i,j}\right)\text{.} $$

In contrast to when there is no MLP, where $Y_{i,j}=\sum_{h,\ell}Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i,j}$ we now have

$$ Y_{i,j}=\sigma\left(\sum_{h}Y^{(h,L)}_{i,j}+\sigma\left(\sum_{h}Y^{(h,L-1)}_{i,j}+\sigma\left(\dots\right)\right)\right)\text{.} $$

Recall that in the proof of Theorem˜5.1 we use the outputs of the transformer to compute the following two functions:

$$ \displaystyle f\left(\left\{A_{k},B_{k},C_{k},D_{k}\right\}_{k=1}^{LH}\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{i,1} \displaystyle g\left(\left\{A_{k},B_{k},C_{k},D_{k}\right\}_{k=1}^{LH}\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{i,i+1}\text{.} $$

We now describe how to recover $LH$ independent matrix products $A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}$ , thus completing the proof. This is formalized in the following inductive lemma.

#### Lemma B.10.

Recall that we index $k\in[LH]$ as $(h,\ell)$ . For all $0\leq\ell\leq L$ , there is an eAC of size $O(H(L-\ell)N^{2})$ that computes $\left\{A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right\}$ for $k=(h,p)$ with $p\geq\ell$ , $\left\{\prod_{p=t}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(p)}_{i_{0},1}\right)\right\}_{t\in[\ell-1,L],i_{0}}$ , and $\left\{\prod_{p=t}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(p)}_{i_{0},i_{0}+1}\right)\right\}_{t\in[\ell-1,L],i_{0}}$ .

#### Proof.

For the base case, fix $\ell=L$ . Then, for fixed $k=(h_{0},L)$ and $i_{0},j_{0}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{i,1} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}Y_{i_{0},1} \displaystyle=\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(L)}_{i_{0},1}\right)\frac{\partial Y^{(h_{0},L)}_{i_{0},1}}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}\text{.} $$

In the second equality, we keep only summands depending on $C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}$ and in the third, we apply the chain rule and observe that only $Y^{(h_{0},\ell)}_{i_{0},1}$ in $Y_{i_{0},1}^{(L)}$ depends on $C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}$ . Since $\sigma$ is eAC gradient efficient, we can compute $\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(L)}\right)$ with $h\left(\sigma\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(L)}\right)\right)=h(Y_{i_{0},1})$ using the output of the transformer. Over all $h\in[H]$ and $i_{0}\in[N]$ , we use an eAC of size $O(HN)$ . In particular, we can compute

$$ \frac{\partial Y^{(h_{0},L)}_{i_{0},1}}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}=\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}}{h(Y_{i_{0},1})}\text{.} $$

We make a similar argument for $g$ as follows.

$$ \frac{\partial g}{\partial D_{ki_{0}}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial D_{ki_{0}}}Y_{i_{0},i_{0}+1}=\sigma^{\prime}(Y_{i_{0},i_{0}+1}^{(L)})\frac{\partial Y^{(h_{0},L)}_{i_{0},i_{0}+1}}{\partial D_{ki_{0}}}\text{.} $$

An identical proof allows us to recover $\frac{\partial Y^{(h_{0},L)}_{i_{0},i_{0}+1}}{\partial D_{ki_{0}}}$ using an eAC of size $O(HN)$ .

Since in Theorem˜5.1, we showed how to compute the products from $\frac{\partial Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i_{0}1}}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}$ and $\frac{\partial Y^{(h,\ell)}_{i_{0},i_{0}+1}}{\partial D_{ki_{0}}}$ , we can use the above derivatives to recover the matrix products $A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}$ with an eAC of size $O(N^{2})$ . Repeating the above argument for all $H$ gives us a $O(HN^{2})$ eAC that computes all matrix products in the $L$ -th layer. Given the resulting matrix products, we can compute all $Y^{(h,L)}_{i_{0},1}$ with an eAC of size $O(HN^{2})$ by summing the rows of each matrix product. Then, since

$$ Y_{i_{0},1}=\sigma\left(\sum_{h}Y_{i_{0},1}^{(h,L)}+\sigma\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(L-1)}\right)\right) $$

we can compute

$$ \sigma^{\prime}\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(L-1)}\right)=h\left(\sigma\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(L-1)}\right)\right)=h\left(\sigma^{{}_{1}}(Y_{i_{0},1})-\sum_{h}Y_{i_{0},1}^{(h,L)}\right) $$

for all $i_{0}$ with an eAC of size $O(HN)$ . Note that this is only step where we require $\sigma$ to be invertible. In particular, we have described how to compute the following quantities:

$$ \left\{\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(L-1)}_{i_{0},1}\right)\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y_{i_{0,1}}^{(L)}\right)\right\}_{i_{0}}\text{, }\left\{A_{k}B_{k}^{\top}\right\}_{k=(h,L)} $$

using an eAC of size $O(HN^{2})$ , completing the base case.

Now, consider the inductive case $\ell<L$ . We argue that all additional required values can be computed with an eAC of size $O(HN^{2})$ . Applying the chain rule, for $k\leftarrow(h_{0},\ell),i_{0},j_{0}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}} \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}Y_{i_{0},1} \displaystyle=\left(\prod_{t=\ell}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(t)}_{i_{0},1}\right)\right)\frac{\partial Y^{(h_{0},\ell)}_{i_{0},1}}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}} $$

following similar logic to the base case. By the inductive hypothesis, we have $\prod_{t=\ell}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(t)}_{i_{0},1}\right)$ from the previous $(\ell+1)$ -th iteration. Thus, with an eAC of size $O(HN)$ we can compute for all $i_{0}$ :

$$ \frac{\partial Y^{(h_{0},\ell)}_{i_{0},1}}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}=\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial C_{ki_{0}j_{0}}}}{\prod_{t=\ell}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(t)}_{i_{0},1}\right)}\text{.} $$

From here, we again follow the proof of Theorem˜5.1 to recover

$$ \left\{A_{k}B_{k}\right\}_{k=(h,\ell)} $$

and sum up matrix rows to obtain $\left\{Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell)}\right\}_{i_{0}}$ with an eAC of size $O(HN^{2})$ . Then, since

$$ Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{h}Y_{i_{0},1}^{(h,\ell)}+\sigma\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell-1)}\right) $$

we can compute

$$ \sigma^{\prime}\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell-1)}\right)=h\left(\sigma\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell-1)}\right)\right)=h\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell)}-\sum_{h}Y_{i_{0},1}^{(h,\ell)}\right) $$

for all $i_{0}$ using an eAC of size $O(HN)$ . Using our inductive hypothesis, we compute for all $i_{0}$ ,

$$ \prod_{t=\ell-1}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(t)}_{i_{0},1}\right)=\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y_{i_{0},1}^{(\ell-1)}\right)\prod_{t=\ell}^{L}\sigma^{\prime}\left(Y^{(t)}_{i_{0},1}\right) $$

with $O(N)$ size eAC, completing the inductive case. A similar argument holds for the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $D_{ki_{0}}$ . ∎

The above lemma allows us to conclude the proof, computing all $LH$ matrix products. ∎

## Appendix C Head Aggregation

Consider a transformer with $L$ layers of $H$ heads with embedding dimension $m$ . There are two standard ways to aggregate the outputs of the heads in the $\ell$ -th layer, denoted $X^{(\ell)}$ , given the input $X^{(\ell-1)}$ : summation and concatenation. Summation aggregation is described in Definition˜2.6. In concatenation aggregation (see e.g. [VSP+17]), each attention head maps each row of dimension $m$ into dimension $m/H$ . The output is then

$$ X^{(\ell)}=\Psi_{\ell}\left(X^{(\ell-1)}+\begin{pmatrix}\mathrm{Att}_{Q_{1},K_{1},V_{1}}\left(X^{(\ell-1)}\right)&\mathrm{Att}_{Q_{2},K_{2},V_{2}}\left(X^{(\ell-1)}\right)&\dots&\mathrm{Att}_{Q_{H},K_{H},V_{H}}\left(X^{(\ell-1)}\right)\end{pmatrix}\right) $$

where $\Psi$ denotes the MLP applied after concatenation.

We show such a transformer can simulate a transformer with summation aggregation and embedding dimension $m/H$ , so that any lower bound against transformers with summation aggregation and embedding dimension $m/H$ also hold against transformations with concatenation aggregation and embedding dimension $m$ .

#### Proposition C.1.

Assume $H\leq m$ divides $m$ . Suppose $T$ is a transformer with input length $N$ , embedding dimension $m/H$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads per layer, and summation aggregation.

Then, there is a transformer $T^{\prime}$ with input length $N+1$ , embedding dimension $m+H$ , $L$ layers, $H$ heads per layer and concatenation aggregation such that there is a linear function $f:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m}$ such that $f(T^{\prime}(X))=T(X)$ for all inputs $X$ . Furthermore, the following hold:

- 1. If $T$ is computable by an eAC, so is $T^{\prime}$ .

- 2. If each embedding map of $T$ is computable by an AC of size $O(m/H)$ , then all embedding maps of $T$ in one layer are computable by an AC of size $O(m)$ .

- 3. If $T$ has no MLPs, then neither does $T^{\prime}$ .

- 4. If $T$ has MLPs or GLU MLPs with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=O(m/H)$ and activation function $\sigma$ , then $T^{\prime}$ has an MLP with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=O(m)$ and activation function $\sigma$ (see Definition˜B.3 and Definition˜B.1).

In particular, Theorem˜3.1 implies that whenever $m/H=N^{o(1)}$ , the standard $LHN^{2+o(1)}$ time algorithm to compute transformers with concatenation aggregation is optimal, and Theorem˜5.1 implies that whenever $m/H=\Theta(N)$ , the corresponding $LHN^{\omega+o(1)}$ time algorithm is optimal. Furthermore, the reduction preserves whatever assumptions we make on the MLPs, either in the main body or Appendix˜B.

#### Proof.

We show that each layer can be simulated. Let $Y^{(\ell)}$ be the output of the $\ell$ -th layer of $T$ . In addition, let $Y^{(\ell,h)}$ be the output of the $h$ -th attention head in the $\ell$ -th layer of $T$ before the summation. By definition, $Y^{(\ell)}=\Psi_{\ell}\left(Y^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{h}Y^{(\ell,h)}\right)$ for $\ell\geq 1$ (in the case where $T$ does not have MLP, $\Psi_{\ell}$ is simply the identity map). Consider a single layer of $T^{\prime}$ with input $X^{(\ell-1)}$ , where we view it as a concatenation of $H$ blocks:

$$ \begin{pmatrix}X^{(\ell-1)}_{1}&X^{(\ell-1)}_{2}&\dots&X^{(\ell-1)}_{H}\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

We define the input of the transformer $T^{\prime}$ as $X_{1}^{(0)}=Y^{(0)}$ and $X_{h}^{(\ell-1)}:=0_{N\times(m/H)}$ for all $h>1$ . We will prove two cases separately: when $T$ has no MLPs, and when $T$ has MLPs with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=O(m)$ and activation function $\sigma$ .

#### Case 1: $T$ has no MLPs.

We proceed with the inductive hypothesis

$$ \sum_{h=1}^{H}X_{h}^{(\ell-1)}=Y^{(\ell-1)}\text{.} $$

That is, the sum of all the blocks is the output of the $(\ell-1)$ -th layer of $T$ . Note that the base case is satisfied by construction.

Consider the $h$ -th attention head. Fix an attention head of $T$ with embedding maps $Q_{h},K_{h},V_{h}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times(m/H)}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N\times(m/H)}$ (recall that $T$ has embedding dimension $m/H$ ). We design attention heads with similar embedding maps. Define the map $g:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m/H}$ where

$$ g:v\mapsto v\begin{pmatrix}I_{m/H}\\
\vdots\\
I_{m/H}\end{pmatrix}:=vW_{g} $$

so that $g(v)_{i}=\sum_{i\equiv i^{\prime}\mod(m/H)}v_{i}$ .

If $T$ has no MLPs, we design embedding maps $Q^{\prime}_{h},K^{\prime}_{h},V^{\prime}_{h}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N\times(m/H)}$ as

$$ \displaystyle Q^{\prime}_{h}=Q_{h}\circ g,K^{\prime}_{h}=K_{h}\circ g,V^{\prime}_{h}=V_{h}\circ g\text{.} $$

Note here that if $Q_{h}:X\rightarrow XW_{Q_{h}}$ can be described as a linear function, so can $Q^{\prime}_{h}:X\rightarrow XW_{g}W_{Q_{h}}$ (and analogously for $K_{h},V_{h}$ ). Under the inductive hypothesis, we have that

$$ Q^{\prime}_{h}\left(\begin{pmatrix}X^{(\ell-1)}_{1}&X^{(\ell-1)}_{2}&\dots&X^{(\ell-1)}_{H}\end{pmatrix}\right)=Q_{h}\left(\sum_{h}X^{(\ell-1)}_{h}\right)=Q_{h}(Y^{(\ell-1)}) $$

is exactly the embedding computed by the $h$ -th head of the $\ell$ -th layer of $T$ . A similar argument holds for $K^{\prime}_{h},V^{\prime}_{h}$ . As a result, the concatenated attention heads outputs

$$ \begin{pmatrix}Y^{(\ell,1)}&\dots&Y^{(\ell,H)}\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

The output of the layer is then

$$ \begin{pmatrix}Y^{(\ell,1)}+X^{(\ell-1)}_{1}&\dots&Y^{(\ell,H)}+X^{(\ell-1)}_{H}\end{pmatrix} $$

so that

$$ \sum_{h}Y^{(\ell,h)}+X^{(\ell-1)}_{h}=Y^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{h}Y^{(\ell,h)}=Y^{(\ell)} $$

satisfying the inductive hypothesis.

At the final layer, the transformer $T^{\prime}$ outputs

$$ \begin{pmatrix}Y^{(L,1)}&Y^{(L,2)}&\dots&Y^{(L,H)}\end{pmatrix} $$

so that $g(T^{\prime}(X))=T(X)$ . To conclude the proof, note that $g$ is easily implemented by an AC (and therefore eAC) of size $O(m)$ . Since every embedding map $Q_{h},K_{h},V_{h}$ takes the same input (i.e. the output of $g$ ), we can implement all $H$ embedding maps with an AC of size $O(m)$ .

#### Case 2: $T$ has MLPs or GLU MLPs with ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=O(m/H)$ and $\sigma$ activation.

If $T$ has MLPs with hidden dimension ${d_{\textup{hid}}}=O(m)$ and activation function $\sigma$ , we instead proceed with the inductive hypothesis

$$ X_{1}^{(\ell-1)}=Y^{(\ell-1)}\text{ and }X_{h}^{(\ell-1)}=0_{N\times m}\text{ for $h>1$.} $$

That is, $X_{1}^{(\ell-1)}$ is the output of the $(\ell-1)$ -th layer of $T$ and the remaining blocks are $0$ . The base case again holds by definition.

Consider the $\ell$ -th layer. Define the maps $\pi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m/H}$ as

$$ \pi:v\mapsto v\begin{pmatrix}I_{m/H}\\
0_{(m-m/H)\times(m/H)}\end{pmatrix}=(v_{1},\dots,v_{m/H})\text{.} $$

Furthermore, for $a\leq b$ , define $i:\mathbb{R}^{a}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{b}$ as the map $i:v\mapsto(v,0_{b-a})$ as the injective map with padding $0$ . For every fixed attention head $h$ , define $Q_{h}^{\prime}=Q_{h}\circ\pi$ and $K_{h}^{\prime},V_{h}^{\prime}$ analogously. Here, observe that $Q_{h}^{\prime},K_{h}^{\prime},V_{h}^{\prime}$ are embeddings that can in fact be implemented with AC of size $O(m/H)$ , so all embedding maps can be implemented with an AC Of size $O(m)$ .

Now, for the MLP, if $T$ has MLPs given by $W_{1}:\mathbb{R}^{(m/H)+1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{{d_{\textup{hid}}}},W_{2}:\mathbb{R}^{{d_{\textup{hid}}}+1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m},\sigma$ , we let $T^{\prime}$ have MLPs given by

$$ W_{1}^{\prime}(X):=\begin{pmatrix}X&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}I_{m/H}&0_{(m/H)\times 1}\\
\vdots&\vdots\\
I_{m/H}&0_{(m/H)\times 1}\\
0_{1\times(m/H)}&1\end{pmatrix}W_{1},\quad W_{2}^{\prime}(X):=\begin{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X&1\end{pmatrix}W_{2}&0_{1\times(m-(m/H))}\end{pmatrix} $$

and $\sigma$ activation function. Note that both $W_{1},W_{2}$ can be implemented as eAC of size $O(m)$ .

We claim that the construction yields the desired result. By the inductive hypothesis, the output of the attention heads (after concatenation) in the $\ell$ -th layer is

$$ Z:=\begin{pmatrix}Y^{(\ell,1)}&Y^{(\ell,2)}&\dots&Y^{(\ell,H)}\end{pmatrix}\text{.} $$

In particular, the first linear map of the MLP $W_{1}^{\prime}$ computes

$$ \displaystyle W_{1}^{\prime}\left(Y^{(\ell-1)}+Z\right) \displaystyle=W_{1}^{\prime}\left(\begin{pmatrix}Y^{(\ell,1)}+Y^{(\ell-1)}&Y^{(\ell,2)}&\dots&Y^{(\ell,H)}\end{pmatrix}\right) \displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}Y^{(\ell-1)}+\sum_{h}Y^{(\ell,h)}&1_{N\times 1}\end{pmatrix}W_{1} $$

is exactly the input to activation function $\sigma$ computed by $T$ . This completes the proof of the inductive case, as the $W_{2}^{\prime}$ outputs the output of the MLP into $X_{1}^{(\ell)}$ and $0$ everywhere else. A similar modification applies to GLU MLPs by modifying $W_{0}$ analogously to $W_{1}$ . ∎

# Deterministic Monotone Min-Plus Product and Convolution

**Authors:** Ce Jin ††thanks: University of California Berkeley. cejin@berkeley.edu. Supported by the Miller Research Fellowship at the Miller Institute for Basic Research in Science, UC Berkeley. Jaewoo Park ††thanks: University of California San Diego. pjaewoo@ucsd.edu. Supported by NSF HDR TRIPODS Phase II grant 2217058 (EnCORE Institute). ## Abstract

The Monotone Min-Plus Product problem is a useful primitive that has seen many algorithmic applications over the past decade. It also generalizes various other structured Min-Plus products studied in the literature, such as Bounded Difference Min-Plus Product and Bounded Integer Min-Plus Product. In this problem, we are given two $n\times n$ integer matrices $A$ and $B$ , where each row of $B$ is a monotone non-decreasing sequence of integers from $\{1,\dots,n\}$ , and the goal is to compute their Min-Plus product, defined as the $n\times n$ matrix $C$ with $C_{i,j}=\min_{k}\{A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\}$ . The fastest known algorithm for this task [Chi, Duan, Xie, and Zhang, STOC’22] runs in $n^{(\omega+3)/2+o(1)}=\mathcal{O}(n^{2.686})$ time, significantly improving over the brute-force cubic algorithm. However, its main disadvantage is that it requires randomization, which is then inherited by all downstream applications.

Our main result is a deterministic algorithm for Monotone Min-Plus product with the same time complexity $n^{(\omega+3)/2+o(1)}=\mathcal{O}(n^{2.686})$ as its randomized counterpart, improving upon the previous deterministic bound $\mathcal{O}(n^{2.875})$ [Gu, Polak, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu, ICALP’21]. Our derandomization also applies to previously studied extensions and variants (e.g., [Dürr, IPL’23]), including rectangular matrices, bounded range $[n^{\mu}]$ , and column-monotone matrices. As an immediate consequence, we derandomize state-of-the-art algorithms for multiple problems, including Language Edit Distance, RNA Folding, Optimum Stack Generation, unweighted Tree Edit Distance, Batched Range Mode, and Approximate All-Pairs Shortest Paths.

Our techniques also yield a deterministic algorithm for the Monotone Min-Plus Convolution problem that runs in $n^{1.5+o(1)}$ time, nearly matching the best-known randomized time complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1.5})$ [Chi, Duan, Xie, and Zhang, STOC’22]. This algorithm can be used to derandomize state-of-the-art algorithms for Jumbled Indexing for binary strings and several variants of Knapsack.

## 1 Introduction

One of the most fundamental problems in algorithm design is the All-Pairs Shortest Paths problem (APSP), which asks us to compute pairwise distances in an $n$ -node weighted graph. APSP is known to be asymptotically equivalent to Min-Plus product [26], where we are given two $n\times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$ and need to compute an $n\times n$ matrix $A\star B$ such that

$$ (A\star B)_{i,j}:=\min_{1\leq k\leq n}\{A_{i,k}+B_{k,j}\}. $$

The fastest known algorithm for these problems runs in $n^{3}/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time, due to Williams [29], and further improving this running time remains a major open problem. In fact, a popular hypothesis in fine-grained complexity is that APSP, or equivalently Min-Plus product, does not admit an $\mathcal{O}(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ -time algorithm for any $\varepsilon>0$ ; see [28] for a survey on fine-grained complexity.

Despite the difficulty of designing faster algorithms for Min-Plus product, researchers have identified several structured cases where it admits truly subcubic-time algorithms. For instance, bounded integer Min-Plus product, where both matrices have entries from $[M]$ 11 1 For a positive integer $m$ , $[m]$ denotes $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ . for some integer $M$ , can be computed in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(Mn^{\omega})$ time [2].22 2 In this paper, we use $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}$ to hide $n^{o(1)}$ factors and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ to hide $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log n$ factors.33 3 $\omega\leq 2.372$ [1] denotes the square matrix multiplication exponent; that is, $\omega$ is the smallest constant such that the product of two $n\times n$ matrices can be computed in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\omega})$ arithmetic operations. More generally, we use $\omega(a,b,c)$ to denote the smallest constant such that the product of an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ matrix and an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrix can be computed in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{\omega(a,b,c)})$ arithmetic operations. A generalization of bounded integer Min-Plus product is bounded difference Min-Plus product, where adjacent entries in the input matrices differ by at most $M$ . Bringmann, Grandoni, Saha, and Vassilevska Williams [6] first studied this setting and gave an $\mathcal{O}(n^{2.825})$ -time randomized algorithm and an $\mathcal{O}(n^{2.861})$ -time deterministic algorithm for the case $M=\mathcal{O}(1)$ . They used bounded difference Min-Plus product as a tool to obtain the first subcubic-time algorithms for Language Edit Distance, RNA Folding, and Optimum Stack Generation.

An important setting that further generalizes bounded difference Min-Plus product, and is the focus of this paper, is monotone Min-Plus product; see [19] for a discussion of this generalization. An $n\times n$ matrix $B$ is called row-monotone if

- • for every $1\leq i,j\leq n$ , we have $B_{i,j}\in[n]$ ;

- • for every $1\leq i\leq n$ and $1\leq j<n$ , we have $B_{i,j}\leq B_{i,j+1}$ .

Column-monotone matrices are defined analogously. The task of computing the Min-Plus product between an arbitrary integer matrix $A$ and a row-monotone matrix $B$ is called the monotone Min-Plus product problem. The importance of monotone Min-Plus product is reflected in its wide range of applications, including Language Edit Distance [6], RNA Folding [6], Optimum Stack Generation [6], Batched Range Mode [27, 19, 14], unweighted Tree Edit Distance [23, 14, 24], Single-Source Replacement Paths [19, 14], approximate APSP [13, 14, 25], and $k$ -Dyck Edit Distance [17, 14].

The fastest algorithm for monotone Min-Plus product is due to Chi, Duan, Xie, and Zhang [11] and runs in time $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{(3+\omega)/2})=\mathcal{O}(n^{2.686})$ . Unfortunately, this running time is achieved by a randomized algorithm, making the fastest algorithms for applications of monotone Min-Plus product randomized as well. More frustratingly, for many of these algorithms, the only source of randomness is the black-box call to monotone Min-Plus product; see Table 1 and Table 2 for examples. Thus, prior to our work, obtaining deterministic algorithms for these applications required replacing the randomized monotone Min-Plus product algorithm with a slower deterministic one, such as the $\mathcal{O}(n^{2.875})$ -time algorithm of [19], or the $\mathcal{O}(n^{2.861})$ -time bounded difference Min-Plus product algorithm of [6].

#### Remark.

We briefly explain how some of the randomized running times in Table 1 and Table 2 are obtained. The randomized running times for Language Edit Distance, RNA Folding, and Optimum Stack Generation in Table 1 are obtained by replacing the bounded difference Min-Plus product algorithm of [6] with the monotone Min-Plus product algorithm of [11]. For every positive integer $k$ , the algorithm of [25] for $+2k$ -approximate APSP in Table 2 runs in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}(n^{2+x/(k+1)})$ time, where $x$ is the solution to $1+2x=\omega(1-\frac{k-1}{k+1}x,1-x,1-\frac{k-2}{k+1}x)$ , and uses the monotone Min-Plus product oracle as its only source of randomness. For $2k\geq 8$ , this is the fastest known algorithm. The work of [21] improves the running times of the $+4$ - and $+6$ -approximation algorithms of [25] using deterministic algorithms, and further improves the running time for $+2$ -approximation using a randomized algorithm whose randomness comes from a source other than the monotone Min-Plus product oracle.

A problem closely related to Min-Plus product is Min-Plus convolution. In the Min-Plus convolution problem, the input consists of two length- $n$ arrays $A=(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{n})$ and $B=(B_{1},B_{2},\ldots,B_{n})$ , and the output is an array $A\diamond B$ indexed by $k=2,\dots,2n$ , where

$$ (A\diamond B)_{k}=\min_{1\leq i\leq k-1}\{A_{i}+B_{k-i}\}, $$

with out-of-bounds entries set to $\infty$ . The fastest algorithm for this problem runs in $n^{2}/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}$ time, which can be obtained by combining Williams’ APSP algorithm [29] with the reduction in [3]. A popular hypothesis in fine-grained complexity is the Min-Plus convolution hypothesis, which postulates that Min-Plus convolution cannot be solved in $\mathcal{O}(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ time for any $\varepsilon>0$ ; see [12, 22]. It is known that the Min-Plus convolution hypothesis implies the Min-Plus product hypothesis [3].

Similar to Min-Plus product, Min-Plus convolution admits significantly faster algorithms when the input is structured. A length- $n$ array $A$ is called monotone if

- • for every $1\leq i\leq n$ , we have $A_{i}\in[n]$ ;

- • for every $1\leq i<n$ , we have $A_{i}\leq A_{i+1}$ .

When both input arrays are monotone, Chan and Lewenstein [8] gave an $\mathcal{O}(n^{1.859})$ -time randomized algorithm and an $\mathcal{O}(n^{1.864})$ -time deterministic algorithm. Chi, Duan, Xie, and Zhang [11] improved the randomized running time to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1.5})$ . Bringmann, Dürr, and Polak [5] generalized this result to a randomized $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{1+\mu/2})$ -time algorithm for arrays with entries in $[n^{\mu}]$ and with only one of the input arrays being monotone.

Monotone Min-Plus convolution also has a wide range of applications. Examples include Jumbled Indexing [8], Knapsack problems with bounded weights and profits [4, 5], and weak approximation schemes for Knapsack problems [4, 10].55 5 These Knapsack results use Max-Plus convolution instead of Min-Plus convolution, but the two are equivalent up to a sign change. Due to the gap between the best-known randomized and deterministic algorithms for monotone Min-Plus convolution, the best-known running times for all these applications are achieved by randomized algorithms.
