# Furthest Pair Requires Quadratic Time in Superconstant Dimension under SETH

**Authors:** Barna Saha ††thanks: Supported by NSF HDR TRIPODS Phase II grant 2217058 (EnCORE Institute). Affiliation: University of California San Diego Email: bsaha@ucsd.edu Yinzhan Xu11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of California San Diego Email: xyzhan@ucsd.edu Christopher Ye11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of California San Diego Email: czye@ucsd.edu

## Abstract

Several fundamental problems in computational geometry admit algorithms with running time $f(d)\cdot n^{2-\Theta(1/d)}$ for $n$ points in $d$ dimensions, making them among the most prominent examples of barely subquadratic computation. Notable members of this class include Furthest Pair, Bichromatic Closest Pair, (Bichromatic) Maximum Inner Product, and Hopcroft’s Problem. Chen [Theory Comput. 2020] proved that, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), these problems require $n^{2-o(1)}$ time when the dimension satisfies $d=2^{\Theta(\log^{*}n)}$ . We extend this lower bound to all efficiently constructible dimensions $d=\omega(1)$ . Thus, assuming SETH, the dependence of the best known algorithms on the dimension is essentially unavoidable. The proof utilizes techniques in OpenAI’s recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture.

The proof was initially discovered by ChatGPT 5.5 Pro. The authors have validated and substantially edited the proof to improve the presentation.

## 1 Introduction

Furthest Pair and Closest Pair are among the most fundamental problems in computational geometry. Given a set of $n$ points in $d$ dimensions, Furthest Pair (resp. Closest Pair) asks to find a pair of points that are furthest (resp. closest) to each other in Euclidean distance. Their applications reach far beyond computational geometry [SH75, Tou83, MB02, Har01], ranging over spatial databases [CMTV00, CMTV04, GCI+16, MMC21], data mining [Epp00, NTM01, Gon85, XWL+11], computer vision [SSC08, CLS+18], and robotics [LC91, GJK88, RLMK05].

Despite analogous definitions, Closest Pair and Furthest Pair have markedly different algorithmic complexities, observed as early as 1976 [BS76]: Currently, the best algorithms for Closest Pair run in $f(d)\cdot n\log^{O(d)}(n)$ time [BS76, KM95, DHKP97] (which is truly subquadratic as long as $d=o(\log n/\log\log n)$ ), while the best algorithms for Furthest Pair run in $f(d)\cdot n^{2-\Theta(1/d)}$ time [Yao82, AESW90] (which stops being truly subquadratic for any superconstant $d$ ).

Furthest Pair is not the only fundamental problem with a $f(d)\cdot n^{2-\Theta(1/d)}$ running time. Other examples include:

- • Bichromatic Closest Pair [AESW90]. In this problem, we are given two sets of points $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ , and we need to find $a\in A,b\in B$ that minimizes $\lVert a-b\rVert_{2}$ . A priori, it may be surprising that the complexity of Bichromatic Closest Pair is more comparable to that of Furthest Pair than to that of Closest Pair. Similar to Furthest Pair and Closest Pair, Bichromatic Closest Pair is a fundamental problem with applications in various domains. In fact, some of the applications listed earlier specifically apply to this Bichromatic version of Closest Pair (e.g., [LC91, GJK88]).

- • Maximum Inner Product ( $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP) [AESW90, Yao82, Mat92]. In this problem, we are given two sets of points $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ , and we need to find $a\in A,b\in B$ that maximizes $a\cdot b$ . It is one of the central problems in similarity search with a myriad of applications [HIM12, AI08, RR07, RG12, SL14, AINR14, AIL+15, AR15, NS15, SL15, Val15, AW15, KKK18, APRS16, TG17, CP17, Chr17].

- • Hopcroft’s problem (also known as $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV) [Mat93, Cha93]. In this problem, we are given two sets of points $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ , and we need to determine whether there exists $a\in A,b\in B$ such that $a\cdot b=0$ . Hopcroft’s problem, first posed by John Hopcroft in the early 1980s, is a basic problem related to a range of computational geometry problems [Eri95]. Finding faster algorithms for Hopcroft’s problem in various settings remains an active research direction [CZ24, ABV24].

Prior work [Wil18, Che20] has studied the fine-grained hardness of these problems under the following Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis (OVH), which is known to hold under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [Wil05].

#### Definition 1.1 (OVH).

For every $\delta>0$ there is a constant $c=c(\delta)$ such that any algorithm that, given two sets of $n$ Boolean vectors in dimension $c\log n$ , determines whether there is a pair of orthogonal vectors cannot run in time $O(n^{2-\delta})$ .

Straightforward transformations [Wil05, AW15] from Orthogonal Vectors show that Furthest Pair, Bichromatic Closest Pair, Maximum Inner Product, and Hopcroft’s problem require $n^{2-o(1)}$ time when $d=\omega(\log n)$ under OVH. Williams [Wil18] improved the dependence to $d=\operatorname{poly}\log\log n$ , and Chen [Che20] further improved it to $d=2^{\Theta(\log^{*}n)}$ . However, there remained a key gap between the upper and lower bounds:

Is there a superconstant $d$ where any of Furthest Pair, Bichromatic Closest Pair, Maximum Inner Product, or Hopcroft’s problem in dimension $d$ can be solved in truly subquadratic time?

This paper resolves this gap and shows that these problems are already hard for any superconstant dimension (as long as the dimension is efficiently computable).

#### Theorem 1.2 (Informal Theorem 4.7).

Under OVH or SETH, Furthest Pair, Bichromatic Closest Pair, Maximum Inner Product, and Hopcroft’s problem (also known as $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV) require $n^{2-o(1)}$ time for any efficiently constructible dimension $d=\omega(1)$ .

Some of these problems, in particular Maximum Inner Product and Bichromatic Closest Pair, have been reduced to other problems in a black-box way, including some linear algebra problems on geometric graphs [ACSS20], dynamic detection of firing neurons [ALS+23], and attention computation [GHS+26]. Hence, Theorem 1.2 also directly implies improved lower bounds for these downstream applications.

### 1.1 Technical Overview

We now give an overview of the techniques in this work. The hardness of exact $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP, Furthest Pair and Bichromatic Closest Pair follows from reductions from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV, based on reductions in [Wil18, Che20]. See Appendix B for details. Hence, we focus on $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV.

Recall in the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV problem, we are given two sets of points $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ , and we need to determine whether there exists $x\in A,y\in B$ such that $x\cdot y=0$ . The key technical contribution of this work is to design a better reduction from OV to $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV.

Generally, such reductions proceed as follows: given Boolean vectors $x,y$ , split each $d$ -dimensional vector into $L$ blocks of size $b$ . Then map each $b$ -bit block $x^{(i)}$ in $x$ and each $b$ -bit block $y^{(i)}$ in $y$ into $w=O(1)$ integers using (efficiently computable) maps $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively. For a $d=bL$ -dimensional vector $x$ , $\alpha(x)$ applies the map $\alpha$ to each block. This way, $\alpha(x)\cdot\beta(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha(x^{(i)})\cdot\beta(y^{(i)})$ . The goal is to show the existence of a set $V$ such that

$$ \alpha(x)\cdot\beta(y)\in V\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\cdot y=0\text{.} $$

Checking membership in $V$ can be simulated by $|V|$ calls to $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV (with one extra dimension), since for a fixed $v\in V$ , $x\cdot y=v$ iff $(x,v)\cdot(y,-1)=0$ . Thus, the reduction is efficient as long as $|V|=n^{o(1)}$ and the entries of the mapped vectors are small.

Consider the first step in [Che20]’s reduction. Given $b$ distinct primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{b}>L$ , the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) gives a one-to-one correspondence $\alpha$ between $\{0,1\}^{b}$ and a subset of $[0,\prod p_{j})$ (note that in the approach, $\beta=\alpha$ ). In particular, for the $i$ -th block of $x$ , $\alpha(x^{(i)})\equiv x_{j}^{(i)}\pmod{p_{j}}$ for $j\in[b]$ , i.e. we can recover the $j$ -th bit of the $i$ -th block of $x$ from $\alpha(x^{(i)})$ modulo $p_{j}$ . In other words,

$$ \alpha(x)\cdot\alpha(y)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha(x^{(i)})\cdot\alpha(y^{(i)})\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{L}x^{(i)}_{j}y^{(i)}_{j}\pmod{p_{j}}\text{.} $$

Since the latter sum is in $[0,L]\subseteq[0,p_{j})$ , it is zero iff $\sum_{i=1}^{L}x^{(i)}_{j}y^{(i)}_{j}=0$ . In other words, $x\cdot y=0$ iff $\alpha(x)\cdot\alpha(y)\equiv 0\pmod{p_{j}}$ for all $j\in[b]$ . Furthermore, the values of the product $\alpha(x)\cdot\alpha(y)$ are at most $L\cdot\left(\prod p_{j}\right)^{2}$ so it suffices to take $V$ to be the set of integers in this range that are $0$ modulo all $p_{j}$ . Here, we note that typically (e.g. [Che20]) $|V|$ is simply bounded by the range of $\alpha(x)\cdot\alpha(y)$ . Unfortunately, since we need $b$ distinct primes, we have $\prod p_{j}=b^{\Omega(b)}$ . Thus, if we want to use the same bound $|V|\leq L(\prod p_{j})$ we need $b^{b}=n^{o(1)}$ to ensure an efficient reduction. Since $bL=d=\Theta(\log n)$ , the requirement $b^{b}=n^{o(1)}$ forces $b\log b=o(\log n)=o(bL)$ or $L=\omega(\log b)$ . The above approach establishes hardness of $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $\omega(\log\log n)$ . Through a recursive refinement of this approach, [Che20] achieves hardness for dimensions $2^{\Theta(\log^{*}n)}$ .

At a high level, the previous approach was bottlenecked by the density of primes in $\mathbb{Z}$ . In the reduction above, we use the fact that there are $b$ distinct primes bounded by $O(b\log b)$ . If, hypothetically, one had access to $b$ distinct primes bounded by a constant, then one could use CRT to map $b$ bits into integers of size $2^{O(b)}$ , which is $2^{o(bL)}=n^{o(1)}$ for any superconstant $L$ . Interestingly, a similar density barrier appears in Erdős’s $n^{1+c/\log\log n}$ lower bound of the unit distance problem [Erd46], where the relevant primes are those congruent to $1$ modulo $4$ . The breakthrough result of [Ope26] on the unit distance problem bypasses this barrier, and instead constructs number fields in which selected rational primes split into many prime ideals. Indeed, the number theory machinery of [Ope26] is exactly what allowed us to overcome the barrier faced by previous attempts to establish the hardness of $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV.

We now briefly discuss how the number theory machinery helps us achieve the desired reduction. First, a few definitions (we will try to keep these as minimal as possible). A ring is a set closed under addition and multiplication (the classical example is the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ ). An ideal is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication. An ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ is prime if whenever $ab\in\mathfrak{p}$ , either $a\in\mathfrak{p}$ or $b\in\mathfrak{p}$ . A field is a ring with multiplicative inverses (the classical example is $\mathbb{Q}$ ). A (finite) field extension is obtained by adjoining to $\mathbb{Q}$ the roots of some polynomials (for example, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ is the extension obtained by adjoining roots of $x^{2}-2$ ). Every number field is equipped with a ring of integers, the set of elements that are roots of monic polynomials with integer coefficients. If we take a prime $q\in\mathbb{Z}$ and the ideal generated by $q$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , $q$ may no longer be prime, but it factors uniquely into prime ideals (analogous to how integers have a unique prime factorization in $\mathbb{Z}$ ). A prime $q$ splits completely in $K$ if the factorization of $q$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ has (1) no repeated factors, and (2) for every factor $\mathfrak{p}$ , the residue field $\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}\cong\mathbb{F}_{q}$ . An embedding of a field extension $K$ is a homomorphism $K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ that fixes $\mathbb{Q}$ .

Proposition 3.20 shows that for any sufficiently large $b$ and $L$ , there is a degree $O(b)$ field extension $K$ , its corresponding ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ and a constant number of primes $\mathcal{Q}=\{q_{1},\dots,q_{T}\}$ , each of size $\Theta(\sqrt{L})$ satisfying:

- 1. Each $q_{t}$ splits completely into $\Theta(b)$ distinct prime ideals in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

- 2. For each $j\in[b]$ , there are two primes $q_{j,1},q_{j,2}\in\mathcal{Q}$ and corresponding prime ideal factors $\mathfrak{p}_{j,1},\mathfrak{p}_{j,2}$ .

- 3. For every bit vector $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ , there is a corresponding element $u_{a}\in K\setminus\{0\}$ such that: (a) $|\sigma(u_{a})|=1$ for every embedding $\sigma$ . (b) $Q^{2}u_{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ where $Q:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t}$ . (c) For every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ , $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a})=2a_{j}$ and $\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(c(u_{a}))=-2a_{j}$ , where $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x)$ denotes the valuation of $x$ at $\mathfrak{p}$ (roughly speaking, how many times $\mathfrak{p}$ divides $x$ )11 1 We note that a valuation can be negative. For example, in the field $\mathbb{Q}$ , $1/9=3^{-2}$ . and $c$ denotes the complex conjugation automorphism on $K$ (e.g. $i\mapsto-i$ if $K=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ ).

#### Embedding $\{0,1\}^{b}$ into $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

Our first step is to embed binary $b$ -bit vectors into the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Formally, for each prime $q_{t}$ , map $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ to $F_{t}(a):=(Q^{2}c(u_{a}))^{q_{t}-1}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .22 2 In the actual proof, we define $F_{t}$ as a map on $u_{a}$ . Define $G_{t}(a):=Q^{2}c(u_{a})$ so that $F_{t}(a)=G_{t}(a)^{q_{t}-1}$ . Define $K_{t}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{L}F_{t}(x^{(i)})F_{t}(y^{(i)})$ . If $x\cdot y=0$ and $u\cdot v>0$ , then we claim $K_{t}(x,y)\neq K_{t}(u,v)$ for some $t$ . Note that if we apply the map $F_{t}$ to each block, the dot product of the resulting vector is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}F_{t}(x^{(i)})F_{t}(y^{(i)})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}K_{t}(x,y)\text{.} $$

By additivity of valuations33 3 In general, $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(xy)=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x)+\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(y)$ and $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x+y)\geq\min(\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x),\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(y))$ . and 3(c) above,

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(G_{t}(x^{(i)})G_{t}(y^{(i)}))=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(Q^{4}c(u_{x^{(i)}})c(u_{y^{(i)}}))=2(2-x^{(i)}_{j}-y^{(i)}_{j}) $$

where $x^{(i)}_{j}$ is the $j$ -th bit of $x^{(i)}$ , i.e. the valuation is $0$ iff $x^{(i)}_{j}y^{(i)}_{j}=1$ (see Lemma 3.21). In other words, if $x,y$ are orthogonal, then every prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ divides $G_{t}(x^{(i)})G_{t}(y^{(i)})$ for all $i\in[L]$ , while if $x,y$ are not orthogonal, say $x^{(i)}_{j}y^{(i)}_{j}=1$ , then some prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ does not divide $G_{t}(x^{(i)})G_{t}(y^{(i)})$ . In the residue field $\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}\cong\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ ,44 4 Here we use the fact that $q_{t}$ splits completely. we have $G_{t}(x^{(i)})G_{t}(y^{(i)})\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}$ for all $i,j$ in the former case and non-zero for some $i,j$ in the latter case.

We now examine $K_{t}$ . When $x,y$ are orthogonal, $F_{t}(x^{(i)})F_{t}(y^{(i)})\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}$ for all selected prime ideals so that $K_{t}(x,y)\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}$ . When $x,y$ are not orthogonal, Fermat’s Little Theorem implies that $F_{t}(x^{(i)})F_{t}(y^{(i)})\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}$ for some $i,j$ , since any non-zero element taken to the $(q_{t}-1)$ -th power in $\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ is $1$ . For such a $j\in[b]$ , let

$$ 0<k:=|\{i\mid x_{j}^{(i)}=y_{j}^{(i)}=1\}|\leq L $$

denote the number of blocks where the $j$ -th bit is not orthogonal. Since $q_{j,1}q_{j,2}>L\geq k$ at least one of $q_{j,1},q_{j,2}$ will not divide $k$ . In particular, since each non-zero coordinate contributes $1$ and the remaining terms contribute $0$ , we have $K_{t}(x,y)\equiv k\not\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}$ for the corresponding prime $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ lying above $q_{j,r}\nmid k$ .

#### Embedding $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ into $\mathbb{C}$ .

Next, we embed $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ into $\mathbb{C}$ via $\sigma$ , with the guarantee that $K_{t}(x,y)\neq K_{t}(u,v)$ implies that $|\sigma(K_{t}(x,y))-\sigma(K_{t}(u,v))|\geq\exp(-O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ , i.e. distinct elements in the ring of integers are mapped to sufficiently separated elements of $\mathbb{C}$ (Lemma 3.23). As before, note that if we apply $\sigma$ entry-wise, the resulting dot product of the mapped vectors is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma(F_{t}(x^{(i)}))\sigma(F_{t}(y^{(i)}))=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sigma(K_{t}(x,y))\text{.} $$

Fix $\Delta:=K_{t}(x,y)-K_{t}(u,v)$ . First, observe that any embedding is not too large:

$$ |\sigma(F_{t}(a))|=Q^{2(q_{t}-1)}|\sigma(c(u_{a}))|^{q_{t}-1}=Q^{2(q_{t}-1)}=\exp(O(\sqrt{L}\log L)) $$

since $\sigma(c(u_{a}))=\overline{\sigma(u_{a})}$ has absolute value $1$ and $Q$ is the product of $O(1)$ primes in the range $\Theta(\sqrt{L})$ . A similar bound holds for $\Delta$ .

To conclude, we claim that the product $\prod_{\sigma}|\sigma(\Delta)|$ over all embeddings $\sigma$ is a non-zero integer (i.e. at least $1$ ). Note that this immediately ensures $|\sigma(\Delta)|\geq\exp(-O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ for any embedding $\sigma$ , since the number of embeddings is equal to the degree of $K$ , or $O(b)$ . To bound the product, we note that $\Delta\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. In particular, the product of all its embeddings is (up to sign) a power of the constant coefficient, an integer.

#### Embedding $\mathbb{C}$ into $\mathbb{Z}$ .

So far, we have mapped each block of $b$ bits into $T$ -dimensional vectors in $\mathbb{C}$ via $\sigma(F_{t}(a))$ with the guarantee that $|\sigma(K_{t}(x,y))-\sigma(K_{t}(u,v))|\geq\delta:=\exp(-O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ for some $t$ whenever $0=x\cdot y<u\cdot v$ . For each $q_{t}$ , we construct maps $f_{t},g_{t}:\mathbb{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{4}$ such that $f_{t}(x)\cdot g_{t}(y)\simeq M^{2t}\operatorname{Re}(N^{2}xy)+M^{2t+1}\operatorname{Im}(N^{2}xy)$ for some sufficiently large $N\gg 1/\delta$ and $M$ . (Here, note that we will not be able to define $f_{t},g_{t}$ to equal the right-hand side exactly, since $xy$ may not be integral, but they will be close to the desired value up to rounding error. We will ignore the rounding errors and treat the above equality as exact in this overview.) If we apply $f_{t},g_{t}$ entry-wise to the $L$ coordinates corresponding to prime $q_{t}$ , then the dot product of the resulting $\mathbb{Z}$ -vectors is

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{L}\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(\sigma(F_{t}(x^{(i)})))\cdot g_{t}(\sigma(F_{t}(y^{(i)})))=\sum_{t=1}^{T}M^{2t}\operatorname{Re}(N^{2}\sigma(K_{t}(x,y)))+M^{2t+1}\operatorname{Im}(N^{2}\sigma(K_{t}(x,y)))\text{.} $$

Now, we observe that $|N^{2}\sigma(K_{t}(x,y))|=\operatorname{poly}(1/\delta)\cdot L^{O(\sqrt{L})}=\exp(O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ so that if we set $M\gg\exp(O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ , we can recover the individual summands from the dot product. By setting $N\gg 1/\delta$ , we can see that either the real parts or imaginary parts of $N^{2}\sigma(K_{t}(x,y))$ and $N^{2}\sigma(K_{t}(u,v))$ will disagree if $|\sigma(K_{t}(x,y))-\sigma(K_{t}(u,v))|\geq\delta$ .

Thus, combined with our previous guarantees, we can ensure that (1) the images of vector pairs with $x\cdot y=0$ and $u\cdot v>0$ are disjoint, and (2) the entries of the vectors, the size of the possible dot products, and the output set $V$ have size bounded by $\exp(O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ . In particular, we can reduce OV to $\exp(O(b\sqrt{L}\log L))$ instances of $O(L)$ -dimensional $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV.

## 2 Preliminaries

Given a field $K$ , let $K^{\times}$ denote its multiplicative group. Given a real number $x\in\mathbb{R}$ , we let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denote its floor, $\lceil x\rceil$ its ceiling, and $\lfloor x\rceil$ its nearest integer. For a complex number $z$ , let $\operatorname{Re}(z)$ denote its real part and $\operatorname{Im}(z)$ its imaginary part. Throughout the paper, we use $\log$ to denote natural logarithm.

We define constructible dimension functions. Formally, to ensure that our reduction is efficient, we require that the number of dimensions in the constructed $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV instance can be computed efficiently.

#### Definition 2.1 (Constructible dimension function).

A function $D:\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$ is constructible if $D(n)$ can be computed exactly in $n^{o(1)}$ time.

We use the following standard tools from number theory.

#### Theorem 2.2 (Prime Number Theorem).

Let $\pi(n)$ denote the number of primes $\leq n$ . Then,

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\pi(n)}{n/\log n}=1\text{.} $$

#### Theorem 2.3 (Chinese Remainder Theorem).

Given $d$ pairwise co-prime integers $q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{d}$ , and $d$ integers $r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{d}$ , there is exactly one integer $0\leq t<\prod_{i=1}^{d}q_{i}$ such that

$$ t\equiv r_{i}\pmod{q_{i}}\text{ for all }i\in[d]\text{.} $$

We call this the Chinese remainder representation (or the $\operatorname{CRR}$ encoding) of the $r_{i}$ ’s (with respect to these $q_{i}$ ’s). We also denote

$$ t=\operatorname{CRR}(\{r_{i}\};\{q_{i}\}) $$

for convenience. We sometimes omit the sequence $\{q_{i}\}$ for simplicity, when it is clear from the context. Moreover, $t$ can be computed in polynomial time with respect to the total bits of all the given integers.

## 3 An Improved Local Reduction to $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV

The goal of this section is to obtain a better reduction to $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV. We formally state the required reduction below.

#### Lemma 3.1.

There exist absolute constants $K_{0},L_{0},w_{0}$ such that for all integers $b\geq 1$ and $L\geq L_{0}$ , there exist functions $\alpha,\beta:\{0,1\}^{b}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{w_{0}}$ and $V\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ satisfying the following properties. Let $B=\lceil L^{K_{0}b\sqrt{L}}\rceil$ . Then:

- 1. (Entry Bound) For all $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ and $k\in[w_{0}]$ , $\alpha(a)_{k},\beta(a)_{k}<B$ and for all $v\in V$ , $v\leq B$ . Also, $|V|\leq B$ .

- 2. (Product Bound) For all $x,y\in\{0,1\}^{bL}$ , let $x_{i},y_{i}$ denote the $i$ -th block of size $b$ in $x,y$ respectively. Then

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha(x_{i})\cdot\beta(y_{i})\leq B $$

- 3. (Correctness) For all $x,y\in\{0,1\}^{bL}$ and $x_{i},y_{i}$ as above,

$$ x\cdot y=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha(x_{i})\cdot\beta(y_{i})\in V\text{.} $$

For clarity, we will occasionally denote $\alpha,\beta,V$ as $\alpha_{b,L},\beta_{b,L},V_{b,L}$ to make the dependence on $b,L$ explicit. Lemma 3.1 has been formally verified in Lean 4 (see Appendix C for details).

### 3.1 Number Theory Preliminaries

We begin with several standard notions from algebraic number theory, with some simple examples to illustrate the definitions.

#### Definition 3.2 (Number field).

A number field is a finite-dimensional field extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$ . Its degree, denoted $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ , is the dimension of $K$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$ .

As an example $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})=\{a+b\sqrt{2}\mid a,b\in\mathbb{Q}\}$ is a degree-2 extension (also called a quadratic extension). $\mathbb{Q}(2^{1/3})$ is a degree-3 extension (also called a cubic extension).

#### Definition 3.3 (Real embedding).

An embedding of $K/\mathbb{Q}$ into $\mathbb{C}$ is a homomorphism $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ that fixes $\mathbb{Q}$ . An embedding is real if its image is contained in the real numbers: $\sigma(K)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and complex otherwise.

#### Definition 3.4 (Totally real and totally imaginary field).

A number field $K$ is totally real if every embedding $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is real. A number field $K$ is totally imaginary if every embedding $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is complex.

For example, $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ is totally real (an embedding must send $\sqrt{2}$ to $\sqrt{2}$ or $-\sqrt{2}$ ), while $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is totally imaginary ( $i$ must be mapped to $i$ or $-i$ ).

#### Definition 3.5 (Infinite Place).

An infinite place of $K/\mathbb{Q}$ into $\mathbb{C}$ is an equivalence class of embeddings $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ , where two embeddings $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are equivalent if $\tau=\sigma$ or $\tau=\overline{\sigma}$ . An infinite place is real if $\sigma(K)\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ for one (equivalently every) representative embedding $\sigma$ and complex otherwise.

We observe that for a real place, the equivalence class consists of one homomorphism, since $\sigma_{1}=\overline{\sigma_{2}}$ implies $\sigma_{1}=\sigma_{2}$ . For a complex place, the equivalence class consists of two homomorphisms that are complex conjugates of each other. For a field extension $K/L$ , we say an infinite place $w$ of $K$ lies above an infinite place $v$ of $L$ if the restriction to $L$ of any representative of $w$ represents the place $v$ .

#### Lemma 3.6 ([Mil03, Proposition 2.1(b)]).

Let $K/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite extension of degree $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ . Then, there are exactly $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$ .

#### Definition 3.7 (CM field ([Ope26, Definition A.4])).

A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension $K/L$ of a totally real field. The nontrivial automorphism of $K/L$ , also known as the complex conjugation automorphism, is denoted $c$ . If $K=L(i)$ with $L$ totally real, then for every complex embedding $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ , $\sigma(c(\alpha))=\overline{\sigma(\alpha)}$ .

For example $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is a CM field and the complex conjugation automorphism maps $i$ to $-i$ . When $K=L(i)$ with $L$ totally real, since $\sigma(c(c(\alpha)))=\sigma(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ is an automorphism, we have $c(c(\alpha))=\alpha$ is the identity map.

#### Definition 3.8 (Ring of integers).

Let $K$ be a number field. Its ring of integers is

$$ \mathcal{O}_{K}=\{x\in K:x\text{ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in }\mathbb{Z}\}. $$

For example, $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{Z}$ .

#### Definition 3.9 (Ideal).

Given a ring $R$ , a subset $I\subseteq R$ is an ideal if: (i) $a+b\in I$ for all $a,b\in I$ and (ii) $ra\in I$ for all $r\in R$ and $a\in I$ . An ideal is proper if $I\subsetneq R$ . An ideal is principal if it is generated by a single element.

Given two ideals $I,J\subseteq R$ , their product $IJ$ is the ideal generated by $\{ab\mid a\in I,b\in J\}$ .

#### Definition 3.10 (Prime and Maximal ideals).

A proper ideal $I\subsetneq R$ is prime if for all $a,b\in R$ , $ab\in I$ implies that $a\in I$ or $b\in I$ . A proper ideal $I\subsetneq R$ is maximal if there is no proper ideal $I^{\prime}$ satisfying $I\subsetneq I^{\prime}\subsetneq R$ .

For an ideal $I$ , we say that a prime ideal $P$ divides $I$ if $I\subseteq P$ . Since rings of integers of number fields are Dedekind Domains (see e.g. Theorem 3.29 of [Mil20]), every ideal factors uniquely into a product of prime ideals. We use the following standard fact regarding prime ideals of the ring of integers.

#### Fact 3.11 (Theorem 3.1 of [Neu13]).

Every non-zero prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is maximal. Since quotients by maximal ideals are fields, $\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}$ is a field.

To distinguish prime ideals and prime numbers, we say a prime $q$ is rational if $q\in\mathbb{Z}$ . In a number field $K$ , the ideal generated by $q$ in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is denoted $q\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Note that $q\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is not necessarily a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For an extension $K/L$ and prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{L}$ , observe that if a prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}$ lies above the ideal generated by $\mathfrak{p}$ , denoted $\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , then since $\mathfrak{p}\subseteq\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathcal{O}_{L}$ , $\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathcal{O}_{L}$ is prime and therefore equal to $\mathfrak{p}$ .

#### Definition 3.12 (Local ring).

Let $K$ be a number field and let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . The local ring of $K$ at $\mathfrak{p}$ is

$$ \mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}:=\left\{\frac{a}{b}:a,b\in\mathcal{O}_{K},\;b\notin\mathfrak{p}\right\}\text{.} $$

#### Definition 3.13 (Residue field).

If $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , the field $\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}$ is the residue field of $\mathfrak{p}$ .

From Chapter 1 Corollary 11.2 of [Neu13], we have for any prime (and therefore maximal) ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ , an isomorphism $\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}/\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}$ .

#### Definition 3.14 (Residue degree).

Let $K$ be a number field and let $q$ be a rational prime. For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ above $q$ , the residue degree of $\mathfrak{p}$ over $q$ is $f(\mathfrak{p}\mid q):=[\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}:\mathbf{F}_{q}]$ .

#### Definition 3.15 (Splitting completely (as in Definition A.2 of [Ope26])).

Let $q$ be a rational prime. We say that $q$ is unramified in $K$ if

$$ q\mathcal{O}_{K}=\prod_{i=1}^{g}\mathfrak{p}_{i}^{e(\mathfrak{p}_{i}|q)}\text{.} $$

where the prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_{i}$ are distinct and the exponents (called ramification indices) $e(\mathfrak{p}_{i}|q)=1$ . We say $q$ splits completely if it further satisfies $g=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ or equivalently $f(\mathfrak{p}_{i}|q)=1$ i.e. each residue field is

$$ \mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}_{i}\cong\mathbb{F}_{q}\text{.} $$

As an example, $7$ splits completely in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2})$ , since $(3+\sqrt{2})(3-\sqrt{2})\equiv 0\pmod{7}$ . Furthermore, for the prime ideal $(7,3-\sqrt{2})$ , we can see that any element in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is $a+b\sqrt{2}\equiv a+3b\pmod{(7,3-\sqrt{2})}$ and thus an element of $\mathbb{F}_{7}$ . The following definition will only be used in Appendix A but we state it here as it depends on the above definitions.

#### Definition 3.16 (Definition A.2 of [Ope26]).

An infinite ramification of an extension $K/F$ is a real place $v:F\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that there is a complex place $w:K\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ lying above $v$ . An extension $K/F$ is everywhere unramified if there is no finite ramification (i.e. all finite primes of $F$ are unramified) and no infinite ramification.

We require some additional preliminaries regarding prime ideals.

#### Definition 3.17 (Conjugate prime ideals).

Let $c$ be the complex conjugation automorphism of a CM field $K$ . If $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , then $c\mathfrak{p}=\{c(x)\mid x\in\mathfrak{p}\}$ is also a prime ideal. The pair $\{\mathfrak{p},c\mathfrak{p}\}$ is called a conjugate pair of prime ideals.

The fact that prime ideals are preserved under automorphism is standard in commutative algebra (see e.g. Chapter 1 of [Neu13] or [AM18]).

#### Definition 3.18 (Valuation at a prime ideal (see e.g. Chapter 3 of [Mil20])).

Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For a nonzero element $x\in K^{\times}$ , the valuation $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x)$ is the exponent of $\mathfrak{p}$ appearing in the factorization of the principal ideal $(x)$ .

For example, if $q$ splits completely, then $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(q)=1$ for all $\mathfrak{p}$ dividing $q$ and $0$ otherwise. Note that valuation satisfies:

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(xy)=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x)+\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(y)\text{, }\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x+y)\geq\min(\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x),\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(y))\text{.} $$

We will require the following standard lemma.

#### Lemma 3.19.

Let $K$ be a CM field with complex conjugation automorphism $c$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Then, for any $z\in K^{\times}$ ,

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(c(z))=\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{p}}(z)\text{.} $$

#### Proof of Lemma 3.19.

Consider the unique factorization of $(z)$ into prime ideals:

$$ (z)=\prod_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}\mathfrak{p}_{i}^{\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}(z)}\text{.} $$

Applying the automorphism $c$ we have

$$ (c(z))=c((z))=\prod_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}(c\mathfrak{p}_{i})^{\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}(z)} $$

where each $(c\mathfrak{p}_{i})$ is a prime ideal. In particular, we have $\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{p}_{i}}(c(z))=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{i}}(z)$ . Observe that $c=c^{-1}$ (see discussion below Definition 3.7). Setting $\mathfrak{p}:=(c\mathfrak{p}_{i})$ , we have $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(c(z))=\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{p}}(z)$ , for any $\mathfrak{p}$ with nonzero valuation in $(c(z))$ . Otherwise, if $\mathfrak{p}$ has zero valuation in $(c(z))$ , then $c\mathfrak{p}$ also has zero valuation in $(z)$ , preserving the equality. ∎

### 3.2 Proof of Lemma 3.1

We will prove Lemma 3.1 assuming the following Proposition 3.20, with all necessary preliminaries introduced above. This section contains a proof of Lemma 3.1 assuming Proposition 3.20. See Appendix A for a proof of Proposition 3.20.

#### Proposition 3.20 (Medium-Prime Norm-One Codebook).

There exist absolute constants $C_{0}>0$ and $T\geq 16$ such that the following holds for all sufficiently large $L$ and $b$ . Put $Y:=\left\lceil 4\sqrt{L}\right\rceil$ . There exist:

- (i) a CM field $K$ with complex conjugation $c$ and degree $[K:\mathbb{Q}]\leq C_{0}b$ ;

- (ii) $T$ distinct rational primes $q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}\in[Y,2Y]$ , each splitting completely in $K$ , and $Q:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t}$ ;

- (iii) for each block bit $j\in[b]$ , two prime ideals

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{j,1},\mathfrak{p}_{j,2}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K} $$

lying above two distinct rational primes $q_{j,1},q_{j,2}\in\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}\}$ , with $q_{j,1}q_{j,2}>L$ ;

- (iv) for every $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ , an element $u_{a}\in K^{\times}$ ;

with the following properties. For every $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle u_{a}c(u_{a}) \displaystyle=1, \displaystyle|\sigma(u_{a})| \displaystyle=1\quad\text{for every complex embedding }\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}, \displaystyle Q^{2}u_{a} \displaystyle\in\mathcal{O}_{K}. $$

Moreover, for every selected prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a}) \displaystyle=2a_{j} \displaystyle\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a}) \displaystyle=-2a_{j}\text{.} $$

Because each selected rational prime splits completely in $K$ , one also has

$$ \mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}\cong\mathbb{F}_{q_{j,r}}. $$

Fix parameters $b,L$ with $L$ sufficiently large and let $K,q_{1},\dots,q_{T}$ be guaranteed by Proposition 3.20. Let

$$ E_{t}:=q_{t}-1\qquad(t=1,\ldots,T). $$

Since $q_{t}=\Theta(\sqrt{L})$ and $T$ is constant,

$$ Q=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t}=L^{O(1)},\qquad Q^{O(E_{t})}=\exp(O(\sqrt{L}\log L)). $$

For a block $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ , let $u_{a}$ be guaranteed by Proposition 3.20 and define

$$ F_{t}(a):=Q^{2E_{t}}\,c(u_{a}^{E_{t}})\in K. $$

By (1), we have $Q^{2}u_{a}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ and therefore $c(Q^{2}u_{a})=Q^{2}c(u_{a})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ since $c$ is an embedding fixing $\mathbb{Q}$ and therefore $Q^{2}$ . In particular, $F_{t}(a)=Q^{2E_{t}}c(u_{a})^{E_{t}}=(Q^{2}c(u_{a}))^{E_{t}}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For block vectors

$$ x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L}),\qquad y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L}),\qquad x_{i},y_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{b}, $$

define

$$ K_{t}(x,y):=\sum_{i=1}^{L}F_{t}(x_{i})F_{t}(y_{i})\in\mathcal{O}_{K}\text{.} $$

#### Lemma 3.21 (Valuation Table).

Let $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ lie above the rational prime $q_{t}$ . Then, for every block $a$ ,

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(F_{t}(a))=2E_{t}(1-a_{j}). $$

Consequently, for any blocks $a,b$ ,

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(F_{t}(a)F_{t}(b))=2E_{t}(2-a_{j}-b_{j}). $$

In particular, this product has valuation $0$ exactly when $a_{j}=b_{j}=1$ , and has valuation at least $2E_{t}$ otherwise.

#### Proof.

Since the rational prime $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ , it is unramified; hence $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(q_{t})=1$ . For any other rational prime $q$ dividing $Q$ , we claim $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(q)=0$ so that $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(Q)=1$ . This follows as $\gcd(q,q_{t})=1$ so that Bezout’s identity guarantees integers $a,b$ such that $aq+bq_{t}=1$ . In other words, if $q,q_{t}\in\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ , then $\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ is not a proper ideal, a contradiction. By (3) and Lemma 3.19,

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(c(u_{a}))=-2a_{j}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(F_{t}(a))=E_{t}(2\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(Q)+\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(c(u_{a})))=E_{t}(2-2a_{j})=2E_{t}(1-a_{j})\text{.} $$

The product formula follows by additivity of valuations. ∎

#### Lemma 3.22 (Multi-Characteristic Anti-Cancellation).

For $x,y\in\{0,1\}^{bL}$ , written in $L$ blocks of length $b$ , the following are equivalent:

$$ x\cdot y=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{for all }t\text{ and all selected }\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}\mid q_{t},\;\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(K_{t}(x,y))\geq 2E_{t}. $$

In particular, if $x\cdot y=0$ and $x^{\prime}\cdot y^{\prime}>0$ , then

$$ (K_{1}(x,y),\ldots,K_{T}(x,y))\neq(K_{1}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\ldots,K_{T}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})). $$

#### Proof.

If $x\cdot y=0$ , then for every block $i\in[L]$ and bit $j\in[b]$ we never have $x_{i,j}=y_{i,j}=1$ . By Lemma 3.21, every summand $F_{t}(x_{i})F_{t}(y_{i})$ has valuation at least $2E_{t}$ at every selected prime over $q_{t}$ . Hence the sum $K_{t}(x,y)$ has valuation at least $2E_{t}$ at every such prime, since the valuation of the sum is at least the minimum of the valuations (see discussion below Definition 3.18).

Conversely suppose $x\cdot y>0$ . Then there exists a bit $j$ for which

$$ k:=\#\{i\in[L]:x_{i,j}=y_{i,j}=1\} $$

satisfies $1\leq k\leq L$ . The bit $j$ has two selected prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}_{j,1},\mathfrak{p}_{j,2}$ lying over distinct rational primes $q_{j,1}$ and $q_{j,2}$ with $q_{j,1}q_{j,2}>L$ . Therefore $k$ is not divisible by at least one of $q_{j,1},q_{j,2}$ (otherwise $k\geq q_{j,1}q_{j,2}$ ). Choose such a prime and write it as $q_{t}$ , with corresponding selected prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}$ .

For a bad block, $a_{j}=1$ , Lemma 3.21 implies that the element $F_{t}(a)$ has valuation $0$ at $\mathfrak{p}$ . Since $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ and $\mathfrak{p}$ lies above $q_{t}$ , we also have $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(q_{t})=1$ . Furthermore, since $a_{j}=1$ , Proposition 3.20 gives

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a}))=2\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(q_{t})+\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(c(u_{a}))=2-2a_{j}=0\text{.} $$

Next, we claim $q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a})$ is in the local ring $\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}$ . Write $Q=q_{t}Q^{\prime}$ so that $Q^{\prime}\not\in\mathfrak{p}$ (as argued in Lemma 3.21, $\mathfrak{p}$ does not divide any other rational prime in $Q$ ) and $(Q^{\prime})^{2}\not\in\mathfrak{p}$ . Then, $q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a})=(Q^{2}c(u_{a}))/(Q^{\prime})^{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}$ . Since the valuation of $q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a})$ at $\mathfrak{p}$ is $0$ , we also have $q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a})\in\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}^{\times}$ and has a well-defined nonzero residue modulo $\mathfrak{p}$ . Reducing modulo $\mathfrak{p}$ and observing that $\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}/\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{O}_{K,\mathfrak{p}}\simeq\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}\simeq\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ since $q_{t}$ splits completely, we have that $q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a})$ is a non-zero element in $\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ . Fermat’s Little Theorem then implies that

$$ (q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a}))^{E_{t}}\equiv(q_{t}^{2}c(u_{a}))^{q_{t}-1}\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{p}}\text{.} $$

Also $(Q^{\prime})^{2E_{t}}\equiv((Q^{\prime})^{E_{t}})^{2}\equiv 1^{2}\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{p}}$ . Hence $F_{t}(a)\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{p}}$ , and similarly $F_{t}(b)\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{p}}$ for the right block $b$ when $b_{j}=1$ . Thus every bad product satisfies

$$ F_{t}(a)F_{t}(b)\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{p}}. $$

The other summands are divisible by $\mathfrak{p}$ , since the valuation is at least $2E_{t}$ . Therefore

$$ K_{t}(x,y)\equiv k\pmod{\mathfrak{p}}. $$

Since the residue characteristic is $q_{t}$ and $q_{t}\nmid k$ , this residue is nonzero. Hence

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(K_{t}(x,y))=0<2E_{t}. $$

This proves the equivalence and the separation of orthogonal from nonorthogonal algebraic value vectors. ∎

#### 3.2.1 Constructing the Reduction

We now proceed to describe the reduction. First, we embed binary vectors into the complex vectors with entries in $\mathbb{C}$ . Fix one complex embedding $\sigma:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ . For $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ , set

$$ z_{t}(a):=\sigma(F_{t}(a)). $$

Then

$$ \sigma(K_{t}(x,y))=\sum_{i=1}^{L}z_{t}(x_{i})z_{t}(y_{i}). $$

Because $|\tau(u_{a})|=1$ for every embedding $\tau$ , (4) gives an absolute constant $C_{2}$ such that

$$ |\tau(F_{t}(a))|\leq\exp(C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L) $$

for every $t,a,\tau$ .

#### Lemma 3.23 (Product-Formula Separation).

There is an absolute constant $C_{3}$ such that if

$$ (K_{1}(x,y),\ldots,K_{T}(x,y))\neq(K_{1}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}),\ldots,K_{T}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})), $$

then, for some $t$ ,

$$ |\sigma(K_{t}(x,y)-K_{t}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}))|\geq\exp(-C_{3}b\sqrt{L}\log L). $$

#### Proof.

Choose $t$ with $\Delta:=K_{t}(x,y)-K_{t}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\neq 0$ . By construction $\Delta\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For every embedding $\tau$ ,

$$ |\tau(\Delta)|\leq 2L\exp(2C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L)\leq\exp(C_{4}\sqrt{L}\log L) $$

for large $L$ after enlarging $C_{4}$ .

We now define the field norm, $\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x):=\prod_{\tau:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}}\tau(x)$ , where the product is taken over all embeddings $\tau$ . From Lemma 3.6, there are $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ such embeddings. We claim that $\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(x)\in\mathbb{Z}$ for any $x\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Since $x\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , $x$ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}$ , e.g. $x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_{0}=0$ . Let $m_{x}$ denote the minimal polynomial with degree $n$ . We claim that each root of $m_{x}$ appears equally often in the set $\{\tau(x)\}$ . In particular, the product of $\tau(x)$ over all $\tau$ is $(-1)^{w}a_{0}^{v}$ for some integers $w,v$ , and therefore an integer. To see this, let $\alpha$ be a root of $m_{x}$ . By Proposition 2.1(b) of [Mil03], $\alpha$ determines an embedding

$$ \rho_{\alpha}:\mathbb{Q}(x)\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C},\qquad x\mapsto\alpha\text{.} $$

Since $K=\mathbb{Q}(x)(\gamma)$ (see e.g. Theorem 5.1 of [Mil03] and Definition A.2 for the required definition of separable) for some $\gamma\in K$ , applying Proposition 2.12 of [Mil03] to the extension $K/\mathbb{Q}(x)$ shows that $\rho_{\alpha}$ extends to exactly $[K:\mathbb{Q}(x)]$ embeddings $K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ . Hence each root $\alpha$ of $m_{x}$ occurs exactly $[K:\mathbb{Q}(x)]$ times among the values $\tau(x)$ .

Since $\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Delta)$ is a nonzero integer,

$$ 1\leq|\operatorname{N}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Delta)|=\prod_{\tau:K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}}|\tau(\Delta)|. $$

Here the product is over all $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ complex embeddings, counted individually rather than by conjugate pairs. Isolating the fixed embedding $\sigma$ and bounding every other factor by the displayed Archimedean upper bound gives

$$ |\sigma(\Delta)|\geq\exp(-C_{4}([K:\mathbb{Q}]-1)\sqrt{L}\log L). $$

The degree of $K$ is $O(b)$ by Proposition 3.20, so

$$ |\sigma(\Delta)|\geq\exp(-C_{3}b\sqrt{L}\log L) $$

for a suitable absolute constant $C_{3}$ . ∎

We now map the binary vectors into $\mathbb{Z}$ -vectors.

#### Proposition 3.24 (Nonuniform Finite Integer Block Gadget).

There are absolute constants $C_{5}$ and $L_{*}\geq 2$ such that, for every $b\geq 1$ and every $L\geq L_{*}$ , there exist two blockwise maps

$$ \Phi_{A},\Phi_{B}:\{0,1\}^{bL}\to\mathbb{Z}^{r},\qquad r=O(L), $$

and a finite set $V_{b,L}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ such that

$$ x\cdot y=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Phi_{A}(x)\cdot\Phi_{B}(y)\in V_{b,L}. $$

Here blockwise means that there are local maps $\alpha_{b,L},\beta_{b,L}:\{0,1\}^{b}\to\mathbb{Z}^{w}$ , with $w=O(1)$ , such that

$$ \Phi_{A}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L})=(\alpha_{b,L}(x_{1}),\ldots,\alpha_{b,L}(x_{L})) $$

and similarly for $\Phi_{B}$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\|\Phi_{A}(x)\|_{\infty},\;\|\Phi_{B}(y)\|_{\infty},\;\max_{v\in V_{b,L}}|v| \displaystyle\leq 2^{C_{5}b\sqrt{L}\log L}, \displaystyle|V_{b,L}| \displaystyle\leq 2^{C_{5}b\sqrt{L}\log L}\text{.} $$

#### Proof.

Let $b_{*}$ be the finite threshold in Proposition 3.20. Choose once and for all an absolute $L_{*}$ dominating the $L$ -threshold in Proposition 3.20, the prime-number-theorem threshold needed in the finite fallback below, and the finitely many lower bounds on $L$ used in the rounding inequalities. We prove the claim for $L\geq L_{*}$ . We split into two cases.

#### Case 1: $b<b_{*}$ .

If $b<b_{*}$ , we use the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) to directly construct the required maps. Since $b<b_{*}$ is constant, the Prime Number Theorem implies that the interval $(L,2L]$ contains at least $b_{*}$ primes. Choose $b$ distinct primes

$$ p_{1},\ldots,p_{b}\in(L,2L]. $$

Then

$$ P:=\prod_{j=1}^{b}p_{j}\leq(2L)^{b}\leq L^{Cb} $$

for an absolute constant $C$ depending only on $b_{*}$ . For a block $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ , let $t(a)\in[0,P)$ be the CRR encoding with $t(a)\equiv a_{j}\pmod{p_{j}}$ for all $j\in[b]$ . Put one local coordinate on each side, $\alpha(a)=\beta(a)=t(a)$ . Then for full block vectors,

$$ D(x,y):=\sum_{i=1}^{L}t(x_{i})t(y_{i}) $$

satisfies $D(x,y)\equiv\sum_{i}x_{i,j}y_{i,j}\pmod{p_{j}}$ . For each fixed $j$ , the integer

$$ s_{j}:=\sum_{i=1}^{L}x_{i,j}y_{i,j} $$

lies in $[0,L]$ . Because $p_{j}>L$ , the congruence $s_{j}\equiv 0\pmod{p_{j}}$ is therefore equivalent to $s_{j}=0$ . Hence

$$ D(x,y)\equiv 0\pmod{P}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s_{j}=0\text{ for every }j\in[b]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\cdot y=0. $$

Taking

$$ V=\{z\in[0,LP^{2}]\cap\mathbb{Z}:z\equiv 0\pmod{P}\} $$

gives coordinate, value, and cardinality bounds $L^{O(b)}$ , which are stronger than the claimed $2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}$ for sufficiently large $L$ . Hence we may assume $b\geq b_{*}$ and use the arithmetic construction.

#### Case 2: $b\geq b_{*}$ .

Let

$$ N:=\left\lceil\exp(C_{6}b\sqrt{L}\log L)\right\rceil $$

with $C_{6}$ sufficiently large. For every $t$ and block $a$ , define integers

$$ X_{t}(a):=\lfloor N\operatorname{Re}(z_{t}(a))\rceil,\qquad Y_{t}(a):=\lfloor N\operatorname{Im}(z_{t}(a))\rceil. $$

For two blocks $a,b^{\prime}$ (we use $b^{\prime}$ to avoid confusion with the parameter $b$ ), define

$$ \displaystyle R_{t}(a,b^{\prime}) \displaystyle:=X_{t}(a)X_{t}(b^{\prime})-Y_{t}(a)Y_{t}(b^{\prime}), \displaystyle I_{t}(a,b^{\prime}) \displaystyle:=X_{t}(a)Y_{t}(b^{\prime})+Y_{t}(a)X_{t}(b^{\prime}). $$

These are rounded versions of $N^{2}\operatorname{Re}(z_{t}(a)z_{t}(b^{\prime}))$ and $N^{2}\operatorname{Im}(z_{t}(a)z_{t}(b^{\prime}))$ . Indeed, write

$$ X_{t}(a)=N\operatorname{Re}(z_{t}(a))+\xi_{a},\qquad Y_{t}(a)=N\operatorname{Im}(z_{t}(a))+\eta_{a}, $$

with $|\xi_{a}|,|\eta_{a}|\leq 1/2$ , and similarly for $b^{\prime}$ . Using (5), for each block pair

$$ \displaystyle|R_{t}(a,b^{\prime})-N^{2}\operatorname{Re}(z_{t}(a)z_{t}(b^{\prime}))| \displaystyle\leq C_{7}N\exp(C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L)+C_{7}, \displaystyle|I_{t}(a,b^{\prime})-N^{2}\operatorname{Im}(z_{t}(a)z_{t}(b^{\prime}))| \displaystyle\leq C_{7}N\exp(C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L)+C_{7}. $$

Let $M_{0}$ be an integer larger than twice the absolute value of every possible component sum

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{L}R_{t}(x_{i},y_{i}),\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{L}I_{t}(x_{i},y_{i}). $$

By (5), (8), and the choice of $N$ (7), we may take

$$ M_{0}\leq 2^{C_{8}b\sqrt{L}\log L} $$

for a sufficiently large $C_{8}$ .

For each block $a$ , include, for every $t=1,\ldots,T$ , the four left local coordinates

$$ M_{0}^{2t}X_{t}(a),\quad M_{0}^{2t}Y_{t}(a),\quad M_{0}^{2t+1}X_{t}(a),\quad M_{0}^{2t+1}Y_{t}(a), $$

and the four right local coordinates

$$ X_{t}(b^{\prime}),\quad-Y_{t}(b^{\prime}),\quad Y_{t}(b^{\prime}),\quad X_{t}(b^{\prime}). $$

Concatenating these local maps over the $L$ blocks gives $r=4TL=O(L)$ coordinates. For block vectors $x,y$ , their integer dot product is

$$ \Phi_{A}(x)\cdot\Phi_{B}(y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}M_{0}^{2t}\sum_{i=1}^{L}R_{t}(x_{i},y_{i})+\sum_{t=1}^{T}M_{0}^{2t+1}\sum_{i=1}^{L}I_{t}(x_{i},y_{i}). $$

The packing is injective on component sums. If two packed sums are equal, subtract them and divide by the smallest used power of $M_{0}$ , namely $M_{0}^{2}$ , and then reindex the remaining exponents from $0$ . We get an identity $\sum_{s}D_{s}M_{0}^{s}=0$ . Each $D_{s}$ is the difference of two possible component sums, so the choice of $M_{0}$ gives $|D_{s}|<M_{0}$ . Reducing modulo $M_{0}$ gives $D_{0}=0$ ; dividing by $M_{0}$ and repeating gives every $D_{s}=0$ . Hence equality of packed dot products is equivalent to equality of all real and imaginary component sums.

By Lemma 3.23, an orthogonal algebraic value vector and a nonorthogonal algebraic value vector differ in some complex component by at least

$$ \delta_{0}:=\exp(-C_{3}b\sqrt{L}\log L). $$

Therefore either the corresponding real parts or imaginary parts differ by at least $\delta_{0}/\sqrt{2}$ . Summing (8) over the $L$ blocks, the total rounding error in any component sum is at most

$$ L\bigl(C_{7}N\exp(C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L)+C_{7}\bigr). $$

Choosing $C_{6}$ sufficiently large (recall this ensures $N$ is sufficiently large) ensures

$$ N^{2}\delta_{0}/\sqrt{2}>2L\bigl(C_{7}N\exp(C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L)+C_{7}\bigr). $$

Indeed, after dividing the dominant right-hand term by $N$ , the comparison is between exponents

$$ (C_{6}-C_{3})b\sqrt{L}\log L\quad\text{and}\quad C_{2}\sqrt{L}\log L+O(\log L). $$

Since $b\geq b_{*}\geq 1$ in the arithmetic case, one fixed choice of $C_{6}>C_{3}+C_{2}+O(1)$ works for all large $L$ ; the remaining additive term $2LC_{7}$ is then smaller as well. Thus after rounding, no orthogonal pair and nonorthogonal pair have the same packed dot product. Define

$$ V_{b,L}:=\{\Phi_{A}(x)\cdot\Phi_{B}(y):x\cdot y=0\}. $$

Then (6) follows. The coordinate and value bounds follow from (5), the choices of $N$ and $M_{0}$ , and the fact that $T$ is constant. Since all possible dot products lie in an interval of length $2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}$ , the same bound holds for $|V_{b,L}|$ . ∎

We are now ready to prove Lemma 3.1. From Proposition 3.24, we simply need to shift the coordinates so that all values are nonnegative.

#### Proof of Lemma 3.1.

Let $L_{0}:=L_{*}$ , where $L_{*}$ is the absolute threshold from Proposition 3.24. Assume $L\geq L_{0}$ . The (possibly negative) coordinates in the vectors produced by Proposition 3.24 have magnitude at most $2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}=L^{O(b\sqrt{L})}$ . Let $V^{\rm old}_{b,L}$ be the old value set, let $r_{s}$ be the full dimension of the vectors (i.e. $r_{s}=4TL$ ), and choose an integer $B\geq 1$ that bounds both the magnitude of every signed coordinate and $|v|$ for every $v\in V^{\rm old}_{b,L}$ . This still has $B=L^{O(b\sqrt{L})}$ by Proposition 3.24. Replace each signed left coordinate $a_{i}$ and right coordinate $b_{i}$ by the nonnegative pair

$$ (B+a_{i},B-a_{i}),\qquad(B+b_{i},B-b_{i}). $$

The contribution of this pair is

$$ (B+a_{i})(B+b_{i})+(B-a_{i})(B-b_{i})=2B^{2}+2a_{i}b_{i}. $$

Therefore the full transformed dot product equals

$$ 2r_{s}B^{2}+2D_{\rm old}(x,y), $$

where $D_{\rm old}$ is the signed dot product from Proposition 3.24. Since each signed product has magnitude at most $B^{2}$ and there are $r_{s}$ signed coordinates,

$$ |D_{\rm old}(x,y)|\leq r_{s}B^{2} $$

for every pair $x,y$ . Define the new value set explicitly by

$$ V^{+}_{b,L}:=\{2r_{s}B^{2}+2v:v\in V^{\rm old}_{b,L}\}. $$

The choice of $B$ makes every element of $V^{+}_{b,L}$ nonnegative, and the displayed bound also makes every transformed dot product nonnegative. Moreover every transformed dot product is at most $4r_{s}B^{2}$ . Since $r_{s}=O(L)$ , $b\geq 1$ , and $L\geq 2$ , this is still $L^{O(b\sqrt{L})}$ ; the same bound holds for the shifted values and the transformed coordinates. Membership in the value set is preserved exactly. This doubles the local width and changes the exponent only by an absolute constant. Enlarging $K_{0}$ bounds the coordinates, the values in $V^{+}_{b,L}$ , its cardinality, and all possible dot products by $\left\lceil L^{K_{0}b\sqrt{L}}\right\rceil$ . ∎

## 4 $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV Lower Bound via Uniform Local Reductions

At this point, Lemma 3.1 already gives a nonuniform reduction from (Boolean) OV to $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV. We can, for example, modify Theorem B.3 of [Che20] to obtain a uniform reduction, and therefore the desired lower bound. The setting here is slightly different from [Che20]’s setting. One key difference is that the reduction here is for the blockwise bichromatic setting, where [Che20] assumes a single map for both sets of vectors. For completeness, we include a proof in this section, which closely follows [Che20]’s approach.

First, we restate Lemma 3.1 in the language of a nonuniform local reduction (similar to [Che20]).

#### Definition 4.1 (Local Bichromatic Nonnegative Reduction).

A local bichromatic nonnegative $(b,L,\kappa)$ -reduction of width $w=O(1)$ consists of maps

$$ \alpha,\beta:\{0,1\}^{b}\to\{0,1,\ldots,\left\lceil L^{\kappa b}\right\rceil-1\}^{w} $$

and a set $V\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ such that

$$ |V|\leq\left\lceil L^{\kappa b}\right\rceil,\qquad\max_{v\in V}v\leq\left\lceil L^{\kappa b}\right\rceil, $$

every possible full dot product is at most $\left\lceil L^{\kappa b}\right\rceil$ , and for all block vectors $x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{L})$ and $y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L})$ ,

$$ x\cdot y=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha(x_{i})\cdot\beta(y_{i})\in V. $$

It is uniform if $\alpha,\beta$ can be evaluated and $V$ can be generated in time $L^{O(\kappa b)}\operatorname{poly}(b)$ .

It is easy to see that Lemma 3.1 implies the following.

#### Corollary 4.2.

There are absolute constants $K_{0}$ and $L_{0}\geq 2$ , and a fixed width $w_{0}=O(1)$ , such that, for every $b\geq 1$ and every $L\geq L_{0}$ , there is a (possibly nonuniform) local bichromatic nonnegative $(b,L,K_{0}\sqrt{L})$ -reduction of width $w_{0}$ , consisting of maps $\alpha_{b,L},\beta_{b,L}$ and a set $V_{b,L}$ .

#### Lemma 4.3 (CRT Composition for Local Two-Map Reductions).

There is an absolute constant $C_{\rm crt}$ with the following property. Suppose $\kappa\geq 1$ and there is a local bichromatic nonnegative $(m,L,\kappa)$ -reduction (called the micro-reduction) of constant width $w$ . Let $B\geq m$ and put $q:=\left\lceil B/m\right\rceil$ . If $q\leq L^{\kappa m}$ , then there is a local bichromatic nonnegative $(B,L,C_{\rm crt}\kappa)$ -reduction of the same constant width. If the micro-reduction is given uniformly, the composed reduction can be evaluated and its value set generated in time

$$ L^{O(\kappa B)}\operatorname{poly}(B) $$

plus the corresponding micro-reduction construction time.

#### Proof.

Pad a $B$ -bit block with zeros and view it as $q$ chunks of length- $m$ blocks. Let $(\alpha,\beta,V)$ be the micro-reduction. By Definition 4.1, all values of $V$ and all possible micro full dot products are nonnegative and at most

$$ D_{\rm micro}:=\left\lceil L^{\kappa m}\right\rceil. $$

If $D_{\rm micro}$ is below a fixed absolute threshold $D_{0}$ , then $q\leq D_{\rm micro}\leq D_{0}$ . For each of the finitely many pairs $(D_{\rm micro},q)$ with $1\leq q\leq D_{\rm micro}\leq D_{0}$ , hardwire the first $q$ primes larger than $D_{\rm micro}$ into the uniform construction. Their product is bounded by an absolute constant, which is absorbed in $L^{O(\kappa B)}$ after enlarging $C_{\rm crt}$ . Thus we may assume $D_{\rm micro}$ is large. Choose $q$ distinct primes $p_{1},\ldots,p_{q}$ in the interval

$$ [D_{\rm micro}^{2},2D_{\rm micro}^{2}]. $$

For large $D_{\rm micro}$ , the prime number theorem gives

$$ \#\{p\in[D_{\rm micro}^{2},2D_{\rm micro}^{2}]:p\text{ prime}\}=\Theta\left(\frac{D_{\rm micro}^{2}}{\log D_{\rm micro}}\right), $$

which is larger than $q$ because $q\leq D_{\rm micro}$ . Thus such a choice is possible, and each selected prime satisfies $p_{h}>D_{\rm micro}$ . Put $P:=\prod_{h=1}^{q}p_{h}$ . Since every $p_{h}\leq 2D_{\rm micro}^{2}$ ,

$$ P\leq(2D_{\rm micro}^{2})^{q}\leq L^{O(\kappa mq)}=L^{O(\kappa B)}. $$

To find these primes deterministically, scan the interval $[D_{\rm micro}^{2},2D_{\rm micro}^{2}]$ and run a primality test on each integer until $q$ primes have been collected. The interval length is $D_{\rm micro}^{2}\leq L^{O(\kappa m)}\leq L^{O(\kappa B)}$ , and each primality test costs polynomial time in $\log D_{\rm micro}=O(\kappa m\log L)$ , so this search fits within the final stated time bound.

For a large block $a=(a^{(1)},\ldots,a^{(q)})$ and each local coordinate $r\in[w]$ , define $\alpha^{\prime}(a)_{r}$ as the unique integer in $[0,P)$ satisfying

$$ \alpha^{\prime}(a)_{r}\equiv\alpha(a^{(h)})_{r}\pmod{p_{h}}\qquad\text{for all }h\in[q]. $$

Define $\beta^{\prime}$ analogously from $\beta$ . For full block vectors $x,y$ , let

$$ D^{\prime}(x,y):=\sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha^{\prime}(x_{i})\cdot\beta^{\prime}(y_{i}). $$

For every chunk index $h$ ,

$$ D^{\prime}(x,y)\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{L}\alpha(x_{i}^{(h)})\cdot\beta(y_{i}^{(h)})\pmod{p_{h}}. $$

Because $p_{h}>D_{\rm micro}$ , this residue identifies the integer micro dot product exactly. Moreover,

$$ x\cdot y=\sum_{h=1}^{q}\sum_{i=1}^{L}x_{i}^{(h)}\cdot y_{i}^{(h)}, $$

and every summand is a nonnegative integer because the vectors are Boolean. Therefore $x\cdot y=0$ if and only if each chunked dot product $\sum_{i=1}^{L}x_{i}^{(h)}\cdot y_{i}^{(h)}$ is zero. By the micro-reduction property, this is equivalent to requiring that, for every $h$ , the identified micro dot product lies in $V$ .

The possible range of $D^{\prime}$ is explicit:

$$ 0\leq D^{\prime}(x,y)\leq D_{\rm max}^{\prime}:=LwP^{2}. $$

Define

$$ V^{\prime}:=\{z\in[0,D_{\rm max}^{\prime}]\cap\mathbb{Z}:z\bmod p_{h}\in V\text{ for every }h\in[q]\}. $$

Then $(\alpha^{\prime},\beta^{\prime},V^{\prime})$ is the desired composed reduction. The coordinate bound follows from $\alpha^{\prime}(a)_{r},\beta^{\prime}(a)_{r}<P\leq L^{O(\kappa B)}$ , and the full dot-product range is at most $LwP^{2}\leq L^{O(\kappa B)}$ . For the value-set size, note that $V^{\prime}\subset[L^{O(\kappa B)}]$ . After increasing $C_{\rm crt}$ , all bounds fit the definition of a $(B,L,C_{\rm crt}\kappa)$ -reduction.

Uniform evaluation uses $q$ micro-evaluations and CRT reconstruction for each coordinate. To generate $V^{\prime}$ , enumerate the

$$ |V|^{q}\leq\left\lceil L^{\kappa m}\right\rceil^{q}\leq L^{O(\kappa mq)}\leq L^{O(\kappa B)} $$

residue tuples and reconstruct their residue classes $r\in[0,P)$ modulo $P$ . For each such $r$ , list the integers $r+aP$ with $a\geq 0$ and $r+aP\leq D_{\rm max}^{\prime}$ . There are at most $1+D_{\rm max}^{\prime}/P\leq L^{O(\kappa B)}$ representatives per tuple. Output the generated representatives with duplicates removed, for example by sorting; the total generated list length is $L^{O(\kappa B)}$ , so this remains within the stated time. Arithmetic is on $O(\kappa B\log L)$ -bit integers and contributes only polynomial factors. ∎

#### Lemma 4.4 (Base Search).

For every fixed $C>0$ and absolute integer width bound $W\geq 1$ , there are thresholds $L_{\rm bs}=L_{\rm bs}(C,W)$ and $b_{\rm bs}=b_{\rm bs}(C,W)$ with the following property. Let $L\geq L_{\rm bs}$ and $b\geq b_{\rm bs}$ , and assume

$$ m,L\leq C\log\log\log b,\qquad 1\leq\kappa\leq(\log\log\log b)^{C}. $$

Suppose a local bichromatic nonnegative $(m,L,\kappa)$ -reduction of width at most $W$ exists. Then exhaustive search over widths at most $W$ finds a local bichromatic nonnegative $(m,L,C_{\rm bs}\kappa)$ -reduction, for a constant $C_{\rm bs}=C_{\rm bs}(W)$ , in time

$$ b^{o(1)}\leq L^{O(\kappa b)} $$

for the ranges used in Lemma 4.5.

#### Proof.

Choose a sufficiently large absolute constant $C_{0}$ and put

$$ R:=\left\lceil L^{C_{0}\kappa m}\right\rceil. $$

In the application $W=w_{0}$ from Corollary 4.2. Enumerate all widths $1\leq w\leq W$ and all pairs of local maps

$$ \alpha,\beta:\{0,1\}^{m}\to\{0,1,\ldots,R-1\}^{w}. $$

Since a $(m,L,\kappa)$ -reduction of some width at most $W$ exists, one of the enumerated candidates contains the witnessing maps after enlarging $C_{0}$ if necessary. The number of candidates, summing over $w\leq W$ , is

$$ \sum_{w\leq W}R^{2w2^{m}}=L^{O(\kappa m2^{m})}=b^{o(1)} $$

under (9). Indeed,

$$ \log\!\left(L^{O(\kappa m2^{m})}\right)=O(\kappa m2^{m}\log L). $$

Here $\kappa,m,\log L\leq(\log\log\log b)^{O(1)}$ by (9), while

$$ 2^{m}\leq 2^{O(\log\log\log b)}=(\log\log b)^{O(1)}. $$

Therefore the logarithm of the search space is bounded by a fixed power of $\log\log b$ , which is $o(\log b)$ . Exponentiating gives $L^{O(\kappa m2^{m})}=b^{o(1)}$ .

For each candidate, compute all one-block contributions

$$ g(a,b^{\prime}):=\alpha(a)\cdot\beta(b^{\prime}),\qquad a,b^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}^{m}, $$

and mark whether $a\cdot b^{\prime}=0$ . Use dynamic programming over the $L$ block positions to compute two sets of sums: $S_{\rm good}$ , obtainable with all block pairs orthogonal, and $S_{\rm bad}$ , obtainable with at least one nonorthogonal block pair. Initially $S_{\rm good}=\{0\}$ and $S_{\rm bad}=\varnothing$ . If $G_{\rm good}$ and $G_{\rm bad}$ are the one-block contribution sets from orthogonal and nonorthogonal block pairs, and $G_{\rm all}:=G_{\rm good}\cup G_{\rm bad}$ , update by

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm good}^{\prime} \displaystyle=S_{\rm good}+G_{\rm good}, \displaystyle S_{\rm bad}^{\prime} \displaystyle=(S_{\rm bad}+G_{\rm all})\cup(S_{\rm good}+G_{\rm bad}), $$

and deduplicate after each step.

Let

$$ R_{\rm out}:=\left\lceil L^{C_{1}\kappa m}\right\rceil $$

with $C_{1}$ much larger than $C_{0}$ and $W$ . In the DP, keep only sums in $[0,R_{\rm out}]$ and record an overflow flag; during either update, if a sum in $S_{\rm good}+G_{\rm good}$ , $S_{\rm bad}+G_{\rm all}$ , or $S_{\rm good}+G_{\rm bad}$ falls outside this interval, set the flag. Any candidate with the overflow flag set is rejected, so for an accepted candidate no reachable sum has been discarded. A candidate is accepted only if

$$ S_{\rm good}\cap S_{\rm bad}=\varnothing,\qquad|S_{\rm good}|\leq R_{\rm out},\qquad\max(S_{\rm good}\cup S_{\rm bad})\leq R_{\rm out}. $$

For an accepted candidate take $V=S_{\rm good}$ . Then all coordinates are at most $R\leq R_{\rm out}$ after increasing $C_{1}$ if necessary, all actual full dot products and all values of $V$ are at most $R_{\rm out}$ , and $|V|\leq R_{\rm out}$ . Hence the output is a local $(m,L,C_{\rm bs}\kappa)$ -reduction for a constant $C_{\rm bs}=C_{\rm bs}(W)$ .

Existence of a local $(m,L,\kappa)$ -reduction guarantees that at least one candidate passes the test, because its actual orthogonal value set and full dot-product range are bounded by $\left\lceil L^{\kappa m}\right\rceil\leq R_{\rm out}$ . The DP states are subsets of $[0,R_{\rm out}]$ , so the verification time per candidate is $L^{O(\kappa m)}2^{O(m)}\operatorname{poly}(m)=b^{o(1)}$ in the stated range. Multiplying by the $b^{o(1)}$ candidate count still gives total search time $b^{o(1)}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 4.5 (Two-Parameter Uniformization).

There are absolute constants $K_{1},L_{1},B_{1}$ such that, for every $L\geq L_{1}$ and $b\geq B_{1}$ with

$$ 2\leq L\leq\log\log\log b, $$

there is a uniform local bichromatic nonnegative $(b,L,K_{1}\sqrt{L})$ -reduction. The maps can be evaluated and the value set can be generated in time

$$ L^{O(b\sqrt{L})}\operatorname{poly}(b)=2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}\operatorname{poly}(b). $$

#### Proof.

By Corollary 4.2, for every block length and every $L\geq L_{0}$ there exists a nonuniform local reduction with parameter $\Lambda:=K_{0}\sqrt{L}$ , where $L_{0},K_{0}$ , and the width bound $w_{0}$ are absolute. Fix an absolute constant $C_{*}$ large enough that the bounds verified below imply (9) with $C=C_{*}$ . Let $L_{1}$ dominate $L_{0}$ and the threshold $L_{\rm bs}(C_{*},w_{0})$ from Lemma 4.4. The constants $K_{0},w_{0},L_{1}$ are fixed once and for all and hardwired into the uniform search. After enlarging $K_{0}$ if necessary, $\Lambda\geq 1$ for $L\geq L_{1}$ .

Set $b_{0}:=b$ . For $s=1,2,3$ , define

$$ b_{s}:=\max\left\{1,\left\lceil\frac{\log b_{s-1}}{\Lambda\log L}\right\rceil\right\}. $$

Then $b_{3}=O(\log\log\log b)$ . Also $\Lambda=K_{0}\sqrt{L}\leq(\log\log\log b)^{C_{*}}$ after increasing $C_{*}$ , so (9) holds for $m=b_{3}$ , $\kappa=\Lambda$ , and $C=C_{*}$ . Let $A:=\log\log\log b$ and $D:=\Lambda\log L$ . Since $2\leq L\leq A$ , we have $D\leq C\sqrt{A}\log A$ for an absolute $C$ . For large $b$ , the quantities $\log b_{s-1}/D$ are larger than $1$ for $s=1,2,3$ , so the maxima in the definition of $b_{s}$ are inactive. Also $\left\lceil x\right\rceil\geq x$ , and

$$ \log(3D)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}A $$

for all large $A$ . Therefore

$$ b_{1}\geq\frac{\log b}{2D},\qquad b_{2}\geq\frac{\log b_{1}}{2D}\geq\frac{\log\log b}{3D},\qquad b_{3}\geq\frac{\log b_{2}}{2D}\geq\frac{A}{4D} $$

hold after enlarging a single absolute lower bound on $b$ if necessary. Indeed, the first bound is weaker than $b_{1}\geq\log b/D$ ; the second follows from $\log b_{1}\geq\log\log b-\log(2D)\geq(2/3)\log\log b$ ; and the third follows from $\log b_{2}\geq\log\log\log b-\log(3D)\geq A/2$ . Hence $b_{3}\geq c\sqrt{A}/\log A\to\infty$ uniformly for $2\leq L\leq A$ . Choose the threshold $B_{1}$ large enough that, for every $b\geq B_{1}$ , all preceding displayed inequalities hold and $b\geq b_{\rm bs}(C_{*},w_{0})$ . Thus the nonuniform reduction with block length $b_{3}$ , width bound $w_{0}$ , and parameter $\Lambda$ exists, and Lemma 4.4 with $W=w_{0}$ finds a base reduction with parameter $C_{\rm bs}\Lambda$ in time $b^{o(1)}$ .

Compose upward. For each $s=3,2,1$ , use Lemma 4.3 to pass from block length $b_{s}$ to block length $b_{s-1}$ . The number of chunks $q_{s}:=\left\lceil b_{s-1}/b_{s}\right\rceil$ satisfies

$$ q_{s}\leq L^{C\Lambda b_{s}} $$

for an absolute constant $C$ , by the definition of $b_{s}$ : if $b_{s}>1$ , then

$$ b_{s}\geq\frac{\log b_{s-1}}{\Lambda\log L}, $$

so

$$ b_{s-1}\leq e^{\Lambda b_{s}\log L}=L^{\Lambda b_{s}} $$

up to an absolute constant factor coming from the ceiling, and hence

$$ q_{s}=\left\lceil b_{s-1}/b_{s}\right\rceil\leq b_{s-1}+1\leq L^{C\Lambda b_{s}}. $$

If $b_{s}=1$ , then also $b_{s-1}\leq e^{\Lambda\log L}=L^{\Lambda}$ by the maximality in the definition of $b_{s}$ , so the same bound holds after enlarging $C$ . Absorbing $C$ into the current parameter, the hypothesis of Lemma 4.3 holds. Each composition multiplies the parameter by at most an absolute constant, so after three compositions the parameter is still $O(\Lambda)=O(\sqrt{L})$ .

The construction time is the base search time plus the three CRT composition times. The latter are bounded by

$$ L^{O(\Lambda b_{0})}\operatorname{poly}(b)=L^{O(b\sqrt{L})}\operatorname{poly}(b), $$

and dominate $b^{o(1)}$ for large $b$ . This gives the desired uniform family after increasing $K_{1}$ . ∎

### 4.1 Hardness of Low-Dimensional $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV

#### Proposition 4.6 (Dimensionality Reduction to $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV).

For all sufficiently large $L$ and sufficiently large $b$ , let $2\leq L\leq d$ , $b=\lceil d/L\rceil$ , and assume $L\leq\log\log\log b$ . Boolean $OV_{n,d}$ reduces in time

$$ n\cdot 2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}+2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}\operatorname{poly}(b) $$

to

$$ 2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)} $$

instances of $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV on two sets of $n$ vectors in dimension $O(L)$ , with entry bit-length $O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)$ .

#### Proof.

Pad each Boolean vector with zeros so that its dimension is exactly $bL$ , and split it into $L$ blocks of length $b$ . Use the uniform local maps $\alpha,\beta$ and value set $V$ supplied by Lemma 4.5. Let $\Phi_{A},\Phi_{B}$ be their blockwise concatenations. For every $v\in V$ , create a $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV instance by replacing

$$ a\in A\quad\text{with}\quad(\Phi_{A}(a),-v),\qquad y\in B\quad\text{with}\quad(\Phi_{B}(y),1). $$

Then

$$ (\Phi_{A}(a),-v)\cdot(\Phi_{B}(y),1)=\Phi_{A}(a)\cdot\Phi_{B}(y)-v. $$

Hence the original Boolean instance has an orthogonal pair iff at least one of the produced $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV instances has a zero inner-product pair. The number of instances, dimension, bit-length, and reduction time follow from Lemma 4.5. Arithmetic on $O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)$ -bit integers contributes only polynomial factors in that bit-length. ∎

Finally, we prove the main theorem.

#### Theorem 4.7 (Main Theorem).

Assume OVH or SETH. Let $D(n)=\omega(1)$ be a constructible dimension function. Then, for every fixed $\delta>0$ , $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV on two $n$ -point sets in dimension at most $D(n)$ , with $O(\log n)$ -bit entries, has no $O(n^{2-\delta})$ -time algorithm.

We remark that hardness of exact $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP, Furthest Pair and Bichromatic Closest Pair follows from reductions from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV, based on reductions from [Wil18, Che20]. See Appendix B for details.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.7.

Fix $\delta>0$ . It is enough to consider $0<\delta<1$ ; otherwise replace $\delta$ by $1/2$ . Suppose, toward contradiction, that $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension at most $D(n)$ with $O(\log n)$ -bit entries has an $O(n^{2-\delta})$ -time algorithm. Let $d=\left\lceil c\log n\right\rceil$ , where $c$ is the OVH constant for $\delta/4$ .

All constants and finite lower thresholds required by the reduction are fixed independent of $n$ . Let $L_{0}$ and $b_{0}$ dominate the finitely many lower bounds on $L$ and $b$ that occur in those statements.

Choose

$$ L=L(n):=\left\lfloor\min\left\{\frac{D(n)}{C_{9}},\frac{\log\log\log\log n}{C_{9}}\right\}\right\rfloor $$

for a sufficiently large constant $C_{9}$ . By Definition 2.1, this value of $L$ , and hence $b=\left\lceil d/L\right\rceil$ , can be computed in $n^{o(1)}$ time; this cost is included in the reduction time below. Since $D(n)=\omega(1)$ , for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $L\geq\max\{2,L_{0}\}$ and $L=\omega(1)$ . With $b=\lceil d/L\rceil$ , we have

$$ b\geq\frac{c\log n}{L}, $$

so

$$ \log b=\log\log n-\log L+O(1)=(1+o(1))\log\log n $$

because the second bound term in the minimization gives $\log L=o(\log\log n)$ . Hence

$$ \log\log\log b=(1+o(1))\log\log\log\log n. $$

In particular $b\to\infty$ , so $b\geq b_{0}$ for all sufficiently large $n$ . Choosing $C_{9}$ large enough, this implies

$$ L\leq\log\log\log b $$

for large $n$ , so the uniform reduction applies. The first term in the minimization ensures that the final $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV dimension $O(L)$ is at most $D(n)$ for sufficiently large $C_{9}$ ; if the assumed algorithm is stated for exactly dimension $D(n)$ rather than at most $D(n)$ , pad all vectors with zero coordinates.

By Proposition 4.6, the number of produced $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV instances is

$$ 2^{O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)}=\exp\left(O\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{L}}\log L\right)\right)=n^{o(1)}. $$

Indeed, $d=O(\log n)$ and $L=\omega(1)$ , so

$$ O\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{L}}\log L\right)=O\left(\log n\cdot\frac{\log L}{\sqrt{L}}\right)=o(\log n). $$

Their dimensions are $O(L)$ and their bit-length is

$$ O(b\sqrt{L}\log L)=O\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{L}}\log L\right)=o(\log n), $$

so in particular it is $O(\log n)$ . The reduction time is

$$ n\cdot n^{o(1)}+n^{o(1)}\operatorname{poly}(b)=n^{1+o(1)}, $$

because $b=\lceil d/L\rceil=O(\log n)$ and therefore every fixed polynomial in $b$ is $n^{o(1)}$ .

Running the assumed $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV algorithm on all instances takes

$$ n^{o(1)}\cdot n^{2-\delta}=n^{2-\delta+o(1)}. $$

Together with the $n^{1+o(1)}$ reduction time, this is at most $n^{2-\delta/2}$ for sufficiently large $n$ , contradicting OVH for the choice of $c=c(\delta/4)$ . ∎
