## Appendix A Tools from Number Theory

The goal of this section is to prove Proposition 3.20. This section begins with Theorem A.30, from which the remaining proof of Proposition 3.20 will be self-contained.

### A.1 Further Group Theory and Number Theory Preliminaries

We begin with the necessary preliminaries (beyond those given in Section 3.1). We use $H_{2}(x)=x\log(1/x)+(1-x)\log(1/(1-x))$ to denote the binary entropy function with natural logarithms. Let $G$ be a group. A subgroup $H\triangleleft G$ is normal if $gHg^{-1}=H$ for all $g\in G$ , i.e. it is invariant under conjugation. The order of a group is its size $|G|$ . A normal subgroup $H\triangleleft G$ has index $[G:H]=|G/H|$ .

#### Definition A.1 (Normal Extension (Chapter 13 of [DF04])).

The extension field $K/F$ is called a splitting field for the polynomial $f(x)$ if $f(x)$ factors completely into linear factors (or splits completely) in $K[x]$ (i.e. splits into degree- $1$ polynomials with coefficients in $K$ ) and $f(x)$ does not factor completely into linear factors over any proper subfield of $K$ containing $F$ . An extension $K/F$ is normal if $K$ is the splitting field for some collection of polynomials. The normal closure of an extension $K/F$ is the smallest normal extension $K/F\subseteq N/F$ .

#### Definition A.2 (Separable (Chapter 13 of [DF04])).

A polynomial over $F$ is called separable if it has no multiple roots (i.e., all its roots are distinct). The field $K$ is said to be separable (or separably algebraic) over $F$ if every element of $K$ is the root of a separable polynomial over $F$ (equivalently, the minimal polynomial over $F$ of every element of $K$ is separable).

#### Definition A.3 (Galois Extension ([DF04, Chapter 14])).

A finite extension $K/F$ is Galois if $|\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)|=[K:F]$ . In this case, the Galois group of $K/F$ is $\operatorname{Gal}(K/F)=\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ .

We note that Galois extensions are normal and separable. Furthermore, since any extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is separable, such an extension is Galois iff it is normal.

#### Definition A.4 (Fixed Field [DF04]).

If $H$ is a subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(K/F)$ , the subfield of $K$ fixed by all the elements of $H$ is called the fixed field of $H$ , denoted $K^{H}$ .

Next, we define $p$ -groups and pro- $p$ groups.

#### Definition A.5.

A finite group $G$ is a $p$ -group if every element has order that is a power of $p$ .

#### Definition A.6 (Inverse Limits [Wil20]).

A partially ordered set $(J,\preceq)$ is an inverse system if for any $i,j\in J$ there is some $k\in J$ such that $k\preceq i$ and $k\preceq j$ .

An inverse system of groups $(J,\preceq)$ consists of: (1) group $G_{j}$ for each $j\in J$ and, whenever $i\preceq j$ , we have some homomorphism $\phi_{ij}:G_{i}\rightarrow G_{j}$ such that $\phi_{ii}=\mathrm{id}_{G_{i}}$ and $\phi_{ik}=\phi_{jk}\circ\phi_{ij}$ when $i\preceq j\preceq k$ .

The inverse limit of an inverse system of groups (more informally, the inverse limit of the groups $G_{j}$ ) is the group, denoted $\underset{\leftarrow}{\lim}G_{j}$ , of sequences $(g_{j})_{j\in J}$ such that $g_{j}\in G_{j}$ for all $j$ and $\phi_{ij}(g_{i})=g_{j}$ for all $i\preceq j$ .

#### Definition A.7 (Pro- $p$ Groups [Wil20]).

Let $p$ be a prime. A pro- $p$ group is an inverse limit of an inverse system of finite $p$ -groups.

#### Definition A.8 (Maximal unramified pro-p extension (Definition A.3 of [Ope26])).

For a number field $F$ , $F^{\mathrm{ur},p}$ denotes the compositum of all finite everywhere-unramified Galois extensions of $F$ whose Galois groups are finite $p$ -groups. Its Galois group $\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{ur},p}/F)$ is a pro- $p$ group, and its finite quotients correspond to finite everywhere-unramified Galois $p$ -group extensions of $F$ .

Pro- $p$ groups are equipped with the following topology.

#### Definition A.9 ([Wil20]).

Let $(G_{j})_{j\in J}$ be an inverse system of finite groups. Endow each $G_{j}$ with the discrete topology (every subset is open and closed), and give $\prod G_{j}$ the product topology (open sets are the full group $G_{j}$ in all but finitely many coordinates). The topology on $\underset{\leftarrow}{\lim}\,G_{j}\subseteq\prod G_{j}$ is the subspace topology.

#### Definition A.10 (Frattini Subgroup (Definition 4.1.1 of [Wil20])).

The Frattini subgroup of group $G$ , denoted $\Phi(G)$ , is the intersection of all maximal proper subgroups of $G$ .

We define generator rank and relation rank of pro- $p$ groups.

#### Definition A.11 (Generator rank [Wil20]).

Let $G$ be a topological group and let $S$ be a subset of $G$ . We say $S$ is a (topological) generating set for $G$ if the subgroup $\langle S\rangle$ generated by $S$ is a dense subgroup of $G$ .66 6 A subset is dense if it intersects every non-empty open set. Equivalently, its closure is the whole set. The group $G$ is (topologically) finitely generated if it has a finite topological generating set. The generator rank of $G$ , denoted $d(G)$ , is the minimum size of a (topological) generating set.

For a topologically finitely generated pro- $p$ group $G$ , we have $H_{1}(G,\mathbb{F}_{p}):=G/\Phi(G)\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d(G)}$ (see e.g. Proposition 4.1.13 of [Wil20], and Proposition A.26).

#### Definition A.12 (Relation rank (Section 5.4.2 of [Wil20])).

Let $G$ be a topologically finitely generated pro- $p$ group, and let $d(G)$ denote its minimal number of topological generators. A finite pro- $p$ presentation of $G$ is an isomorphism

$$ G\cong F/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle\text{,} $$

where $F$ is a finitely generated free pro- $p$ group and $\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle$ denotes the closed normal subgroup of $F$ topologically normally generated by $R$ . The relation rank of $G$ , denoted $r(G)$ , is the minimum cardinality of such a set $R$ , taken over pro- $p$ presentations of $G$ in which $F$ is freely generated by $d(G)$ elements.

For a topologically finitely generated pro- $p$ group $G$ , one has

$$ r(G)=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}H^{2}(G,\mathbb{F}_{p})\text{,} $$

where $H^{2}$ denotes the second cohomology group (see e.g. Definition 5.1.16 and Theorem 5.4.28 of [Wil20]). In particular, $r(G)$ is intrinsic to $G$ and does not depend on the choice of a minimal topological generating set.

#### Definition A.13 (Trace (see e.g. Corollary 2.20 of [Mil20])).

Let $L/K$ be a separable extension so that there are $n=[L:K]$ distinct embeddings of $L$ fixing $K$ , denoted $\{\sigma_{i}\}$ . Then, define for $x\in L$ , $\Tr_{L/K}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}(x)$ .

#### Definition A.14 (Relative Discriminant ([Mil20])).

Let $L/K$ be a separable extension of degree $n=[L:K]$ and $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in L$ . Then their discriminant is

$$ \disc(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\det(\Tr_{L/K}(x_{i}x_{j}))\text{.} $$

The relative discriminant $\mathfrak{d}_{L/K}$ is the ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ generated by $\disc(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})$ for all $x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{O}_{L}$ .

#### Definition A.15 (Absolute Discriminant ([Mil20])).

The absolute discriminant of a number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is defined

$$ |\Delta_{K}|=|\disc(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})| $$

where $\{x_{i}\}$ is (any) $\mathbb{Z}$ -basis of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

We use the following properties of the discriminant given in [Ope26].

#### Definition A.16 (Discriminant (Definition A.6 of [Ope26])).

The root discriminant of a number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is $\operatorname{rd}(K)=|\Delta_{K}|^{1/[K:\mathbb{Q}]}$ . Finite unramified extensions preserve root discriminant.

For an extension $M/F$ , the relative discriminant $\mathfrak{d}_{M/F}$ is an ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{F}$ , and the tower formula is

$$ |\Delta_{M}|=|\Delta_{F}|^{[M:F]}N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{d}_{M/F}). $$

Thus $\mathfrak{d}_{M/F}=\mathcal{O}_{F}$ is equivalent to no finite ramification in $M/F$ . Here, $N_{F/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{a})=[\mathcal{O}_{F}:\mathfrak{a}]$ denotes the absolute norm of an ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ .

Next, we define the class number.

#### Definition A.17 (Fractional Ideal [Neu13]).

A fractional ideal of $K$ is a finitely generated $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ -submodule $\mathfrak{a}\neq 0$ of $K$ . The ideal group of $K$ , denoted $J_{K}$ is the group of fractional ideals of $K$ , with identity $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ and inverse $\mathfrak{a}^{-1}=\{x\in K\mid x\mathfrak{a}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}\}$ . The fractional principal ideals of $K$ , denoted $P_{K}$ , form a subgroup of $J_{K}$ .

#### Definition A.18 (Class Number [Neu13]).

The class group of $K$ is the group $J_{K}/P_{K}$ . The class number of $K$ , denoted $\operatorname{h}(K)$ is $\operatorname{h}(K)=|J_{K}/P_{K}|$ .

Next, we define the Frobenius representative.

#### Definition A.19 (Frobenius Representative [Mar18]).

Let $L/K$ be a Galois extension. Let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ that is unramified in $L/K$ , and $\mathfrak{P}$ a prime lying above $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_{L}$ . The Frobenius automorphism of $\mathfrak{P}$ , denoted $\phi_{\mathfrak{P}}$ is the unique $\phi\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ such that $\phi_{\mathfrak{P}}(\alpha)\equiv\alpha^{|\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}|}\pmod{\mathfrak{P}}$ for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{O}_{L}$ .

We state the necessary preliminaries for decomposition groups.

#### Definition A.20 (Decomposition Group [Mar18, Mil20]).

Let $L/K$ be an extension and $\mathfrak{p}$ a prime ideal in $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . For a prime $\mathfrak{P}$ above $\mathfrak{p}$ in $\mathcal{O}_{L}$ , the decomposition group $D(\mathfrak{P}\mid\mathfrak{p})$ is the set of automorphisms in $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ satisfying $\sigma(\mathfrak{P})=\mathfrak{P}$ .

For an infinite place $v$ of $K$ and $w$ above $v$ (i.e. agreeing with $v$ on $K$ ), the decomposition group of $w$ , denoted $D_{w}$ , is the set of automorphisms in $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ such that $\sigma(w)=w$ .

#### Definition A.21 (Chapter 7 of [Mil20]).

For any prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ of number field $K$ , the $\mathfrak{p}$ -adic absolute value is given by $|x|_{\mathfrak{p}}=(1/e)^{\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}}(x)}$ for some constant $e>1$ . The standard choice is $e=\mathbb{N}\mathfrak{p}:=|\mathcal{O}_{K}/\mathfrak{p}|$ (Chapter 4 of [Mil20]). Let $\mathbb{Q}_{p}$ denote the completion of $\mathbb{Q}$ with the $p$ -adic absolute value.

#### Definition A.22 (Chapter 7 of [Mil20]).

Let $K$ be a field and $|\cdot|$ a non-trivial absolute value. A sequence $\{x_{i}\}$ is Cauchy if for all $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists $N$ such that $|x_{i}-x_{j}|<\varepsilon$ for all $i,j\geq N$ . A field $K$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence has a limit in $K$ .

#### Claim A.23 (Theorem 7.23 of [Mil20]).

Let $K$ be a field with an absolute value $|\cdot|$ . Then there exists a complete field $\hat{K}$ and a homomorphism $K\rightarrow\hat{K}$ preserving the absolute value that is universal in the following sense: every homomorphism $K\rightarrow L$ from $K$ into a complete field $L$ preserving the absolute value, extends uniquely to a homomorphism $\hat{K}\rightarrow L$ .

For a place $v$ of $K$ , we let $K_{v}$ denote the completion of $K$ w.r.t. $v$ . For a prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ , $K_{\mathfrak{p}}$ denotes the completion of $K$ w.r.t. the $p$ -adic absolute value $|\cdot|_{\mathfrak{p}}$ .

#### Claim A.24 (Theorem 7.38, Corollary 7.42 of [Mil20]).

Let $K$ be a complete field w.r.t. a discrete absolute value $|\cdot|_{K}$ and $L/K$ be a finite, separable extension. Then $[L:K]=ef$ where $e$ is the ramification index and $f$ is the residue field degree.

In particular, for a number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ , a rational prime $q$ , and a prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}$ of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ lying above $q$ , the completion $K_{\mathfrak{P}}$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_{q}$ (see e.g. Remark 8.3 of [Mil20]), and $[K_{\mathfrak{P}}:\mathbb{Q}_{q}]=e(\mathfrak{P}|q)f(\mathfrak{P}|q)$ .

#### Claim A.25 (Proposition 8.10 of [Mil20]).

Let $L/K$ be a finite Galois extension of number field $K$ . Let $v$ be an infinite place of $K$ and $w$ a place of $L$ lying above $v$ . Let $K_{v}$ denote the completion of $K$ with respect to $v$ and $L_{w}$ the completion of $L$ with respect to $w$ . Then, $K_{v},L_{w}$ are either isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ (see Remark 7.49 of [Mil20]) and $D_{w}\cong\operatorname{Gal}(L_{w}/K_{v})$ .

We will use the following facts.

#### Proposition A.26 (Proposition 3.3 of [Ope26]).

Let $G$ be a finitely generated pro- $p$ group. Then $d(G)=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(G/\Phi(G))$ . If $g_{1},\dots,g_{k}\in\Phi(G)$ and $N$ is their closed normal closure, then $d(G/N)=d(G)$ and $r(G/N)\leq r(G)+k$ .

#### Proposition A.27 (Golod-Shafarevich Inequality ([Ope26, Proposition 3.4])).

If a finite non-trivial pro- $p$ group has generator rank $d$ and relation rank $r$ , then $r>d^{2}/4$ . Equivalently, a nontrivial finitely generated pro- $p$ group with $r\leq d^{2}/4$ is infinite.

#### Proposition A.28 (Shafarevich Relation-Rank Estimate (Proposition 3.5 of [Ope26])).

Let $F$ be a totally real cubic field, so $\zeta_{3}\not\in F$ , and let $G=\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{ur},3}/F)$ be the Galois group of its maximal everywhere-unramified pro- $3$ extension. Then $r(G)\leq d(G)+C_{0}$ for an absolute constant $C_{0}$ .

#### Proposition A.29 (Proposition 3.7 of [Ope26]).

There is an absolute constant $C_{\mathrm{class}}>0$ such that every number field $K$ satisfies $h(K)\leq\max(2,\operatorname{rd}(K))^{C_{\mathrm{class}}[K:\mathbb{Q}]}$ . The constant $C_{\mathrm{class}}$ is absolute: it is independent of the field $K$ , its degree, and its signature. For fields with $\operatorname{rd}(K)\geq 2$ , this is simply $h(K)\leq\operatorname{rd}(K)^{O([K:\mathbb{Q}])}=|\Delta_{K}|^{O(1)}$ .

### A.2 Proof of Theorem A.30

We now state Theorem A.30 and provide its proof. Every subsequent statement in this section is proved below from Theorem A.30.

#### Theorem A.30 (Number-Theoretic Input from [Ope26]).

There are absolute constants $C_{\rm Sha},C_{\rm class},C_{\rm rd}>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large integers $\ell$ , there is a totally real cyclic cubic field $F_{\ell}$ with the following properties. Let

$$ G_{\ell}:=\operatorname{Gal}(F_{\ell}^{\rm ur,3}/F_{\ell}) $$

be the Galois group of the maximal everywhere-unramified pro- $3$ extension of $F_{\ell}$ , and let $\Phi(G_{\ell})$ be its Frattini subgroup. Then:

- (i) $d(G_{\ell})\geq\ell-1$ and $r(G_{\ell})\leq d(G_{\ell})+C_{\rm Sha}$ , where $d$ and $r$ denote generator and relation ranks;

- (ii) $\log\operatorname{rd}(F_{\ell})\leq C_{\rm rd}\ell\log\ell$ ;

- (iii) if $E_{\ell}/F_{\ell}$ is the finite extension corresponding to $G_{\ell}/\Phi(G_{\ell})$ and $N_{\ell}$ is the finite normal closure over $\mathbb{Q}$ of $E_{\ell}(i)$ , then every rational prime $q$ splitting completely in $N_{\ell}$ satisfies $q\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ , splits completely in $F_{\ell}$ , and, for every prime $v\mid q$ of $F_{\ell}$ , has a Frobenius representative in $\Phi(G_{\ell})$ ;

- (iv) if $g_{1},\ldots,g_{k}\in\Phi(G_{\ell})$ and $N$ is their closed normal closure in $G_{\ell}$ , then $d(G_{\ell}/N)=d(G_{\ell})$ and $r(G_{\ell}/N)\leq r(G_{\ell})+k$ ;

- (v) a nontrivial finitely generated pro- $p$ group with generator rank $d$ and relation rank $r\leq d^{2}/4$ is infinite;

- (vi) every number field $K$ satisfies

$$ h(K)\leq\max\{2,\operatorname{rd}(K)\}^{C_{\rm class}[K:\mathbb{Q}]}. $$

#### Proof.

The field $F_{\ell}$ is given by Proposition 3.8 of [Ope26]. We verify each property step by step.

The first property follows from Equation (5) and Equation (7) of [Ope26]. We note that the second inequality follows from the Shafarevich relation-rank estimate (Proposition A.28).

The second property follows from Equation (6) of [Ope26].

We will argue the third property. Let $q$ be a rational prime splitting completely in $N_{\ell}$ , the normal closure over $\mathbb{Q}$ of $E_{\ell}(i)$ . Since $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ , $F_{\ell}$ , and $E_{\ell}$ are subfields of $N_{\ell}$ , complete splitting in $N_{\ell}$ descends to each of these subextensions. Thus $q$ splits in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ , so $q\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ , and $q$ splits completely in $F_{\ell}$ . Moreover, for every prime $v\mid q$ of $F_{\ell}$ , the prime $v$ splits completely in $E_{\ell}/F_{\ell}$ , so its Frobenius class in $\operatorname{Gal}(E_{\ell}/F_{\ell})\cong G_{\ell}/\Phi(G_{\ell})$ is trivial. Hence any Frobenius representative at $v$ in $G_{\ell}$ lies in $\Phi(G_{\ell})$ .

We note that $G_{\ell}$ is finitely generated (as argued in [Ope26]). The fourth property then follows from Proposition A.26, since $G_{\ell}$ is a pro- $3$ group.

The fifth property follows from Proposition A.27.

The sixth property follows from Proposition A.29. ∎

### A.3 Proof of Proposition 3.20

The next proposition provides the modifications we need from Theorem A.30.

#### Proposition A.31.

There are absolute constants $c_{0},C_{H}>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large integers $\ell$ , $F_{\ell},N_{\ell}$ from Theorem A.30 supply integers and constants

$$ T_{\ell}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1},\qquad T_{\ell}\geq c_{0}\ell^{2},\qquad H_{\ell}\geq 1,\qquad\log H_{\ell}\leq C_{H}\ell\log\ell, $$

a totally real base field $L_{0,\ell}:=F_{\ell}$ of degree $d_{\ell}=3$ , and the finite normal extension $N_{\ell}/\mathbb{Q}$ , which contains $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ and the normal closure of $L_{0,\ell}$ , with the following property. For every set $\mathcal{Q}$ of at most $T_{\ell}$ rational primes splitting completely in $N_{\ell}$ , there is an infinite pro- $3$ Galois extension

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}/L_{0,\ell} $$

such that for every finite subextension $L/L_{0,\ell}$ :

- (i) $L/L_{0,\ell}$ is everywhere unramified and totally real;

- (ii) every $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ splits completely in $L$ ;

- (iii) with $K:=L(i)$ , one has

$$ h(K)\leq H_{\ell}^{[L:\mathbb{Q}]}. $$

The constants $N_{\ell},L_{0,\ell},H_{\ell}$ depend only on $\ell$ , not on the particular primes in $\mathcal{Q}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\ell$ large enough that Theorem A.30 applies and that the numerical inequalities below hold. Put

$$ T_{\ell}:=\left\lfloor\frac{(\ell-1)^{2}}{100}\right\rfloor,\qquad c_{0}:=\frac{1}{200}. $$

For sufficiently large $\ell$ , we have $T_{\ell}\geq c_{0}\ell^{2}$ . The field $N_{\ell}$ contains $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ by definition. Since it is normal over $\mathbb{Q}$ and contains $F_{\ell}=L_{0,\ell}$ , it also contains the normal closure of $L_{0,\ell}$ .

Let $\mathcal{Q}$ be any set of at most $T_{\ell}$ rational primes splitting completely in $N_{\ell}$ . For each $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ and each prime $v\mid q$ of $F_{\ell}$ , choose a Frobenius representative $\sigma_{v}\in G_{\ell}$ .77 7 Technically, Frobenius representatives are chosen with respect to some prime above $v$ . Here, since the Frobenius representatives for different choices of primes above $v$ are equivalent up to conjugation (see e.g. [Mar18]), we let $\sigma_{v}$ denote any representative in the conjugacy class. By Theorem A.30 (iii), every such $\sigma_{v}$ lies in $\Phi(G_{\ell})$ and $q$ splits completely in $F_{\ell}$ . Since $F_{\ell}/\mathbb{Q}$ is cubic and $q$ splits completely in $F_{\ell}$ , there are exactly $3|\mathcal{Q}|$ such primes $v$ .

Let $N(\mathcal{Q})$ be the closed normal88 8 Since Frobenius representatives are equivalent up to conjugacy class, the normal subgroup is well defined. subgroup of $G_{\ell}$ generated by these $3|\mathcal{Q}|$ elements (i.e. $\sigma_{v}\in\Phi(G_{\ell})$ ), and set

$$ \overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}:=G_{\ell}/N(\mathcal{Q})\text{.} $$

Write $d:=d(G_{\ell})$ . By Theorem A.30 (i) and (iv),

$$ d(\overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}})=d,\qquad r(\overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}})\leq d+C_{\rm Sha}+3|\mathcal{Q}|\leq d+C_{\rm Sha}+\frac{3(\ell-1)^{2}}{100}. $$

Because $d\geq\ell-1$ , the last term is at most $d+C_{\rm Sha}+3d^{2}/100$ . For all sufficiently large $\ell$ this is strictly less than $d^{2}/4$ . Also $d(\overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}})=d>0$ , so the quotient is nontrivial. Hence Theorem A.30 (v) implies that $\overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ is infinite.

Let $\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ be the fixed field of $N(\mathcal{Q})$ inside $F_{\ell}^{\rm ur,3}$ . By the fundamental theorem of infinite Galois theory (see e.g. Theorem 7.13 of [Mil03]), the intermediate extension $\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ with Galois group $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}/F_{\ell})\cong\overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ is an infinite Galois pro- $3$ extension. Indeed, we have argued the infinite condition above, and quotients of the pro- $3$ group $G_{\ell}$ by closed normal subgroups are pro- $3$ groups.

We now verify the remaining properties. Let $L/L_{0,\ell}$ be a finite subextension. We claim that any finite subextension is everywhere unramified over $F_{\ell}$ . We use the following standard facts (see e.g. Theorems 29 and 31 of [Mar18]):

- 1. if a finite prime is unramified in $L_{1}/K$ and $L_{2}/K$ , then it is also unramified in their compositum (i.e. the extension generated by $L_{1}/K$ and $L_{2}/K$ ),

- 2. if a finite prime is unramified in an extension $M/K$ , then it is unramified in any intermediate extension $K\subseteq M\subseteq L$ .

Consider a finite sub-extension $L=F_{\ell}(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m})$ and a finite prime $p$ . Note each $\alpha_{i}$ lies in some finite everywhere-unramified Galois extension $E_{i}/F_{\ell}$ where $p$ is unramified. Then, $L\subseteq E_{1}E_{2}\dots E_{m}$ is an intermediate extension of a finite compositum of extensions where $p$ is unramified, so that $p$ is unramified in $L$ . To argue infinite primes are unramified, we observe that each finite subextension is totally real. Indeed, if such an $L$ were not totally real, then after passing to its finite Galois closure $E/F_{\ell}$ inside $\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ , some real place of $F_{\ell}$ would have a complex place of $E$ above it. By Claim A.25, the corresponding decomposition group is isomorphic to $\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R})$ and therefore has order $2$ , which is impossible inside the finite quotient $\operatorname{Gal}(E/F_{\ell})$ of the pro- $3$ group. Since $F_{\ell}$ is totally real, so is every finite subextension.

Next, we argue that every prime $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ splits completely in $L$ . For $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ , the prime $q$ splits completely in $F_{\ell}$ by Theorem A.30 (iii). For every prime $v\mid q$ of $F_{\ell}$ , the chosen Frobenius representative $\sigma_{v}$ maps to the identity in $\overline{G}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ by construction. First, take some finite intermediate Galois subextension $E$ , so that Galois correspondence guarantees $E$ is the fixed field of some normal subgroup $U\triangleleft G_{\ell}$ . Since $E\subseteq\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ we have $N(\mathcal{Q})\subseteq U$ so that $\sigma_{v}$ maps to the identity in $G_{\ell}/U$ . Since an unramified prime $v$ splits completely in a normal extension iff the Frobenius representative $\sigma_{v}=1$ (see e.g. Theorem 32 of [Mar18]), $v$ splits completely in every finite Galois subextension of $\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}/F_{\ell}$ . Hence also in every finite subextension (e.g. $L$ ) since we can choose some finite Galois sub-extension $E$ containing $L$ (taking the finite Galois closure of $L/F_{\ell}$ inside $\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}$ ) and above we have argued that $v$ splits completely in $E$ . Since $q$ already splits completely in $F_{\ell}$ and every prime $v$ above $q$ splits completely in $L$ , it follows that $q$ splits completely in every finite subextension $L/F_{\ell}$ .

It remains to prove the class-number bound with a constant independent of $\mathcal{Q}$ . Let $L/F_{\ell}$ be a finite subextension and set $K=L(i)$ . Since $L/F_{\ell}$ is unramified at finite primes, $\operatorname{rd}(L)=\operatorname{rd}(F_{\ell})$ (Definition A.16). Since the two $L$ -embeddings of $K$ are the identity and complex conjugation and $1,i\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , we have that $\mathfrak{d}_{K/L}$ contains

$$ \disc(1,i)=\det\begin{pmatrix}\Tr(1)&\Tr(i)\\
\Tr(i)&\Tr(-1)\end{pmatrix}=\det\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\
0&-2\end{pmatrix}=-4\text{.} $$

Hence, $(4)\subseteq\mathfrak{d}_{K/L}$ , or equivalently, $\mathfrak{d}_{K/L}\mid 4\mathcal{O}_{L}$ . Therefore,

$$ |\Delta_{K}|=|\Delta_{L}|^{2}\,\operatorname{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{d}_{K/L})\leq|\Delta_{L}|^{2}\,4^{[L:\mathbb{Q}]}. $$

The equality follows from Definition A.16 and observing $[K:L]=2$ . The inequality follows from the fact that $(4)\subseteq\mathfrak{d}_{K/L}$ implies $\operatorname{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{d}_{K/L})\leq\operatorname{N}_{L/\mathbb{Q}}((4))=4^{[L:\mathbb{Q}]}$ since every embedding fixes $\mathbb{Q}$ . Taking $2[L:\mathbb{Q}]$ -th roots gives

$$ \operatorname{rd}(K)\leq 2\operatorname{rd}(F_{\ell}). $$

By Theorem A.30 (vi),

$$ h(K)\leq\max\{2,2\operatorname{rd}(F_{\ell})\}^{2C_{\rm class}[L:\mathbb{Q}]}. $$

Define

$$ H_{\ell}:=\max\{2,2\operatorname{rd}(F_{\ell})\}^{2C_{\rm class}}. $$

Then $h(K)\leq H_{\ell}^{[L:\mathbb{Q}]}$ . This $H_{\ell}$ depends only on $\ell$ , not on $\mathcal{Q}$ . Finally, by Theorem A.30 (ii),

$$ \log H_{\ell}\leq 2C_{\rm class}\log\max\{2,2\operatorname{rd}(F_{\ell})\}\leq C_{H}\ell\log\ell $$

for a sufficiently large absolute constant $C_{H}$ and all sufficiently large $\ell$ . This proves every assertion. ∎

#### Theorem A.32 (Medium-Prime Split Tower).

There exist absolute constants

$$ T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 16},\qquad H\geq 1,\qquad C_{\rm ar}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}, $$

with

$$ \gamma:=T\log 2-\log H>TH_{2}(4/T),\qquad H_{2}(\rho):=-\rho\log\rho-(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho), $$

such that the following holds. (We use $H_{2}$ to denote binary entropy with natural logarithms to distinguish from the constant $H$ and class number $h$ ). For every sufficiently large parameter $Y$ there are $T$ distinct rational primes

$$ q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}\in[Y,2Y] $$

and an infinite sequence of CM fields $K_{s}=L_{s}(i)$ , where $L_{s}$ is totally real, satisfying:

- (i) each $q_{t}$ splits completely in every $K_{s}$ ; in particular $q_{t}\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ and every prime of $K_{s}$ above $q_{t}$ has residue field $\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ ;

- (ii) if $f_{s}:=[L_{s}:\mathbb{Q}]$ , then $f_{s}\to\infty$ and

$$ h(K_{s})\leq H^{f_{s}}; $$

- (iii) for every sufficiently large $b$ there is a layer $s=s(b,Y)$ with

$$ C_{\rm ar}b\leq f_{s}\leq 3C_{\rm ar}b. $$

The constants $T,H,C_{\rm ar}$ are independent of $Y$ and $b$ .

#### Proof.

We derive the statement from Proposition A.31. For $\rho\leq 1/2$ ,

$$ H_{2}(\rho)=O\!\left(\rho\log\frac{1}{\rho}\right), $$

and therefore, for $T\to\infty$ ,

$$ TH_{2}(4/T)=O(\log T). $$

For the tower parameter $\ell$ , put

$$ T_{\ell}^{*}:=\left\lfloor(c_{0}/2)\ell^{2}\right\rfloor. $$

Then $T_{\ell}^{*}\leq T_{\ell}$ (recall $T_{\ell}:=\lfloor(\ell-1)^{2}/100\rfloor$ and $c_{0}=1/200$ ) and, along the tower parameters of Proposition A.31,

$$ T_{\ell}^{*}\log 2-\log H_{\ell}\geq\bigl((c_{0}/2)\ell^{2}-1\bigr)\log 2-C_{H}\ell\log\ell=\Omega(\ell^{2}). $$

Choose once and for all a sufficiently large $\ell$ such that $T_{\ell}^{*}\geq 16$ and

$$ T_{\ell}^{*}\log 2-\log H_{\ell}>T_{\ell}^{*}H_{2}(4/T_{\ell}^{*}). $$

Set

$$ T:=T_{\ell}^{*},\qquad H:=H_{\ell},\qquad N:=N_{\ell},\qquad d_{0}:=d_{\ell}=3,\qquad C_{\rm ar}:=\max\{2,d_{0}\}. $$

These constants now depend only on the objects fixed in Proposition A.31.

Let $Y$ be sufficiently large. We now use only the standard Chebotarev Density Theorem for the fixed finite normal extension $N/\mathbb{Q}$ : if $\pi_{N}(x)$ counts rational primes $q\leq x$ that split completely in $N$ , then

$$ \pi_{N}(x)\sim\frac{1}{[N:\mathbb{Q}]}\frac{x}{\log x}\text{.} $$

To see this, recall the Chebotarev Density Theorem below.

#### Definition A.33 (Density (see e.g. [Mil20])).

Let $S$ be a set of rational primes, and let $P$ be the set of all rational primes. We say that $S$ has density $\delta$ if

$$ \delta=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{|\{p\in S\mid p\leq n\}|}{|\{p\in P\mid p\leq n\}|}\text{.} $$

#### Theorem A.34 (Chebotarev Density Theorem (see e.g. [Mil20])).

Let $N/\mathbb{Q}$ be a finite Galois extension. The primes that split completely in $N$ have density $1/[N:\mathbb{Q}]$ .

In particular, combined with the Prime Number Theorem, we have (10). Subtracting the asymptotics at $2Y$ and $Y$ gives

$$ \#\{q\in[Y,2Y]:q\text{ splits completely in }N\}\sim\frac{1}{[N:\mathbb{Q}]}\frac{Y}{\log Y}. $$

For all large $Y$ this number is at least the fixed integer $T$ . Choose distinct primes

$$ q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}\in[Y,2Y] $$

splitting completely in $N$ , and put $\mathcal{Q}:=\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}\}$ . Applying Proposition A.31 to this $\mathcal{Q}$ gives an infinite pro- $3$ Galois extension over $L_{0,\ell}$ . Because Proposition A.31 is uniform in $\mathcal{Q}$ , the same $H$ works for all choices of $Y$ and all choices of the dyadic split primes.

Every $q_{t}$ splits completely in each totally real finite subextension $L/L_{0,\ell}$ by Proposition A.31. Also $N\supseteq\mathbb{Q}(i)$ , so $q_{t}$ splits in $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ since $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is an intermediate extension. Hence $q_{t}\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ by Euler’s criterion. We claim that $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K=L(i)$ , so that every prime of $K$ above $q_{t}$ has residue field $\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ . Indeed $q_{t}$ splits completely in $L$ and $q_{t}\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ so consider a prime $\mathfrak{p}$ above $q_{t}$ in $L$ . $q_{t}\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ implies that $x^{2}+1$ splits into linear factors in $\mathcal{O}_{L}/\mathfrak{p}\cong\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ . Then, each $\mathfrak{p}$ splits completely into two distinct primes in $K$ (see e.g. Theorem 27 of [Mar18]), implying the complete splitting of $q_{t}$ in $K$ .

The same Proposition A.31 gives

$$ h(K)\leq H^{[L:\mathbb{Q}]} $$

for every such layer.

It remains to regularize the degrees. Let $G:=\operatorname{Gal}(\mathcal{L}_{\ell,\mathcal{Q}}/L_{0,\ell})$ , an infinite pro- $3$ group. For every $i\geq 0$ , infinitude of $G$ gives a finite $3$ -group quotient $P$ of order at least $3^{i}$ . Since every finite $3$ -group has a normal subgroup of index $3^{i}$ whenever its order is at least $3^{i}$ (see e.g. Theorem 6.1 of [DF04]), pulling such a subgroup back to $G$ gives a normal subgroup $G_{i}\triangleleft G$ that is both open and closed with

$$ [G:G_{i}]=3^{i}\text{.} $$

Let $L_{i}$ be the corresponding finite layer (i.e. the fixed field of $G_{i}$ ) promised by the infinite Galois correspondence (Theorem 7.13 of [Mil03]). Then,

$$ [L_{i}:\mathbb{Q}]=[L_{i}:L_{0,\ell}][L_{0,\ell}:\mathbb{Q}]=d_{0}\,3^{i}\text{.} $$

For every sufficiently large $b$ , choose the first $i$ with

$$ d_{0}\,3^{i}\geq C_{\rm ar}b. $$

Since $b$ is large, $i\geq 1$ , and minimality gives

$$ d_{0}\,3^{i-1}<C_{\rm ar}b. $$

Thus

$$ C_{\rm ar}b\leq[L_{i}:\mathbb{Q}]=d_{0}\,3^{i}<3C_{\rm ar}b. $$

Taking the sequence of all such finite layers proves the theorem, with constants independent of $Y$ and $b$ . ∎

#### Theorem A.35 (Medium-Prime Norm-One $S$ -Unit Fiber).

There exist absolute constants

$$ T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 16},\qquad C_{\rm ar}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2},\qquad\gamma>0, $$

with

$$ \gamma>TH_{2}(4/T),\qquad H_{2}(\rho):=-\rho\log\rho-(1-\rho)\log(1-\rho), $$

such that the following holds for every sufficiently large parameter $Y$ and every sufficiently large integer $b$ . There is a CM field $K$ with complex conjugation $c$ , an integer $f$ with

$$ C_{\rm ar}b\leq f\leq 3C_{\rm ar}b,\qquad[K:\mathbb{Q}]=2f, $$

and $T$ distinct rational primes $q_{1},\ldots,q_{T}\in[Y,2Y]$ satisfying:

- (i) each $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ ; in particular every prime of $K$ above $q_{t}$ has residue field $\mathbb{F}_{q_{t}}$ , and $q_{t}\equiv 1\pmod{4}$ ;

- (ii) the $T$ rational primes determine $Tf$ conjugate prime-ideal pairs

$$ \{\mathfrak{P}_{m},c\mathfrak{P}_{m}\},\qquad m=1,\ldots,Tf, $$

in $K$ ;

- (iii) there is a vector $\eta\in\{0,1\}^{Tf}$ , a family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{Tf}$ with

$$ |\mathcal{F}|\geq\exp(\gamma f), $$

and, for every $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}$ , an element $u_{\varepsilon}\in K^{\times}$ such that, with $Q:=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t}$ , $\displaystyle u_{\varepsilon}c(u_{\varepsilon})$ $\displaystyle=1,\qquad|\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})|=1\quad\text{for every complex embedding }\sigma,$ $\displaystyle Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}$ $\displaystyle\in\mathcal{O}_{K},$ $\displaystyle\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(u_{\varepsilon})$ $\displaystyle=2(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m}),\qquad\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(u_{\varepsilon})=-2(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ for every $m=1,\ldots,Tf$ .

All constants are independent of $Y$ and $b$ .

#### Proof.

Apply Theorem A.32 with the given $Y$ , and choose the layer with $f=[L_{s}:\mathbb{Q}]$ in the interval $[C_{\rm ar}b,3C_{\rm ar}b]$ . Put $K=K_{s}=L_{s}(i)$ . Each $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ , hence gives $2f$ primes of residue degree and ramification index one. We claim that complex conjugation permutes these primes and fixes none of them. Recall that complex conjugation preserves prime ideals (Definition 3.17) and complex conjugation fixes rational primes, so that if $\mathfrak{P}$ lies above $(q_{t})$ , so does $c\mathfrak{P}$ .

We claim that $c$ fixes no prime $\mathfrak{P}\mid q_{t}$ . Suppose $c\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}$ . Since $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ , we have $e(\mathfrak{P}|q_{t})=f(\mathfrak{P}|q_{t})=1$ . Hence, by the local degree formula for completions (Claim A.24),

$$ [K_{\mathfrak{P}}:\mathbb{Q}_{q_{t}}]=e(\mathfrak{P}|q_{t})f(\mathfrak{P}|q_{t})=1, $$

so $K_{\mathfrak{P}}=\mathbb{Q}_{q_{t}}$ . Consider the injective map $c:K\hookrightarrow K_{c\mathfrak{P}}=K_{\mathfrak{P}}$ given by embedding $K$ into $K_{\mathfrak{P}}$ . Since $c\mathfrak{P}=\mathfrak{P}$ , the automorphism $c$ preserves the $\mathfrak{P}$ -adic valuation and therefore extends to a map $K_{\mathfrak{P}}\rightarrow K_{\mathfrak{P}}$ (Claim A.23) that fixes $\mathbb{Q}_{q_{t}}\subseteq K_{\mathfrak{P}}$ . But $K_{\mathfrak{P}}=\mathbb{Q}_{q_{t}}$ , so this extension is the identity. Hence $c$ is the identity on $K$ , contradicting that $c$ is the complex conjugation automorphism. Thus $c\mathfrak{P}\neq\mathfrak{P}$ .

Since $c^{2}=1$ , the $2f$ primes form exactly $f$ conjugate pairs. Enumerate these pairs as

$$ \{\mathfrak{P}_{m},c\mathfrak{P}_{m}\},\qquad m=1,\ldots,Tf. $$

The class-number bound gives $h(K)\leq H^{f}$ . Let

$$ \gamma:=T\log 2-\log H. $$

By Theorem A.32, $\gamma>TH_{2}(4/T)>0$ .

For each $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{Tf}$ define an integral ideal

$$ \mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}:=\prod_{m=1}^{Tf}\mathfrak{P}_{m}^{\varepsilon_{m}}(c\mathfrak{P}_{m})^{1-\varepsilon_{m}}\text{.} $$

There are $2^{Tf}$ such ideals and at most $h(K)\leq H^{f}$ ideal classes. Hence some ideal class contains a fiber

$$ \mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{Tf},\qquad|\mathcal{F}|\geq\frac{2^{Tf}}{H^{f}}=\exp(\gamma f). $$

Fix one element $\eta\in\mathcal{F}$ . For every $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}$ , the fractional ideal

$$ \mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}\mathfrak{A}_{\eta}^{-1} $$

is principal. Choose $v_{\varepsilon}\in K^{\times}$ with

$$ (v_{\varepsilon})=\mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}\mathfrak{A}_{\eta}^{-1}, $$

and set

$$ u_{\varepsilon}:=v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon}). $$

Then $u_{\varepsilon}c(u_{\varepsilon})=1$ . For any complex embedding $\sigma$ , the embeddings $\sigma$ and $\sigma\circ c$ are complex conjugates on the CM field, so

$$ |\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})|=\frac{|\sigma(v_{\varepsilon})|}{|\sigma(c(v_{\varepsilon}))|}=\frac{|\sigma(v_{\varepsilon})|}{|\overline{\sigma(v_{\varepsilon})}|}=1. $$

Passing from $v_{\varepsilon}$ to $v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon})$ doubles these valuations, giving the displayed valuation pattern for $u_{\varepsilon}$ .

We now prove that $Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . It suffices to show that $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})\geq 0$ for every finite prime ideal $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Recall that $(v_{\varepsilon})=\mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}\mathfrak{A}_{\eta}^{-1}$ , where $\mathfrak{A}_{\varepsilon}=\prod_{m=1}^{Tf}\mathfrak{P}_{m}^{\varepsilon_{m}}(c\mathfrak{P}_{m})^{1-\varepsilon_{m}}$ and $\mathfrak{A}_{\eta}=\prod_{m=1}^{Tf}\mathfrak{P}_{m}^{\eta_{m}}(c\mathfrak{P}_{m})^{1-\eta_{m}}$ . Thus the only prime ideals at which $v_{\varepsilon}$ can have nonzero valuation are the primes $\mathfrak{P}_{m}$ and $c\mathfrak{P}_{m}$ , all of which lie above the selected rational primes $q_{1},\dots,q_{T}$ . Moreover, for each $m$ , we have $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(v_{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m}$ and $\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(v_{\varepsilon})=(1-\varepsilon_{m})-(1-\eta_{m})=-(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ . Since $\varepsilon_{m},\eta_{m}\in\{0,1\}$ , the valuations all lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$ . Furthermore, $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon}))=2(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ and similarly for $\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m}}(u_{\varepsilon})=-2(\varepsilon_{m}-\eta_{m})$ .

Now let $\mathfrak{P}$ be any finite prime of $K$ . If $\mathfrak{P}$ does not lie above any of the selected rational primes $q_{t}$ , then $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon})=0$ and, since complex conjugation permutes the selected primes, $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(c(v_{\varepsilon}))=0$ . Hence $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon}/c(v_{\varepsilon}))=0$ . Since $Q^{2}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , we get $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})\geq 0$ .

It remains to consider the case where $\mathfrak{P}\mid q_{t}$ for some selected rational prime $q_{t}$ . At such a prime, both $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon})$ and $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(c(v_{\varepsilon}))$ lie in $\{-1,0,1\}$ . Therefore $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(v_{\varepsilon})-\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(c(v_{\varepsilon}))\geq-2$ . On the other hand, $q_{t}$ splits completely in $K$ . In particular, $q_{t}$ is unramified in $K$ , so every prime $\mathfrak{P}\mid q_{t}$ has ramification index $1$ . Hence $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(q_{t})=1$ . Since $Q=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q_{t}$ , we have $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2})=2$ . Thus $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2})+\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(u_{\varepsilon})\geq 2-2=0$ . Therefore $\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}}(Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon})\geq 0$ for every finite prime $\mathfrak{P}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{K}$ . Hence $Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}$ is integral, and so $Q^{2}u_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{O}_{K}$ .

∎

See 3.20

#### Proof.

Apply Theorem A.35 with $Y=\left\lceil 4\sqrt{L}\right\rceil$ and the given $b$ . We get a CM field $K$ , a degree parameter $f\in[C_{\rm ar}b,3C_{\rm ar}b]$ , $T$ rational primes $q_{t}\in[Y,2Y]$ splitting completely in $K$ , and a family

$$ \mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{Tf},\qquad|\mathcal{F}|\geq e^{\gamma f}, $$

with associated elements $\{u_{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon\in\mathcal{F}}$ and $\eta$ .

We first extract many shattered valuation coordinates. Let

$$ M:=Tf,\qquad s:=(3C_{\rm ar}+2)b. $$

Since $f\geq C_{\rm ar}b$ , we have

$$ \frac{s}{M}\leq\frac{(3C_{\rm ar}+2)b}{TC_{\rm ar}b}\leq\frac{4}{T}\leq\frac{1}{2}. $$

The Sauer–Shelah lemma says that if $\mathcal{F}$ shatters no set of size $s$ , then

$$ |\mathcal{F}|\leq\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}\binom{M}{i}\leq\exp\bigl(MH_{2}(s/M)\bigr)\leq\exp\bigl(TfH_{2}(4/T)\bigr)\text{.} $$

The entropy slack $\gamma>TH_{2}(4/T)$ in Theorem A.35 makes this strictly smaller than $e^{\gamma f}\leq|\mathcal{F}|$ . Hence $\mathcal{F}$ shatters a coordinate set $S$ of size at least $(3C_{\rm ar}+2)b$ .

Each rational-prime label contributes exactly $f\leq 3C_{\rm ar}b$ coordinates. Our goal is to find a subset of $S$ of size at least $2b$ that contains at most $b$ coordinates of each rational-prime label. If at least two labels have more than $b$ selected coordinates in $S$ , then after truncation those two labels alone contribute $2b$ retained coordinates. If at most one label has more than $b$ selected coordinates in $S$ , then the total number lost is at most $f-b\leq(3C_{\rm ar}-1)b$ , so the retained number is at least

$$ (3C_{\rm ar}+2)b-(3C_{\rm ar}-1)b=3b. $$

Thus in all cases at least $2b$ coordinates remain, and no label occurs more than $b$ times among them. Retain exactly $2b$ of the surviving coordinates. This retained set is a subset of the shattered set $S$ , and hence is itself shattered.

We claim that these coordinates can be partitioned into $b$ pairs whose two members have distinct rational-prime labels. Indeed, suppose an even number $2m$ of coordinates remain and every label class has size at most $m$ . If the maximum multiplicity is exactly $m$ , then at most two label classes have this multiplicity. Remove one coordinate from a largest label class and one coordinate from a different largest class if there are two, or from any different label class if there is only one; in the one-largest-class case such a different class exists whenever $m>0$ , because only $m$ of the $2m$ coordinates have the largest label. All remaining label classes then have size at most $m-1$ . If the maximum multiplicity is already less than $m$ , then it is at most $m-1$ ; remove any two coordinates with distinct labels, which exist unless $m=0$ . Again every remaining label class has size at most $m-1$ , half of the remaining $2m-2$ coordinates. Induction on $m$ (beginning with $m=b$ ) proves the claim.

Label the resulting pairs by $j=1,\ldots,b$ , and write the two coordinates in the $j$ th pair as $m(j,1)$ and $m(j,2)$ . For each $r\in\{1,2\}$ , define the selected prime ideal

$$ \mathfrak{p}_{j,r}:=\begin{cases}\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=0,\\
c\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=1.\end{cases} $$

Now fix $a\in\{0,1\}^{b}$ . For each selected coordinate $m(j,r)$ prescribe the bit

$$ \theta_{j,r}(a):=\begin{cases}a_{j}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=0,\\
1-a_{j}&\text{if }\eta_{m(j,r)}=1.\end{cases} $$

Because the retained coordinates form a shattered subset of $S$ , there exists $\varepsilon(a)\in\mathcal{F}$ with

$$ \varepsilon(a)_{m(j,r)}=\theta_{j,r}(a)\qquad\text{for all }j\in[b],\ r\in\{1,2\}. $$

Define $u_{a}:=u_{\varepsilon(a)}$ . If $\eta_{m(j,r)}=0$ , then

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a})=\operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}}(u_{\varepsilon(a)})=2(\varepsilon(a)_{m(j,r)}-\eta_{m(j,r)})=2a_{j}. $$

If $\eta_{m(j,r)}=1$ , then

$$ \operatorname{val}_{\mathfrak{p}_{j,r}}(u_{a})=\operatorname{val}_{c\mathfrak{P}_{m(j,r)}}(u_{\varepsilon(a)})=-2(\varepsilon(a)_{m(j,r)}-\eta_{m(j,r)})=2a_{j}. $$

In both cases the conjugate prime has valuation $-2a_{j}$ , so (2)–(3) hold. The two rational-prime labels assigned to bit $j$ are distinct and both lie in $[Y,2Y]$ , so their product is at least $Y^{2}>L$ . Finally, $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=2f\leq 6C_{\rm ar}b$ , so the degree bound follows after setting $C_{0}:=6C_{\rm ar}$ . ∎

## Appendix B Reductions from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV

In this appendix, we give reductions from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV to $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP, Furthest Pair, and Bichromatic Closest Pair for completeness.

#### Lemma B.1 (Implicit in [Wil18], Theorem 4.3 in [Che20]).

There is an $O(n\operatorname{poly}(r))$ -time reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $r$ to exact $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP in dimension $O(r^{2})$ . If the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV coordinates have bit-length $B$ , then the produced $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP coordinates have bit-length $O(B)$ .

#### Proof.

Represent

$$ P(x,y)=-(x\cdot y)^{2}=-\sum_{i,j}x_{i}x_{j}y_{i}y_{j} $$

as an ordinary inner product in dimension $r^{2}$ , for example by mapping $x$ to coordinates $x_{i}x_{j}$ and $y$ to coordinates $-y_{i}y_{j}$ . Then $P(x,y)\leq 0$ for all pairs, and $P(x,y)=0$ exactly when $x\cdot y=0$ . Thus a zero inner product exists in the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV instance iff the maximum produced inner product is $0$ . Products of two $B$ -bit integers have $O(B)$ bits, so the bit-length stays $O(B)$ . ∎

Next, we give a reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV to Furthest Pair, which is based on [Wil18, Theorem 1.2].

#### Lemma B.2.

There is an $O(n\operatorname{poly}(r))$ -time reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $r$ to Furthest Pair in dimension $O(r^{2})$ . If the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV coordinates have bit-length $B$ , then the produced Furthest Pair coordinates have bit-length $O(B+\log r)$ .

#### Proof.

We first run the reduction in Lemma B.1 to obtain a $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP instance in dimension $O(r^{2})$ between sets of vectors $U$ and $V$ , where $u\cdot v\leq 0$ for $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , and the goal is to determine if the maximum dot product is $0$ . If there is any zero vector, the maximum dot product is trivially $0$ . So in the following, we assume all vectors are nonzero.

Let $C$ be a sufficiently large integer. For any $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , define

$$ u^{\prime}=(u/\lVert u\rVert_{2},C,0),v^{\prime}=(-v/\lVert v\rVert_{2},0,C). $$

Let the set of $u^{\prime}$ and $v^{\prime}$ be the Furthest Pair instance.

For $u_{1}^{\prime}$ and $u_{2}^{\prime}$ , their squared distance is

$$ \lVert u_{1}^{\prime}-u_{2}^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert u_{1}/\lVert u_{1}\rVert_{2}-u_{2}/\lVert u_{2}\rVert_{2}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4, $$

and similarly,

$$ \lVert v_{1}^{\prime}-v_{2}^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4. $$

Next consider

$$ \lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert u^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}-2u^{\prime}\cdot v^{\prime}=2(C^{2}+1)+\frac{2u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}. $$

For large enough $C$ , the furthest pair must be $u^{\prime},v^{\prime}$ for some $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ . Furthermore, if the furthest pair has squared distance $2(C^{2}+1)$ , then there exists $u\in U,v\in V$ with $u\cdot v=0$ ; otherwise, there does not exist such pair.

The above completes the reduction to Furthest Pair with real coordinates. To convert the vectors to integer coordinates, first consider if $u\cdot v<0$ , then

$$ \frac{u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}\leq-\frac{1}{\operatorname{poly}(r)\cdot 2^{O(B)}}. $$

Let $\Delta$ be the absolute value of the above gap. Next, choose $\delta>0$ be some small real number to be determined. If we round each coordinate $z$ to a nearest multiple $k(z)\delta$ of $\delta$ for $k(z)\in\mathbb{Z}$ , then the squared distance between any two vectors can change by at most $O(\delta r^{2})$ . Hence, we can have $\delta=O(\Delta/r^{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{poly}(r)\cdot 2^{O(B)}}$ , so that the squared distance between any two vectors changes by at most $\Delta/2$ . This way, we can determine whether the maximum inner product before rounding is $0$ , by checking whether the maximum inner product after rounding is larger than $-\Delta/2$ . Finally, after rounding $z$ to $k(z)\delta$ , output the integer coordinate $k(z)$ to obtain integer vectors. ∎

Finally, we give a reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV to Bichromatic Closest Pair, which is based on [Wil18, Corollary 2.1].

#### Lemma B.3.

There is an $O(n\operatorname{poly}(r))$ -time reduction from $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV in dimension $r$ to Bichromatic Closest Pair in dimension $O(r^{2})$ . If the $\mathbb{Z}$ -OV coordinates have bit-length $B$ , then the produced Bichromatic Closest Pair coordinates have bit-length $O(B+\log r)$ .

#### Proof.

We first run the reduction in Lemma B.1 to obtain a $\mathbb{Z}$ -Max-IP instance in dimension $O(r^{2})$ between sets of vectors $U$ and $V$ , where $u\cdot v\leq 0$ for $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , and the goal is to determine if the maximum dot product is $0$ . If there is any zero vector, the maximum dot product is trivially $0$ . So in the following, we assume all vectors are nonzero.

For any $u\in U$ and $v\in V$ , define

$$ u^{\prime}=u/\lVert u\rVert_{2},v^{\prime}=v/\lVert v\rVert_{2}. $$

Let $U^{\prime}=\{u^{\prime}:u\in U\}$ and $V^{\prime}=\{v^{\prime}:v\in V\}$ be the input to Bichromatic Closest Pair.

Consider

$$ \lVert u^{\prime}-v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert u^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lVert v^{\prime}\rVert_{2}^{2}-2u^{\prime}\cdot v^{\prime}=2-\frac{2u\cdot v}{\lVert u\rVert_{2}\lVert v\rVert_{2}}. $$

If the closest pair has squared distance $2$ , then there exists $u\in U,v\in V$ with $u\cdot v=0$ ; otherwise, there does not exist such pair.

The above completes the reduction to Bichromatic Closest Pair with real coordinates. The vectors can be rounded to integers in the same way as Lemma B.2. ∎

- 1. Golod-Shafarevich inequality (Fig. 1(b)): For every prime $p$ , and every nontrivial finite $p$ -group $Q$ , $d(Q)^{2}<4r(Q)$ , where $d(Q)$ and $r(Q)$ denote the generator rank and relation rank of $Q$ respectively. This is exactly Proposition A.27. See, e.g. [GS64, GS65], for references.

- 2. Shafarevich’s relation-rank bound (Fig. 1(c)): for every number field $F$ and every odd prime $p$ , let $G=\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{ur},p}/F)$ , then the following holds: • The second continuous cohomology group $H^{2}(G,\mathbb{F}_{p})$ is finite dimensional over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . • $r(G)\leq d(G)+r_{1}(F)+r_{2}(F)-1+\delta_{p}(F)$ , where $r_{1}(F)$ denotes the number of real places of $F$ , $r_{2}(F)$ denotes the number of complex places of $F$ , and $\delta_{p}(F)$ is $1$ iff $F$ contains a $p$ -th primitive root of unity and $0$ otherwise. Proposition A.28 is a special case of it where $F$ is a totally real cubic field and $p=3$ . See e.g., [Šaf63, Sha66, May15] for references.

- 3. Chebotarev density theorem (Fig. 1(d)): For every number field $N$ , there exists a positive constant $c$ such that the following holds: let $\pi_{N}(n)$ be the number of primes up to $n$ that split completely in $N$ , then $\frac{\pi_{N}(n)}{n}\cdot\log n\sim c$ . This can be deduced from Theorem A.34: Let $\widetilde{N}$ be the Galois closure of $N/\mathbb{Q}$ , then Theorem A.34 implies $c=1/[\widetilde{N}:\mathbb{Q}]$ . See e.g., [Tsc26, Neu13, Mil20], for references.
